It was determined that there was no statistically significant association between asthma exacerbations with exclusive e-cigarette use (OR: 0.88; 95% CI: 0.56-1.38), exclusive cigarette use (OR: 0.80; 95% CI: 0.60-1.05), or dual-use (OR: 0.98; 95% CI: 0.68-1.41) after adjusting for confounding variables. Similarly, there was no statistically significant association comparing asthma symptoms in the past 30 days with exclusive e-cigarette use (OR: 0.98; 95% CI: 0.58-1.64), exclusive cigarette use (OR: 0.89; 95% CI: 0.65-1.20), or dual-use (OR: 1.04; 95% CI: 0.74-1.47). Discussion In this cross-sectional study, a nationally representative sample of the US population from the 2018 ABCS portion of the BRFSS was analyzed to describe demographics, asthma-related healthcare use, and asthma medication use in exclusive e-cigarette, exclusive cigarette, dual users, and never smokers aged 18 years or older. E-cigarette use was more prevalent among men, White people, with incomes less than $75,000, and employed individuals. Notably, e-cigarette use was the highest among young adults aged 18-24 years, which is consistent with previous studies. As per the CDC’s 2018 National Health Interview Survey [ ], younger adults showed higher rates of e-cigarette use in comparison to older adults. This signifies that public health efforts should be focused on addressing reducing rates of e-cigarette use in younger adults. It is particularly important for potential short- and long-term health effects to be investigated given the uncertainty of its consequences and the younger age group of those at risk. The multivariable regression models showed that there was no association between exclusive e-cigarette use and asthma exacerbations or asthma symptoms in the past 30 days in this representative cohort of adults with asthma. This finding differs from prior studies. The 2015-2018 Canadian Community Health Survey found that e-cigarette users with a diagnosis of asthma had twice the odds of having an asthma attack and that dual use was associated with higher health service use [ ]. Another study that conducted a literature search and meta-analysis of epidemiological studies of the general population investigated the association of e-cigarette use with asthma and COPD. They determined that e-cigarette use was associated with respiratory harm and susceptibility to illness [ ]. An additional study analyzing data from 2016 to 2018 BRFSS found that, compared to individuals who never smoked e-cigarettes, individuals who do smoke e-cigarettes had increased odds of self-reported diagnosis of asthma (OR: 1.26; 95% CI: 1.25-1.27) [ ]. It should be noted that our study focused solely on the BRFSS subset of ACBS, which only included individuals diagnosed with asthma. However, this does support that e-cigarette use leads to adverse respiratory effects that impact biological processes involved in asthma. It is hypothesized that individuals with asthma who use e-cigarettes have milder disease, which would be reflected by the type of therapy that they receive to manage their respiratory condition. Analysis of the distribution of medication use, as seen in Table , revealed that exclusive e-cigarette users were more likely to be taking SABAs (21.9%) in comparison to any other medication. In 1995, the Global Initiative for Asthma Guidelines (GINA) was first published, which described treatment initiatives to control and treat asthma symptoms. Since this publication, SABAs have been recommended as the first-line treatment for patients with mild asthma [ ]. GINA has also supported the use of combination therapy of high-dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) and long-acting beta agonist (LABA) as a combination therapy for severe asthma since the late 2000s. It is well documented that patients with severe persistent asthma may need additional therapy, which includes OCS, for both maintenance and treatment [ ]. Notably, only 7.1% of exclusive e-cigarette users were taking an ICS/LABA combination, and 0.3% were on an OCS. This supports the theory that this cohort of individuals with asthma have a milder form of this respiratory condition as most participants on medication were not using chronic steroids or a LABA/ICS combination. In addition, only 6% of exclusive e-cigarette asthmatic users had a history of respiratory disease, which is defined as having been diagnosed with COPD, emphysema, or chronic bronchitis. In comparison, there were 29.1%, 32.9%, and 11.1% of exclusive cigarette users, dual users, and never users, respectively, who had a history of respiratory disease. Most exclusive e-cigarette users were also previously noted to be between 18 and 24 years old. This suggests that e-cigarette users with asthma were more likely to have a clinically milder disease that was not complicated by other respiratory pathologies. This could be attributed to the fact that they were significantly younger than the typical age onset of additional chronic conditions. Thus, overall, individuals with mild asthma would have a decreased susceptibility to both asthma attacks and symptoms. Strengths There were several strengths of this study. An example would be the utilization of a nationally representative survey, allowing it to be generalizable to the US adult population with asthma over the age of 18. The BRFSS/ACBS also contained a large sample size. It provided robust information about each study participant, which was employed to generate descriptive statistics and control for confounding variables in the regression models. By utilizing never smokers as the reference group, the confounding variable of combustible cigarette use and dual use when analyzing the association between e-cigarettes and asthma exacerbations or asthma symptoms was removed. Limitations This study was not without limitations. The BRFSS/ACBS is a cross-sectional study that is subject to recall bias. As a result, participants may not have responded accurately when asked to reflect on their activities, such as any asthma symptoms in the past 30 days, or if they had been accurately and properly diagnosed with asthma as it is based on self-report. In addition, the baseline severity of asthma cannot be determined. Individuals who use e-cigarettes or cigarettes might have asthma that is more or less severe compared to those who do not use these products. Moreover, the number of medications each participant took, and the quantification of their prescribed dosage cannot be deduced. Their medication type, frequency of use, and adherence would all influence susceptibility to asthma attacks, as well as any asthma symptoms in the past 30 days. A final limitation is the inability to establish a temporal relationship between the diagnosis of asthma and the start of e-cigarette or cigarette use. Conclusions There was no association among the three categories of exclusive e-cigarette users, exclusive cigarette users, and dual users with asthma exacerbations or asthma symptoms in the past 30 days in US adults aged 18+. It is possible that the lack of association can be attributed to this study’s composition of participants who had a milder form of asthma as evidenced by the distribution of medication use. This study noted that e-cigarette use was the highest among adults aged 18-24, which is consistent with previous national studies that showed greater use among young adults in comparison to older adults. The results overall emphasize a need to continue e-cigarette use research to assess future health effects further and formulate appropriate public health recommendations, particularly focusing on young adults.

INTRODUCTION Alcohol-associated harm remains a major and largely preventable driver of global morbidity, mortality, and societal costs, extending well beyond health outcomes to include injuries, violence, and productivity losses. – Within this broader burden, alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD) represents one of the clearest manifestations of long-term alcohol exposure and a major contributor to premature death and disability. , Over the past 3 decades, the prevalence of ALD and alcohol-attributable primary liver cancer has continued to rise, underscoring that the global liver health burden is worsening despite the availability of effective prevention strategies. Alcohol exposure often interacts with other major risk factors for chronic liver disease, including type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and obesity. Moreover, alcohol can also cause new infections with hepatitis B and C, and promote an accelerated progression of metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) to advanced fibrosis stages. In this review, we synthesize contemporary evidence on the global epidemiology of ALD, summarizing temporal trends and geographic variation in prevalence and mortality, and highlighting key methodological limitations that can bias burden estimates. Because alcohol exposure is often underreported in clinical and observational data, we discuss more robust approaches to exposure ascertainment (eg, validated questionnaires and objective biomarkers) and their implications for surveillance. We also outline scalable strategies—combining staged fibrosis assessment and triage pathways, to improve case finding, risk stratification, and health system planning. Finally, we discuss high-impact (“best-buy”) alcohol control policies that could benefit people at risk for and living with ALD. GLOBAL ALCOHOL INTAKE AND ITS ECONOMIC IMPACT Overall, alcohol is responsible for about 5% of all global deaths and disability, making it one of the leading modifiable risk factors for disease burden worldwide. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), the global population consumed an average of 5.0 L of pure alcohol per person per year (age ≥15) in 2022. In the same period, the European WHO Region had the highest per-capita alcohol intake (9.1 L), followed by the Region of the Americas (8.0 L). In contrast, the Eastern Mediterranean, African, and Southeast Asia WHO Regions had the lowest per-capita alcohol intake (0.2, 3.5, and 3.6 L, respectively). About 21% of all alcohol consumed worldwide is unrecorded, including home-brewed alcohol, illicit production, and other sources. Globally, alcohol intake per capita has declined over the last decade (from 5.7 L in 2010 to 5.0 L in 2022), but it remains high and may rise in the absence of stronger interventions. Currently, the WHO forecasts that global per-adult consumption could reach up to 5.7 L by 2030, falling short of targets to reduce harmful use. Although 56% of adults report abstaining from alcohol in 2019, a substantial number of current drinkers do so at harmful levels. Among current drinkers, the average consumption is 27 g of pure alcohol per day, roughly equivalent to 2 standard drinks (United States/Canada) daily. Such patterns far exceed healthy limits and fuel alcohol use disorders (AUD), a harmful pattern of alcohol use that seriously impairs health and functioning, and related harms and deaths. WHO has estimated that 400 million people globally (about 7% of the adult population) were living with an AUD in 2019. According to Global Burden of Disease (GBD) estimates, the prevalence of AUD is highest in regions with heavy drinking patterns; for example, Eastern Europe has the greatest burden of AUD, with an age-standardized prevalence of over 3200 per 100,000 population. Globally, men are 3 times more likely to consume alcohol and develop AUD than women. This is reflected in the associated death rates in 2019, which were 2 million in men compared with 0.6 million in women. However, worrying trends of increased drinking, ALD, and AUD among women have been observed in some regions, narrowing the historical gender gap. , Heavy episodic (binge) drinking is defined by an intake of ≥ 60 g of pure alcohol on at least one occasion in the past month, a common pattern that correlates with the development of alcohol harms. According to the WHO, about 38% of current drinkers report periodic heavy episodic (binge) drinking. This pattern of consumption is particularly prevalent among young adults and in Europe, where nearly 1 in 2 drinkers binge (Figure ). Those aged 20–39 years experience a disproportionately high proportion of alcohol’s harms, accounting for about 13% of all alcohol-attributable deaths that occur in young adults. Earlier initiation and sustained alcohol intake contribute substantially to the later development of ALD, the prevalence of which rises sharply with age. A prior study using GBD data reported a 19-fold increase in ALD prevalence from 15–19 to 20–24 years, with a further 2.5-fold increase to 25–29 years. Children and adolescents are especially vulnerable to commercial influences and social pressures that promote alcohol use. Moreover, older adults with ALD show increasing trends of multiple psychiatric comorbidities, with larger rises than in younger patients, especially for major depressive disorder, anxiety, and bipolar disorder. CURRENT GLOBAL AND REGIONAL BURDEN OF ALD AND PROJECTIONS TO 2050 The natural history of ALD Approximately 26% of individuals with hazardous drinking and 55% of those with AUD will develop some form of ALD. In a systematic review of 35 studies that included 513,278 individuals, the prevalence of ALD was estimated to be 3.5% in the general population. In addition, the 10-year incidence of ALD is estimated to be 0.6%. In individuals seeking treatment for AUD, a recent cohort study demonstrated a 7.1% cumulative incidence of ALD after 10 years, increasing to 13% in those with T2DM. About 10%–20% of individuals with ALD will develop cirrhosis. Thus, the prevalence of alcohol-associated cirrhosis is estimated at ~0.3% in the general population, but rises to 12.9% in those with AUD. In addition, the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) among individuals with cirrhosis is estimated at 1%, 3%, and 9% at 1, 5, and 10 years. Given the high levels of alcohol use, prevalence of AUD, and the underreporting of alcohol consumption, it is likely that the prevalence of ALD is vastly underestimated in the overall population. Compared with MASLD, individuals with ALD had a higher proportion of advanced fibrosis and cirrhosis. ALD may progress from steatosis to steatohepatitis, fibrosis, and cirrhosis, with decompensation, liver failure, and death. In alcohol-associated cirrhosis, HCC occurs at a rate of 0.9%–5.6% per year, and long-term heavy alcohol use markedly increases risk. ALD is also linked to substantially higher mortality from infection, cardiovascular disease, and non-hepatic cancers, as well as metabolic, neurologic, and reproductive comorbidities. , Global and regional prevalence of alcohol-associated cirrhosis In 2023, an estimated 3.15 million people were living with alcohol-associated cirrhosis globally. , About 419,429 new cases of alcohol-associated cirrhosis worldwide developed that year, which is 18.3% higher than in 2000. Thus, these differences between crude and age-standardized estimations reflect substantial demographic changes over the last 3 decades. There are important differences in age-standardized prevalence by sex in 2023, with rates estimated at 47.0 and 22.7 per 100,000 inhabitants in men and women, respectively. Between 1990 and 2023, men and women exhibited decreases of 27% and 32% in age-standardized prevalence, respectively. , According to GBD estimates, the European WHO Region has the highest prevalence of alcohol-associated cirrhosis, at 67.5 per 100,000 in 2023, followed by the Region of the Americas at 58.4 per 100,000 inhabitants (Figure ). , This is consistent with the very high alcohol consumption in Europe (particularly Eastern Europe) and the Americas. A systematic review of societal cost estimated that alcohol consumption costs countries 1.5%–2.6% of their gross domestic product in economic losses. Most of these costs are attributable to productivity losses, including workforce absenteeism, unemployment, and reduced output due to alcohol-associated disability and premature mortality. Moreover, the per-capita economic cost has been estimated at about International Dollar 1300 per adult per year when averaging across countries. In lower-income settings, these costs are disproportionately burdensome economically, as resources diverted to managing alcohol-associated harms undermine development. It is important to note that the cost per liter of alcohol consumed, in terms of health burden, is higher in low and middle-income countries than in high-income countries. This indicates that for an equivalent volume of alcohol, poorer populations suffer greater harm, likely due to weaker health systems, comorbidities, and social determinants that amplify alcohol’s impact. It is expected that the economic impact of ALD will be substantial and will continue to increase. In the United States, one simulated scenario analysis projected that ALD could generate ~$880 billion in total costs between 2022 and 2040 (including $355 billion in direct medical spending), with annual ALD expenditures rising from ~$31 billion in 2022 to $66 billion by 2040. A similar pattern is seen in broader alcohol-associated inpatient spending: a recent study estimated that alcohol-associated hospitalizations cost $32.6 billion in 2022 in the United States, indicating increasing costs even after accounting for inflation. In the United States, alcohol-associated hospitalization rates have remained high (around 700 per 100,000 adults per year), while admissions for alcohol-induced medical complications, including alcohol-associated hepatitis and alcohol-associated cirrhosis, increased from about 70–83 per 100,000 between 2016 and 2022. Over the same interval, outcomes for alcohol-associated admissions worsened, with mean length of stay increasing (~5.6–6.2 d) and in-hospital mortality rising from 2.4% to 3.1%. Compared with other inpatients, those hospitalized with ALD often require more resources: one comparative analysis found median costs nearly twice those of age-matched and sex-matched non-ALD admissions and longer median stays. ALD admissions have also been associated with greater acute care needs and much higher mortality, including more frequent transfusion requirements and markedly higher in-hospital death rates (13.2% vs. 0.2% in one series). Similar patterns have been described in other regions; in Europe, ALD constitutes a dominant share of liver care. In Portugal, alcohol-associated cirrhosis represented 38.6% of liver disease discharges and roughly 43% of inpatient liver-disease costs in the 2000s. The COVID-19 pandemic appeared to further intensify ALD-related healthcare utilization and adverse outcomes. , Increases in high-risk drinking during the pandemic coincided with rises in severe ALD presentations, advanced fibrosis, and hospital admissions. , , In the first pandemic year (2019–2020), ALD mortality in the United States increased by more than 20%, with the greatest relative increases among adults younger than 45 years. Moreover, sex-stratified analyses showed that during the COVID-19 pandemic period, hospital admission rates for ALD increased more in women than in men. – SCREENING FOR ALCOHOL INTAKE, AUD, AND ALD Quantification of alcohol use and screening for AUD Routine alcohol use screening is a cornerstone of ALD prevention and supports clinical and epidemiological research. As noted above, alcohol intake is the main modifiable risk factor for ALD, and—together with liver fibrosis—is also the leading risk factor for liver-related mortality in ALD. – For routine clinical practice, it is important to document current alcohol intake (ideally in grams or standard drinks/week), drinking patterns, and prior alcohol exposure. Given that most patients experience dynamic changes in alcohol use over time, a single, static assessment of alcohol use can misclassify the ALD diagnosis. , In the following paragraphs, we will discuss the principal methods to assess alcohol use and AUD, and the potential implications for epidemiologic estimates. Table summarizes commonly used questionnaires and biomarkers, their detection windows, and test characteristics. Brief validated questionnaires remain the core entry point given their speed, feasibility for universal deployment, cost, and acceptable diagnostic performance in primary care. For instance, the Alcohol Use Disorder Identification Test (AUDIT) is a 10-item screening tool for AUD, while its short version, AUDIT–Consumption (AUDIT-C), includes the first 3 AUDIT items and identifies hazardous drinking. The National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) Single Alcohol Screening Question is another useful instrument, in which a positive answer to “How many times in the past year have you had (4 for women or 5 for men) or more drinks in a day?” may trigger further assessment for AUD. Other instruments, including the Timeline Followback and Lifetime Drinking History (LDH) questionnaires, can provide a more comprehensive quantification of current and past drinking, respectively. A scoping review of 9 studies (n=6010 participants) found that LDH demonstrates moderate to strong test–retest reliability and concurrent/construct validity. However, these are not routinely used due to time constraints. There is substantial heterogeneity in the assessment of alcohol use among epidemiological studies. – This heterogeneity arises from differences in measurement tools, definitions, recall periods, and categorization of drinking patterns, jeopardizing adequate comparison between cohorts and regions. Alcohol biomarkers Direct alcohol biomarkers are best viewed as complementary to structured self-report in identifying alcohol exposure. The major advantage of biomarkers is that they mitigate the well-documented limitations of self-report, particularly in specialty care and transplant contexts. Phosphatidylethanol (PEth) is a direct blood biomarker formed only in the presence of ethanol and is typically detectable over ~2–4 weeks, making it suitable for identifying under-reported use, monitoring abstinence or reduction, and supporting longitudinal care plans in chronic liver disease (Table ). , , In a well-characterized cohort of adults at risk of steatotic liver disease, the use of PEth can increase the diagnosis of ALD 3-fold. Moreover, PEth has also demonstrated being a better predictor of liver-related events over time than self-reported alcohol intake. By contrast, ethyl glucuronide (EtG) and ethyl sulfate (EtS) are short-horizon direct metabolites measured most commonly in urine, useful for detecting recent alcohol exposure between 1 and 3 days (Table ). By contrast, ethyl glucuronide (EtG) and ethyl sulfate (EtS) are short-horizon direct metabolites measured most commonly in urine, useful for detecting recent alcohol exposure between 1 and 3 days (Table ). Their main limitations are interpretive: EtG in particular can be vulnerable to false positives or negatives under specific circumstances (eg, bacterial infection), and incidental ethanol exposure can matter at very low cutoffs; measuring EtG and EtS together increases confidence. , Finally, carbohydrate-deficient transferrin (CDT) is an established serum biomarker associated with sustained heavy drinking; it can support detection of ongoing heavy consumption but is less sensitive for intermittent heavy episodic drinking and is typically best used in combination with clinical assessment and/or other biomarkers rather than as a stand-alone screen (Table ). Of note, a positive alcohol biomarker must always be interpreted in the clinical setting. Finally, comparing drinking patterns across clinical settings helps define where each screening modality adds the most value. In primary care, unhealthy alcohol use is common but heterogeneous, as many patients with hazardous or episodic patterns of consumption who may not perceive themselves as “problem drinkers,” making brief tools like AUDIT-C well-suited for universal case-finding. In emergency departments and trauma settings, the prevalence of recent heavy episodic drinking is higher, favoring a combined questionnaire plus blood alcohol concentration (BAC), allowing immediate confirmation to influence care planning. In liver clinics and transplant programs, sustained heavy drinking, relapse detection, and longitudinal monitoring are central, so PEth is often the most informative single biomarker. At a population level, heavy episodic drinking remains common in many regions (with marked sex differences in many settings), reinforcing that screening strategies must capture both volume and pattern of consumption, and that effective implementation depends on matching the tool to the clinical question, the time horizon of interest, and the local prevalence of unhealthy use. The use of alcohol biomarkers, particularly those with a long detection window, demonstrates that individuals often underreport alcohol use across different settings and regions, with underreporting estimated to occur in up to 55% of patients in routine practice and up to 10% of clinical trials. This underreporting impacts the accurate diagnosis of ALD and metabolic dysfunction and alcohol-associated liver disease (MetALD). Moreover, alcohol consumption often changes over time, and ~60% of individuals with alcohol consumption within the MetALD and ALD ranges may change their diagnosis category, mostly because of decreasing alcohol use. Another phenomenon of relevance is the Hawthorne effect, where people change their behavior, often reducing alcohol intake, simply because they know they are being observed or studied. Finally, the assessment of liver fibrosis can also impact alcohol consumption over time. All the factors highlight the limitations in the identification of individuals with ALD, usually resulting in underestimating the true impact of alcohol intake on liver disease. BEST-BUY POLICIES TO REDUCE ALCOHOL INTAKE AND ALD Alcohol-associated public health policy is a core upstream lever for preventing ALD, because alcohol use is the primary attributable and modifiable driver of ALD at the population level. – In 2018, the WHO consolidated the strongest evidence into the 5-dimensional SAFER framework: , S trengthen restrictions on alcohol availability; A dvance and enforce drink-driving countermeasures; F acilitate access to screening, brief interventions, and treatment; E nforce bans or comprehensive restrictions on advertising, sponsorship, and promotion; and R aise prices through excise taxes and pricing policies. , WHO subsequently aligned this approach with the Global Alcohol Action Plan 2022–2030, endorsed by Member States, which aims to reduce per-capita consumption by 20% by 2030 through the scaled implementation of high-impact interventions. Among SAFER components, pricing measures have the most robust and reproducible benefits because they reduce the affordability of alcoholic beverages (Table ). For instance, Scotland enacted minimum unit pricing (MUP) in 2018, which has been associated with a 13.4% reduction in alcohol-specific deaths and a 4.1% reduction in hospitalizations, alongside decreases in ALD-related deaths (11.7%) and ALD-related hospitalizations (9.8%). Similar natural-experiment evidence from British Columbia shows that raising minimum alcohol prices is associated with rapid and sustained decreases in alcohol-attributable admissions, whereas Finland’s large alcohol tax reduction illustrates the reverse: increased affordability was followed by marked increases in alcohol-associated harm, including liver mortality, supporting a causal affordability–harm relationship. At the macro level, cross-jurisdictional analyses further support this policy gradient: stronger composite alcohol-policy environments across countries and stronger state-level policy implementation within the United States are each associated with lower alcohol-associated harms and alcohol-associated cirrhosis mortality. Scaling screening, brief interventions, and referral to treatment can also reduce consumption when implemented at sufficient coverage in primary care, but their impact depends on workforce training, workflow integration, and treatment capacity. Importantly, evidence from countries implementing policy packages suggests additive benefits when multiple SAFER components are combined. Russia’s multi-component alcohol-control measures resulted in substantial declines in alcohol-attributable mortality, including liver deaths, while periods of weakened policy coincided with worsening outcomes, underscoring the value of a sustained, coordinated policy strategy. Similarly, Lithuania’s 2016–2018 reform package combining tax increases, reduced availability, and marketing restrictions was associated with steep declines in consumption and alcohol-associated mortality. These findings align with an ecological study in Latin America that evidenced a significant association between a national plan on alcohol and the prevalence of ALD. Policies targeting alcohol marketing are also directionally supportive. Cross-national econometric work suggests that comprehensive advertising restrictions are associated with modest reductions in per-capita consumption, although effect sizes vary and attribution can be limited by co-interventions. Evidence syntheses further support minimum pricing as a consistent population tool across settings, with reductions in consumption and alcohol-associated harms observed in natural studies and supported by modeling studies where real-world data are limited. , Finally, because policy effectiveness is often constrained more by implementation than evidence, industry interference that delays or dilutes regulation, illustrated by postponed alcohol warning-label implementation in Ireland, highlights the need for transparent governance, protection from conflicts of interest, and accountable delivery to achieve equitable and sustained reductions in ALD burden. The tragedy of alcohol-associated harms and deaths is that there are clear evidence-based policy solutions that are well known but poorly implemented in most jurisdictions. Alcohol policy progress is often slowed, weakened, or blocked by alcohol industry interference, including lobbying to delay or dilute evidence-based regulations, as illustrated by Ireland’s experience with health warning labeling, in which implementation of prominent health warning labels legislated under the Public Health (Alcohol) Act (2018) was postponed following sustained industry pressure and trade-related threats. Taken together, this evidence supports a pragmatic conclusion for ALD prevention: jurisdictions achieve the largest and most equitable reductions in alcohol harm when they implement SAFER as a coherent package—anchored by price and availability levers, reinforced by marketing controls and drink-driving enforcement, and coupled with accessible screening and treatment—while insulating politicians and policymaking from the influence of the alcohol industry, and ensuring sustained, accountable delivery at scale. LOCAL AND INNOVATIVE INITIATIVES TO IDENTIFY INDIVIDUALS AT RISK OF ALD To complement population-level policies, granular, locally-led innovations are improving how ALD is identified and managed across settings (Figure ). Community-based screening vans that bring transient elastography to town centers and workplaces have reached people who rarely seek care; the South West England “Alright My Liver?” pilot reported high acceptability and detection of previously unrecognized advanced fibrosis. Beyond vans, primary care programs that embed transient elastography have demonstrated feasibility and longer-term utility, reinforcing the value of community case-finding. Such outreach can facilitate earlier diagnosis and linkage to hepatology and addiction services. In terms of treatment of AUD, digital cognitive-behavioral-therapy (CBT) programs can expand healthcare access. In a U.S. randomized trial, adding a web-based CBT program (CBT4CBT) to usual care significantly increased abstinent days at 6 months compared with standard care. A 12-week mobile CBT app from South Korea similarly improved end-of-treatment abstinence and reduced craving compared with face-to-face counseling. Allied-health delivery models extend reach: in Australian community pharmacies, brief training enabled pharmacists to screen with AUDIT and provide brief advice with high acceptability—an opportunity to intervene early among individuals who may not present to physicians. Nurse-led and pharmacist-led screening and brief intervention in primary care offers a pragmatic approach to attenuating progression to ALD when coupled with clear referral and follow-up. Within hospitals, “fast-track” ALD pathways link hepatology and addiction care early during admission and through discharge. A U.S. multidisciplinary clinic that enrolled inpatients with alcohol-associated hepatitis or cirrhosis into integrated hepatology–addiction follow-up reported improved liver function and markedly fewer emergency visits/readmissions at 6 months. In the United Kingdom, hospital-based Alcohol Care Teams operationalize similar principles at scale and are associated with reductions in admissions and mortality related to alcohol. In

FUTURE DIRECTIONS AND KNOWLEDGE GAPS Several priorities must be addressed to improve the global evidence base and clinical impact of ALD epidemiology. First, harmonized ALD registries are needed across regions and health-system levels, using standardized case definitions, fibrosis staging frameworks, and longitudinal outcome ascertainment. , Registries should capture alcohol exposure with explicit specification of time horizon (recent vs. sustained), pattern (heavy episodic vs. daily heavy use), and treatment engagement, while integrating core liver endpoints (decompensation, HCC, transplant, mortality) and extrahepatic outcomes that shape prognosis (cardiovascular disease, infections, malignancy). , , Interoperability with electronic health records and linkage to vital statistics would enable near–real-time monitoring and reduce reliance on cross-sectional estimates. Second, enhanced surveillance in low- and middle-income countries remains a critical gap, given that they showed a disproportionate growing burden of ALD. , Many countries face limited access to diagnostic tools (elastography, patented serum panels), constrained laboratory capacity, and incomplete cause-of-death coding, resulting in systematic underestimation of ALD burden. , , Pragmatic and adapted surveillance should prioritize scalable elements: structured alcohol-use assessment, routine laboratories enabling FIB-4 calculation, sentinel-site elastography, and linkage to hepatitis and metabolic disease programs. – Implementation must be paired with workforce development (task shifting, training) and sustainable financing models for diagnostics and referral pathways. , , Third, the field requires rigorous evaluation of integrated genetic and metabolomic risk scores to enable precision prevention. Polygenic risk scores and metabolomic signatures could help identify individuals at disproportionate risk for advanced fibrosis at a given exposure level, but major questions remain around transferability across ancestries, calibration in admixed populations, ethical deployment, and whether risk disclosure improves outcomes without exacerbating stigma. – Finally, PEth-based screening needs robust implementation research. Key gaps include optimal cutoffs by clinical context, sampling frequency for monitoring, handling discordant self-report and biomarker results, patient-centered communication strategies, and comparative effectiveness studies testing whether PEth-guided pathways improve abstinence, reduce decompensation, and enhance equity, especially when embedded within integrated addiction–hepatology care models. , Finally, the most effective and least costly measures to reduce alcohol harms, including the entire spectrum of ALD and death, are preventative, based on the SAFER measures proposed by WHO. Implementation of preventative measures should be a key target of clinical societies and organizations. CONCLUSIONS ALD is a major and increasing cause of preventable liver-related morbidity and mortality worldwide, amplified by diagnostic under-detection and unequal access to effective treatment and surveillance. Clinicians should adopt risk-stratified pathways that combine validated alcohol-use screening with staged fibrosis assessment and ensure rapid linkage to evidence-based alcohol treatment and liver care. Policymakers must implement high-impact alcohol control measures while financing scalable detection and integrated care to reduce the global ALD burden. Researchers should prioritize harmonized registries, surveillance platforms, and trials of biomarker-guided and precision-risk strategies that measure meaningful clinical outcomes and equity.

Introduction The number of drug misusers have sharply increased by 33% worldwide over the past 14 years from 226 million individuals aged 15–64 years in 2010 to 300 million in 2024 [ ]. Simultaneously, 76,000 adolescents and young adults (AYAs) drug misusers under 35 years old were identified, accounting for 86.4% of population of narcotic and psychotropic drug misuse in China [ ]. Drug misuse irreversibly attenuates cortical thickness during adolescent development and increases the likelihood of palpitation by 4.3-fold [ , ], and is even associated with increased mortality [ , ]. In China, the awareness rate of antidrug knowledge among students reached more than 96% in 2020 [ ]. The proportion of adolescents among drug misusers has slowly decreased (approximately 3% per year) [ ]. However, this trend does not account for drug misusers of new psychoactive substances (NPSs). There is a paucity of effective ways to rapidly decrease the proportion of AYAs among drug misusers, as drug addiction is characterized by compulsive or uncontrollable drug seeking, and it is difficult to fully abstain from drugs once individuals becoming habitual users [ ]. Preventing drug-misuse behaviors among high-risk AYAs before they develop into habitual users is essential for reducing drug misuse. Early warning models for screening AYAs at high risk of drug misuse are needed to guide early interventions to address the specific problems of high-risk AYAs and prevent the development of addictive behaviors. Based on the psychosocial model, which explains the causes of addiction in terms of psychological and social factors, the study focused on psychological and social influences (online suppl. eFig. 1; for all online suppl. material, see https://doi.org/10.1159/000551125 ) [ ]. Integrating psychosocial factors associated with drug misuse into prevention and treatment efforts is essential for screening high-risk AYAs and guiding early interventions. Previous studies have highlighted several externalizing behavioral traits linked to addiction susceptibility genes [ ], including sleep dysfunction [ , ], rebellious behavior [ – ], sensation-seeking (SS) [ ], impulsivity [ ], prosocial relationships [ ], and hedonic hunger [ – ], all of which showed strong associations with drug misuse [ ]. These externalized behaviors can be reliably captured by psychometric assessment. Conceptualization of these externalizing behaviors as psychological indicators and incorporating them into risk model of drug misuse can enhance the discrimination and identification of model. Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are not only linked to mental health disorders but also serve as major risk factors for substance use disorders [ ]. ACEs can induce significant biological changes in AYAs during sensitive developmental windows, thereby increasing their susceptibility to mental disorders [ ]. Among AYAs who suffered ACEs, the frequency of substance misuse increases by 10% during the transition from adolescence to adulthood [ ]. Substance misuse has been suggested to be a coping mechanism for relieving stress after childhood maltreatment exposure [ ]. This underscores the importance of addressing ACE-related psychological vulnerabilities in risk models. Furthermore, the harm perception of drug misuse and refusal self-efficacy of drug misuse (RSEDM) are also important factors governing the substance misuse behaviors, as they determine one’s confidence in implementing a specific behavior [ ]. Previous studies have showed that lower RSEDM and lower harm perception of drugs increase drug misuse intention [ , ]. Therefore, it’s necessary to integrate these factors into the analysis of risk factors. Individual perceptions of drug-related benefits and accessibility of substances are also significant risk factors for drug misuse [ , ]. Lack of awareness and knowledge about types and harms of drug misuse and the accessibility of substances are strong risk factors for substance misuse in AYAs [ ]. Despite legal restrictions, with the rapid expansion of logistics and online networks, trafficking channels have become more diversified and concealed, increasing the accessibility of illicit drugs and complicating supervision [ ]. Meanwhile, NPSs, often created through structural modifications of existing compounds and disguised within everyday products, are difficult to detect using routine methods [ , ]. The continuous emergence of newly synthesized substances may also outpace regulatory scheduling, leaving some compounds temporarily unregulated. Therefore, many drugs remain widely accessible [ ]. Assessing social determinants, such as drug availability and harm perception, is essential for a comprehensive risk assessment among AYAs. As stated above, psychological and social factors must be addressed in the risk models of drug misuse among AYAs. Many studies have explored the etiology of addiction in AYAs. Some have reported that assessing the risk of drug misuse by focusing on a limited set of factors while overlooking the complex interactions among the factors is inaccurate [ , ]. An American Indian study examined 22 variables across individual, interpersonal, and environmental domains [ ], while a study in Myanmar included only five factors [ ]. Some have reported that assessing the risk of drug misuse by focusing on a limited set of factors while overlooking the complex interactions among the factors is inaccurate [ , ]. An American Indian study examined 22 variables across individual, interpersonal, and environmental domains [ ], while a study in Myanmar included only five factors [ ]. Such limitations reduce the comprehensiveness of the risk models. According to previous studies, existing screening tools are designed to identify current drug misusers, while AYAs at high risk who do not yet drugs misuse are ignored [ , ]. However, hypothesis testing, which relies on predefined models based on assumptions or specific hypotheses, may limit the exploration of complex relationships within the data. Machine learning (ML) techniques can handle large risk factor sets and automatically select the most relevant features. They allow for the inclusion of a broader range of factors and the modeling of complex, nonlinear interactions, which enhances the ability to generate accurate, individualized risk assessments [ ]. In addition, robustness of ML to noise and outliers makes the models potentially more generalizable out-of-sample. Therefore, modeling based on ML algorithms provides strong risk assessment performance. However, due to the limitations of ML in explaining and representing conditional dependencies or interaction structures among variables, it remains necessary to explore associational pathways among psychosocial factors and their relationships with drug misuse. Moreover, the complexity of psychosocial variables, the absence of prespecified pathway structures, and the lack of strong theoretical assumptions further complicate this exploration. In addition, the mixed variable types and potential nonlinear associations limit the suitability of conventional parametric models for uncovering conditional dependencies. Given these characteristics, a Bayesian Network (BN) model offers a suitable framework for identifying probabilistic association structures among psychosocial factors and drug misuse. BN supports data-driven learning of conditional dependencies without requiring a priori pathway specification and accommodates uncertainty, mixed data types, and nonlinear interactions. This approach allowed us to explore the complex, probabilistic relationships among multiple variables while taking into account the uncertainty and interdependencies in the data. Therefore, this study aimed to construct a risk model for AYAs at high risk of drug misuse by integrating psychosocial factors and exploring their association pathways using ML algorithms and a BN model. Methods Design We conducted a cross-sectional study between June and December 2023 using convenience sampling on AYAs in Guangdong Province, China. Informed consent was obtained from all participants. Participants provided informed consent by reading the consent form and confirming their agreement before proceeding to the questionnaire. This process was recorded electronically within the survey system. The authors assert that all procedures contributing to this work comply with the ethical standards of the relevant National and Institutional Committees on Human Experimentation and with the Helsinki Declaration of 1975, as revised in 2013. Given the sensitivity of research on drug misuse and ethical guidelines from WHO, the Ethics Committee approved a waiver of parental consent, allowing adolescents to provide informed consent independently. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Sun Yat-sen University, approval number L2023SYSU-HL-012, and prospectively registered before patient enrollment. This study adhered to the Transparent Reporting of a Multivariable Prediction Model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis (TRIPOD) and the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) statements (online suppl. TRIPOD & STROBE checklist) [ , ]. Sampling Eligible AYAs aged 14–35 years who were proficiency in Chinese were invited to participate in this study. AYAs unable to complete the questionnaire for physical or psychological reasons were excluded. To ensure that the sample size was adequate for developing a clinical risk model for binary outcomes, Riley [ ] suggests meeting four key aspects, including (1) estimating the outcome proportion with sufficient precision; (2) targeting a small mean absolute prediction error; (3) ensuring a global shrinkage factor ≥0.90; (4) limiting optimism in apparent R 2 to 0.05. We first applied the logistic regression (LR)-based formula corresponding to the mean absolute prediction error criterion. To further validate the sample size requirement, we set the prevalence at 0.039 based on the observed proportion and specifying nine candidate risk factors after feature selection. The resulting shrinkage estimate of 0.944 met the recommended threshold and indicated that at least 604 participants were needed to meet the four criteria above for model construction. Considering the limited number of positive cases, a 6:4 ratio for splitting the dataset into training and testing sets was applied. Therefore, at least 1,007 AYAs were needed to train and validate the model in this study. More details on sample size estimation are presented in online suppl. eText 1 . Measurements A structured and standardized questionnaire was used to collect data (online suppl. Questionnaire and online suppl. eText 2). The primary outcome, drug misuse, was defined as ever using of a substance for a purpose not consistent with legal or medical guidelines, was assessed using a question matrix listing common illicit drugs, with participants indicating whether they had ever used or were currently using these substances. The risk factor variables included demographic characteristics (age, sex, education level, social role, parents’ marital status and education level, being an only child, and level of resident city), psychological factors (sleep quality, externalizing problem behavior [EPB], prosocial tendencies, SS, and hedonic hunger, perceived risks of drug misuse [PRDM], permissive attitude toward drug misuse [PADM], RSEDM, and ACEs), and social factors (working in nightlife venues [WNVs], environmental exposure to drug misusers [EEDM], cognition of traditional drugs and NPS types). Data Collection Participants were recruited both offline in communities and online via the WJX platform ( www.wjx.cn ). We employed lie detection and logic validation techniques to ensure reliability of the online questionnaire. Three specific lie detection questions required participants to select a specific response (e.g., “always”). Participants reported their parents’ marital status in the demographic section and indicated whether their parents were divorced on the ACEs scale. Responses were considered valid if the participants answered all lie detection and logic questions and completed the questionnaire in more than 200 s. Statistical Analysis Descriptive statistics were computed using IBM SPSS Statistics 25, R 4.3.3 ( http://cran.r-project.org ) and Python 3.12.2 ( https://www.python.org/ ) were used for data processing and modeling (online suppl. eTable 1). A detailed description of the statistical analysis is provided in online suppl. eText 3. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Comparisons between drug misusers and nondrug misusers were conducted using Pearson’s χ 2 and Fisher’s exact tests for categorical data and the Wilcoxon rank-sum test for non-normally distributed continuous data. The statistical analysis procedure is illustrated in . Data Preparation The missingness at the individual level was 15.42%, and the overall missing rate across all variables for all individuals was 0.54%. MissForest was used to impute the missing data. We also applied the one-hot encoding method to convert variables with multiple categories into multiple binary variables. We normalized the continuous variables in our data to the same scale between 0 and 1 to accelerate learning for faster convergence in the ML model training process. We conducted the feature selection using the intersection of key risk factors of drug misuse identified by two algorithms for feature selection to enhance the performance of the ML model [ ], including Boruta, a wrapper-based feature selection method that utilizes the random forest algorithm, and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO), which are less prone to overfitting, and provide better model interpretability and accuracy [ ]. The data in this study were imbalanced, with a minority drug misuser to non-misuser ratio of almost 1:25. To address this issue, the adaptive synthetic sampling approach for imbalanced learning (ADASYN), a newly generalized version of the synthetic minority oversampling technique, was applied to the training dataset to generate new samples for the minority class using a weighted distribution. ML Models and Evaluation Using the intersection of features identified by Boruta and LASSO, we first developed eight models for the drug misuse risk assessment tasks based on different classic ML classifiers that are widely used to solve binary classification problems, including LR, random forest, K-nearest neighbor, Extreme Gradient Boosting, support vector machine (SVM), decision trees, naive Bayes (NB), and adaptive boosting (online suppl. eTable 2). The results of the top three classifiers that performed the best in our task were subsequently combined into an ensemble model using a majority vote. We applied a 5-fold cross-validation to train the ML models with the same proportion of the drug misuse in each fold. The bootstrapping method was employed, generating 1,000 subsets to calculate the mean score and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) of measurements, which ensures the robustness of the results. And permutation test was conducted to examine whether the observed performance metrics are significantly better than a null distribution generated by chance. Feature Importance Analysis The feature importance was analyzed using Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) values, which quantified the contribution of each feature to the risk assessment task. Changes in feature importance before and after applying ADASYN were examined, with a focus on the features whose importance scores increased, indicating improved identification of drug misuse cases in our risk model. BN Analysis BN analysis was conducted to explore association pathways of psychosocial factors. Drug misuse was designated as a deterministic node during the BN construction. Outcome variables of drug misuse and nine variables selected by the intersection of features identified by Boruta and LASSO were initially chosen to form the network, with structural constraints imposed by prohibiting arcs from drug misuse to other variables and from other variables to ACEs. The network structure was further refined using bootstrap resampling. Arcs with frequencies greater than 50% were retained to construct the averaged network structure. Structure learning employs an MMHC search algorithm. Categorization of discretized variables is detailed in online suppl. eTable 3. To address potential directional constraints inherent in BN and to evaluate the robustness of association pathways, we additionally fitted a structural equation model based on the BN-derived structure. The detailed analysis and results are provided in online suppl. eText 4–5 and online suppl. eFigure 2. Results In total, 1,071 questionnaires were collected, of which 1,012 (94.49%) were included in the final analyses. In total, 522 (51.58%) participants were male and 734 (72.53%) were students. A total of 39 participants reported a history of drug misuse (3.85%; 29 males [74.36%] and 10 females [25.64%]). Statistically significant differences were observed between drug misusers and nondrug misusers in terms of social role, being an only child, and birthplace level ( ). Statistically significant differences in sleep quality, EPBs, SS traits, hedonic hunger scores, perceived risks, permissive attitudes, RSEDM, ACEs, WNVs, EEDM, and lower levels of cognition of traditional drugs and NPS were found between drug misusers and nondrug misusers (online suppl. eText 5). The Psychosocial Risk Model on Drug Misuse Nine key factors were identified by intersecting the features selected by both LASSO and Boruta (online suppl. eTable 4), including EEDM, WNVs, cognition of traditional drug types, PRDM, PADM, RSEDM, EPB, SS, and ACEs. The results of modeling using 5-fold cross-validation were detailed in online suppl. eTable 5. The NB and LR both achieved the highest recall score (93.14%), followed by SVM (86.90%) (online suppl. eTable 6). Combining the modeling from these three classifiers, the recall score of the voting model increased to 94.10% (95% CI: 93.71%–94.50%), with improvements in accuracy (92.63%; 95% CI: 92.55%–92.71%), precision (34.15%; 95% CI: 33.69%–34.61%), F-score (49.68%; 95% CI: 49.17%–50.19%), and AUC (98.11%; 95% CI: 98.04%–98.17%). The results of the permutation test were detailed in online suppl. eTable 7. The ROC and PR curves are shown in online suppl. eFigure. 3. The SHAP feature importance for the voting classifier ( ) identified WNVs as the most critical risk factor and PRDM as the least impactful. Other important risk factors included EPB, cognition of traditional drug, SS traits, and EEDM. ACEs showed the strongest associations in their influence on drug misuse though multiple pathways. In the BN analysis, we focus on the core association pathway from ACEs to drug misuse, represented as ACEs → EPB → PADM → RSEDM → Drug Misuse, as each edge made a substantial contribution to model fit. Post-test probability showed that participants who neither worked in nightlife venues nor had EEDM showed only 7.3% probability of drug misuse among participants with high cognition of traditional drugs but low RSEDM ( ). This probability increased to 10.5% if they worked in nightlife venues and further to 92.8% with additional EEDM. Discussion This study presented a risk assessment model and explored the structure of associations among psychosocial factors related to drug misuse among AYAs guided by the psychosocial model. Our model identified important risk factors linked to drug misuse. BN analysis enabled the exploration of conditional dependence patterns among variables, offering pathways linking psychosocial factors to drug misuse. Additionally, post-test probability analysis identified four key risk factors for drug misuse. The results of this study may help develop brief screening tools to identify AYAs at high risk of drug misuse and facilitate accurate early intervention efforts. The prevalence of drug misuse among AYAs in this study was approximately 3.9%, 60 times higher than the nationwide prevalence of 0.064% reported in 2023 [ ]. This discrepancy may be attributed to the inclusion of NPS in our definition of drug misuse, underscoring the growing prevalence of NPS being much higher than that of traditional drugs among AYAs. We noticed that the youngest participants who had initiated drug misuse were 11 years old, aligning with previous reports indicating a trend toward earlier onset of drug misuse in China [ ]. Consistent with the national data, methamphetamine was the most commonly misused traditional drug [ , ], whereas laughing gas was the most frequently used NPS, reflecting its rising popularity as a drug substitute among Chinese AYAs [ ]. Interestingly, we found significant differences in being an only child between nondrug misusers and drug misusers. Compared to multiple children families, AYAs from only child families may face excessive parental attention, leading to loneliness, emotional problems, and potentially risky behaviors [ ]. This finding aligns with research from Korea, mentioning that being an only child is a risk factor for engaging in risky behaviors, including sexual activity, which is often correlated with drug misuse [ ]. These findings highlight the urgent need for targeted interventions to address the unique vulnerabilities of only children in China. The post-test probability analysis revealed that AYAs with low level of refusal self-efficacy and cognition, despite having EEDM, had a low risk of drug misusers, showing that passive exposure alone may be insufficient to significantly increase the risk of drug misuse. In contrast, the same individuals WNVs showed a substantially higher risk of drug misusers, which suggests a strong context-dependent shift in risk assessment of drug misuse among AYAs. Nightlife venues provided access and repeated opportunities for illicit drug misuse, which weakened individual resistance of illicit drug and increased the likelihood of drug misuse [ ]. It seems that individual vulnerabilities are not uniformly expressed but activated by environment, supporting the need for specific prevention for special setting and occupation. Our BN analysis confirmed the association of ACEs and EPBs with drug misuse, which is consistent with previous studies [ , ]. ACEs have emerged as an important risk factor for drug misuse, with EPBs and peer effects as association factors [ ], highlighting the complex interrelationships between psychological factors. Our findings emphasize that ACEs were strongly associated with factors that increase vulnerability to drug misuse by disrupting their behavioral responses to stress and negative emotions, thereby increasing their vulnerability to addiction. ACEs have emerged as an important risk factor for drug misuse, with EPBs and peer effects as association factors [ ], highlighting the complex interrelationships between psychological factors. Our findings emphasize that ACEs were strongly associated with factors that increase vulnerability to drug misuse by disrupting their behavioral responses to stress and negative emotions, thereby increasing their vulnerability to addiction. This underscores the need for early interventions targeting upstream factors, such as ACEs, rather than focusing solely on downstream social factors. It is well recognized that ACEs dysregulate behavioral responses to stress and negative emotions, increasing the risk of psychological addiction and physical dependence, which have powerful long-term effects on vulnerability to illicit drug misuse [ , ]. Our analyses imply that early identification of drug misuse in AYAs and interventions targeting individual deficits caused by ACEs, such as dysfunctional stress response systems, behavioral problems, and cognitive deficits, may reduce the probability of drug misuse in the future. A voting classifier that combined the outputs of LR, SVM, and NB was used to construct the model, which showed the best performance in terms of the recall score and balanced the advantages and shortcomings of different risk model to improve the accuracy and stability of modeling [ ]. To address the adverse effect of data imbalance on the interpretive performance of SHAP, we used ADASYN to identify stable and important features of identification of drug misuse [ ]. Recall was prioritized as a key metric to minimize false negatives in identifying drug misusers. Compared to a previous study with an AUC of 0.85 based on 22 risk factors from 1,738 Native American [ ], our model’s performance was highly satisfactory. The joint probability distribution is an important quantity that allows us to calculate the probability of all nodes being in any given set of states [ ], which can quantify the risk of drug misuse in the future. This study has several limitations. Data were collected primarily in Guangdong Province, which may have limited the generalizability of the findings. However, governmental data have shown that drug misusers in Guangdong Province account for 29% of China’s drug misusers [ ], making it a representative region for studying drug misuse issues. In addition, the data imbalance may influence the modeling process. The use of the ADASYN mitigates imbalance but does not fully resolve the trade-off between precision and recall. Actually, we adopted a strategy of “err on the side of caution” in assessing the risk of drug misuse. In such settings, prioritizing recall improves the likelihood that true cases are identified for further confirmation and early intervention. These false positives highlight that the model is suitable only as an early warning or population-level screening tool, not as a standalone decision-making instrument for identifying individuals. Any real-world application would require confirmatory assessment, and the model should not be used to guide punitive or high-stakes actions. Future work with larger numbers of positive cases, model tuning, improved feature representation, and external validation is needed to improve the balance between precision and recall and to better define the appropriate operational thresholds for different use scenarios. Finally, since the cross-sectional design of this study precludes establishing temporal precedence of variables, further longitudinal studies with larger and more diverse samples are needed to provide additional evidence. Conclusions This study identified the key risk factors for drug misuse in AYAs by developing a psychosocial risk assessment model. ACEs and social environments served as key risk factors. Targeted screening of AYAs working in high-risk environments and antidrug education programs to enhance refusal self-efficacy regarding drug misuse should also be prioritized. Further early interventions focusing on the psychological vulnerabilities caused by ACEs are required. The model demonstrated high recall and offers potential value as an early warning or population-level screening tool. Future longitudinal studies with larger and more diverse samples are needed to validate these associations, refine operational thresholds, and further clarify the psychosocial structures linked to drug misuse risk to guide multilevel interventions for mitigating the risk of drug misuse and improving outcomes for vulnerable AYAs. 1 Introduction Metabolic health encompasses the ability to maintain favorable levels of adiposity, blood glucose, blood pressure, lipid profiles and overall energy regulation. Metabolic dysfunction represents a continuum of abnormalities including metabolic syndrome and broader cardiometabolic irregularities that increase risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and other chronic conditions [ , , ]. Recent data indicate only 6.8% of U.S. adults have optimal cardiometabolic health, with significant declines over the past two decades [ ]. Weight reduction of 5%–7% is associated with improvements in glycemic control, blood pressure, and lipid profiles in adults with overweight or obesity [ , ]. While pharmacologic and surgical approaches are increasingly used, lifestyle interventions remain a cornerstone of weight management [ , ]. Calorie-restricted dietary approaches can be effective when nutritionally adequate and sustainable [ , ]. In addition to weight reduction, improving key cardiometabolic risk factors, including central adiposity, glycemic control, blood pressure, and blood lipids, is central to improving metabolic health and lowering the risk of downstream chronic disease [ , , , , , ]. Increasingly, attention has turned to body composition as a key mediator of cardiometabolic risk. Reducing central adiposity (e.g., waist circumference, visceral adiposity) while preserving lean, metabolically active tissue, is recognized as an important determinant of cardiometabolic health [ , , , , ]. Indices of central obesity (e.g. waist circumference ≥102 cm for males, ≥88 cm for females) and excess visceral fat are strong predictors of metabolic syndrome, diabetes, and other cardiometabolic outcomes, beyond body mass index (BMI) alone [ , , , , , ]. One strategy intended to help facilitate weight loss and improve cardiometabolic risk factors is the use of structured commercial meal replacement programs. These programs are designed to provide structured nutrition and lifestyle support through portion control, reduced decision burden, micronutrient fortification during energy restriction, and convenience, along with a focus on other key behavior modification strategies [ , ]. Meal replacement approaches are cited in obesity guidelines as an effective modality for calorie-restricted weight loss [ , , ]; however, their impact on broader metabolic health outcomes when delivered as part of a comprehensive lifestyle intervention warrants further synthesis. Clinicians may benefit from up-to-date, program-specific evidence for the commercial interventions they encounter in routine practice. 1.1 Objective This narrative qualitative evidence review examined published evidence for weight loss interventions utilizing Medifast's structured, higher protein meal replacement plans (5&1®, 4&2&1®, and 5&2&2®) with comprehensive lifestyle intervention and their impact on weight and metabolic health outcomes in adults living with overweight or obesity. 2 Methods 2.1 Study selection and eligibility criteria Studies utilizing a Medifast meal plan (5&1, 4&2&1, and/or 5&2&2 Plans) as a weight loss intervention were identified from a comprehensive repository of all peer-reviewed publications and clinical trials evaluating Medifast meal plans maintained by Medifast's Scientific & Clinical Affairs department. This repository is maintained through ongoing monitoring of literature databases and clinical trial registries (e.g., PubMed, ClinicalTrials.gov ) to ensure all investigator-initiated and Medifast program-sponsored research is captured. To ensure transparency and thoroughness, all identified studies meeting the specific inclusion criteria were reviewed, as summarized in the Study Selection Diagram ( ). To minimize selection bias, all identified studies meeting predefined inclusion criteria were included regardless of study design, outcomes, or publication source. To be included in this review, publications had to meet the following criteria: (1) utilize one of Medifast's three core structured meal plans (5&1, 4&2&1, or 5&2&2), (2) report weight or metabolic health outcomes, and (3) be published in a peer-reviewed journal between January 2010 and June 2025. Publications in which Medifast meal replacements were used without one of the above meal plans, studies with only abstracts, and conference proceedings were excluded. 2.2 Description of Medifast meal plans The Medifast meal plans utilized in the reviewed studies follow standardized nutritional protocols as described in previous publications [ , , ]. These plans combine portion-controlled meal replacements (MRs), self-prepared Lean and Green meals, and, in some plans, “Healthy Snacks.” Individual MRs provide approximately 90–110 kcal, 11–15 g protein, 12–15 g carbohydrate, 4–6 g fiber, and 0–3.5 g fat. They are fortified with at least 20% of the daily value for 20 essential vitamins and minerals, providing 80%–100% of the daily value when consumed as part of Medifast's structured meal plans. Nutritionally, these meal replacements utilize high-quality protein from soy and dairy sources and contain no colors, flavors, or sweeteners from artificial sources. Lean and Green meals consist of 5–7 oz. of cooked lean protein, three servings of non-starchy vegetables, and up to two servings of healthy fats. Healthy Snacks typically consist of one serving of fruit, dairy, starch, or a prepackaged program snack. Lean and Green meals consist of 5–7 oz. of cooked lean protein, three servings of non-starchy vegetables, and up to two servings of healthy fats. Healthy Snacks typically consist of one serving of fruit, dairy, starch, or a prepackaged program snack. More specifically, on a daily basis, the 5&1 Plan provides 800 to 1000 kcal and 80–120 g of protein, the 4&2&1 Plan provides 1000 to 1200 kcal and 120–150 g of protein, and the 5&2&2 Plan provides 1300 to 1500 kcal and 140–170 g of protein. While these plans are designed for weight loss, the program includes a structured transition and maintenance phase where meal replacements are gradually replaced with nutrient-dense whole foods. In the weight maintenance phase, individuals may continue using a reduced number of meal replacements as a weight management tool while continuing the healthy eating habits initiated during weight loss. 2.3 Behavioral and physical activity components The Medifast program integrates structured meal plans with multimodal behavioral support, offering customizable interventions, such as coaching and comprehensive lifestyle curricula, designed to facilitate long-term habit formation. For most of the included studies, physical activity was generally encouraged but not required or standardized except for Beavers et al., 2025 [ ]. 2.4 Data extraction and study classification Data extraction was performed using a standardized Excel template by two reviewers (one of whom is the lead author), with a third reviewer performing quality assurance on the extracted data and in the review process; two of these reviewers were independent team members. For each eligible publication, extracted data included the study design, population characteristics, intervention duration, primary and secondary outcomes and corresponding results. Because several trials (n = 6) had multiple publications, related reports were identified and grouped and treated as a single unique study to avoid duplication of outcomes. When present, the control group for each study was classified (e.g., standard food-based calorie restriction or no structured intervention) to facilitate the interpretation of effects associated with weight loss interventions using Medifast meal plans. In some publications, like chart reviews, there was no control group and, in three studies a Medifast meal plan served as the control [ , , ]. Two randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and two chart reviews included both weight loss and maintenance phases; for cross-study comparability, outcomes and corresponding results were extracted from the weight loss phase only [ , , , ]. This approach aligns with the primary design of the Medifast meal plans and was the focus of most included trials (i.e., weight loss) and the focus of this narrative qualitative evidence review. Across the reviewed publications, several additional outcomes were reported that fell outside the predefined scope of this synthesis, which focused specifically on weight, body composition, and cardiometabolic health. For example, data were reported for inflammatory markers [ , , , , , , , , ], bone biomarkers [ , , ], quality of life [ , , , ], and behavioral adherence [ , , , , ]. While these data were not synthesized here, they provide further context on the multi-dimensional impact of these interventions and are available in the primary and secondary reports of the included trials. 2.5 Computation and standardization of outcomes For all variables, the measurement method, assessment time points, and reported results per the authors were documented. Where the original publication provided baseline and change in measurements but did not report a percent change, these were calculated by the study authors (change/baseline x100). All such calculated values are explicitly identified in the summary tables. Given heterogeneity in study cohorts and protocols in this narrative qualitative evidence review, data were synthesized qualitatively rather than through a pooled meta-analysis. As part of the qualitative review process, statistical significance was recorded as reported by the original publication, distinguishing between-group differences and within-group changes from baseline to end of intervention, or to primary endpoint as reported by the authors. 3 Results Twenty-four publications were reviewed; 17 publications were identified that fit the inclusion criteria ( , ). Study durations ranged from 4 to 26 weeks for the weight loss interventions. 3.1 Weight loss Weight loss outcomes are summarized in . Thirteen of 14 studies reported clinically meaningful weight loss (≥5%) with 7 reporting ≥10%; greater weight loss was generally observed in studies of longer duration. In the reviewed RCTs, mean weight loss typically ranged from approximately 5%–12% of baseline body weight over 4–26 weeks [ , , , , , , , ]. In retrospective chart reviews, average weight loss of approximately 9%–16% over 12–24 weeks were reported [ , , , ]. In most study populations with coexisting conditions (e.g., men awaiting prostatectomy, adults with prediabetes/diabetes), similar magnitudes of weight loss were observed [ , , , ], whereas one pilot trial in individuals with recent ischemic stroke (n = 34) showed a modest, nonsignificant change; the authors noted a weight-gain outlier may have influenced results in this pilot study [ ] ( ). 3.2 Body composition Body composition outcomes are summarized in . Total fat mass reductions ranged from 3.2 to 11 kg across trials [ , , , , ]. Six RCTs utilizing a non-Medifast meal plan control and 1 non-randomized open-label pilot trial reported significant between-group reductions in total fat mass ( p < 0.05) [ , , , , , , ]. Three chart reviews and Normandin et al., 2018 (an RCT with a Medifast meal plan as the control) reported significant within-group reductions ( p < 0.05) [ , , , , ]. Waist circumference decreased by approximately 5–16 cm across 8 RCTs and 3 chart reviews [ , , , , , , ]. Among the 7 RCTs using a non-Medifast meal plan control, 5 reported significant between-group reductions, while the remaining RCT and 3 chart reviews reported significant within-group reductions ( p < 0.05). Visceral fat outcomes were reported in 4 RCTs and 1 non-randomized open-label pilot study. All 4 RCTs reported statistically significant between-group reductions, while the open-label pilot trial (n = 20) did not reach statistical significance for between-group differences. [ , , , , ]. Serra et al. reported the largest reduction in visceral fat of 20.1% at 24 weeks [ ]. Losses in lean mass or fat-free mass were present but comparatively modest.
