chunks.content: 1 Introduction Premature coronary heart disease (CAD) is highly prevalent in India and many developing countries. , The Global Burden of Diseases (GBD) study reported that CAD in the age group 20–54 years led to more deaths in India compared to the USA, China and countries in Europe and Central Asia, and in contrast to these countries, it is increasing in India. The annual mortality from premature CAD in India was 191,053 in the year 2000 and increased to 286,055 in 2019 (absolute increase of 49.7%, +2.5% per year). Studies from India have reported a significant proportion of patients with premature CAD among hospital admissions. , , , , , , , , , , , Case-control and registry-based studies have also reported that both traditional risk factors (smoking, hypercholesterolemia, hypertension, and unhealthy lifestyles) and emerging risk factors (lipoprotein(a), triglycerides and metabolic syndrome) are important. , , INTERHEART study reported that 8 common risk factors (dyslipidemia, hypertension, smoking, diabetes, abdominal obesity, psychosocial stress, unhealthy diet, and sedentary lifestyle) predicted more than 90% acute coronary events in South Asian patients. In a registry-based study, we reported that raised total and non-HDL cholesterol and smoking/tobacco were equally important. Studies have also reported earlier age of escalation of cardiometabolic risk factors in Indians. Prospective studies for the identification of risk factors for cardiovascular diseases in India are limited. The PURE (Prospective Urban Rural Epidemiology) study investigators reported long-term (11.5 years) follow-up data on 33,583 individuals (85% from India) without CAD at baseline and identified 12 common risk factors that predicted 64% of proportionate attributed fraction (PAF) of cardiovascular events and 69% of deaths. Risk factors were hypertension, raised non-HDL cholesterol, diabetes, low education, abdominal obesity, indoor air pollution, tobacco use, and others ( ). This study also reported that raised non-HDL cholesterol, diabetes, low education, indoor air pollution and unhealthy diet were more important in South Asians as compared to participants from high and upper-middle-income countries. More than a third of incident cardiovascular events were not predicted by these risk factors ( ). Identification of risk for premature CAD is clinically important. Early identification of risk can lead to promotion of healthier lifestyles and other interventions which can mitigate or delay the onset of premature CAD. The current literature is overwhelmed with models for predicting the risk of cardiovascular outcomes in the general population ( ). , , However, most have not been externally validated or directly compared on their relative predictive performance, especially in Indian or South Asian populations, making them currently of unknown value for practitioners, policymakers, and guideline developers. Most are not useful for the prediction of premature CAD because in all the tools age is the most important determinant of risk. In this narrative review, we highlight the importance of genetic risk stratification for identification of premature CAD. 2 Genetic risk factors and risk stratification It has been known for decades that CAD runs in families and a positive family history, especially of premature disease CAD has been considered important. , Epidemiologists have reported, based on presence of history of premature familial CAD and studies on identical twins that genetic risk factors account for 40–60% for the predisposition for CAD. Discovery and isolation of these genetic variants are enabled by development of new technologies in the 21st century. These researches have ranged from identification of chromosomal locations responsible for CAD, detection of rare single nucleotide variants (SNPs) that greatly increase the risk of CAD to the more recent combination of multiple SNPs (initially 10–12 to > 6 million currently) into polygenic risk scores that increase CAD risk. , , , , The identification of these SNPs could be important in prediction of premature CAD in susceptible young adults as these data could be available immediately after birth. 3 Monogenic risks In the initial years of gene-risk association studies focus was on differences in SNPs in patients with CAD versus controls. A number of genes were identified but all these studies were underpowered to detect such associations. Small case-control studies have also been performed in India. Most of such studies were futile as they failed to provide any new information. It was only after development of large consortiums in North America, UK and Europe, , often involving hundreds of thousands of CAD cases and matched population-based controls, that significant SNP's and genes were identified ( ). , , , , , One of the first and most consistent has been the finding of mutations in 9p21 chromosomal location. However, functional significance of this finding is not clear. Some of these genes have been identified as important in causation of CAD atherosclerosis or thrombosis via effects on mitosis proliferation, neovascularization and angiogenesis, nitric oxide signaling, vascular remodeling, blood pressure, lipid metabolism, inflammation, transcription gene regulation, etc. However, there is a need

America, UK and Europe, , often involving hundreds of thousands of CAD cases and matched population-based controls, that significant SNP's and genes were identified ( ). , , , , , One of the first and most consistent has been the finding of mutations in 9p21 chromosomal location. However, functional significance of this finding is not clear. Some of these genes have been identified as important in causation of CAD atherosclerosis or thrombosis via effects on mitosis proliferation, neovascularization and angiogenesis, nitric oxide signaling, vascular remodeling, blood pressure, lipid metabolism, inflammation, transcription gene regulation, etc. However, there is a need for studies to identify functional significance of statistically significant SNPs, genes and chromosomal locations. 3.1 Lipid genes and hypercholesterolemia Single genes consistently fail to predict CAD unless it is a rare variant associated with major coronary risk factors. The most researched have been lipid modifying genes that influence levels of low density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, triglycerides, high density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, apolipoproteins, and lipoprotein(a). , , , , , There are well-identified genes that modify these lipid fractions: LDL cholesterol by HMGCR, PCSK9, APOB, NPC1L1, etc.; HDL cholesterol by CETP; triglycerides by APOC3, ANGPTL3, ANGPTL4 and LPL; and lipoprotein(a) by LPA. All these forms of lipid abnormalities are important in premature CAD. For example, association of familial hypercholesterolemia is mediated through LDL-receptors and importance of LDLR and other genes is well known. What is not well known is that the phenotype of familial homozygous or heterozygous hypercholesterolemia can be mediated by more than 500 SNPs in the genes mentioned above. An important contribution to patient care from information of these genes is focused drug development. Richardson et al conducted a large-scale molecular profiling and genotyping to predict effects of therapeutic target on human lipidome and identified eight drug targets (HMGCR, PCSK9, NPC1L1, CETP, APOC3, ANGPTL3, ANGPTL4 and LPL). In recent years, identification of PCSK9 gene, has led to more efficient LDL cholesterol lowering with PCSK9 inhibiting monoclonal antibodies (evolocumab, alirocumab, inclisiran, etc). , , Strategies to increase HDL cholesterol failed by using the CETP inhibitors, despite identification of CETP gene. This has more to do with absence of mendelian randomization evidence of role of HDL cholesterol in the process of atherosclerosis. Similarly, although genetic targets for increased triglycerides have been identified, , , there is still no gene-based drug development molecule in advanced clinical trials. On the other hand, anti-sense molecules and small RNA inhibitors to reduce lipoprotein(a) molecules are under clinical trials. , , Clearly, there is need for more investment in identification of lipid modifying genes and to translate treatment from bench to bedside using modern technology. Genetic studies focused on monogenic and high-rise high-penetrant variants would be of immense help for future drug development. 4 Gene risk scores (GRS) It is well known that coronary atherosclerosis and incidence of myocardial infarction are multi-factorial. The risk factors are well known. Failure to identify single gene or a group of genes resulted in a strategic rethink and led to concept of using combination of genes for risk stratification in CAD and development of polygenic gene risk scores (GRS). , Some of the first studies were conducted in Europe and utilized data from pre-existing cohorts. Ripatti et al, used prospective data from population data from Sweden and Finland (FINRISK cohorts, Malmo Diet and Cancer cohort, and Malmo Preventive Project) and included 3829 persons with prevalent CAD and 48,897 controls free of disease. In this analysis, participants in top quintile of 13 SNP's based genetic risk score had 1.66 times (95% confidence intervals, CI, 1.35–2.04) increased risk in a model that adjusted for traditional risk factors ( ). Paynter et al, used data from Women's Genome Health Study (USA) and evaluated genetic and clinical risk scores in 19,313 white women. Two types of gene risk score were computed, first with 101 SNPs and the second with 12 SNPs (after pruning). Evaluated alone, the genetic risk score had hazard ratio of 1.015 per risk allele (p = 0.006) with 3% greater risk in the lower tertile and 3.7% in the highest risk tertile. The significance disappeared after adjustment for risk factors and it was concluded that there was no significant association with incidence of cardiovascular disease. Combinations of gradually increasing SNPs were analyzed in larger prospective studies. The SNPs identified were based on candidate gene association studies and were weighted according to the degree of risk found. SNPs with higher significance was given more weight and those with lower significance given lesser weights. Tada et al compared a 27 SNP-based score to 50 SNP based GRS using data from the Malmo Diet and Cancer study in 23,595 participants free of CAD at baseline. During a median follow-up of 14.4 years 2213 participants experienced a first CAD event. After adjustment for traditional risk

The SNPs identified were based on candidate gene association studies and were weighted according to the degree of risk found. SNPs with higher significance was given more weight and those with lower significance given lesser weights. Tada et al compared a 27 SNP-based score to 50 SNP based GRS using data from the Malmo Diet and Cancer study in 23,595 participants free of CAD at baseline. During a median follow-up of 14.4 years 2213 participants experienced a first CAD event. After adjustment for traditional risk factors both GRS-27 and GRS-50 were significantly associated with incident CAD; GRS-27: hazard ratio 1.70, CI 1.48–1.98, GRS-50 hazard ratio 1.92, CI 1.67–2.20 ( ). An important finding of this study was that the younger participants in the study had GRS-50 hazard ratio of 2.40 (CI 1.85–3.12) demonstrating better ability of this score for risk stratification in premature CAD. More studies using larger number of SNP's are now available. Khera et al, used a 60 SNP-based GRS using data from the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) and Women Genome Health (WGH) studies. The hazard ratio of highest vs lowest quintile in ARIC was 1.75 (CI 1.46–2.10) and in WGS was 1.94 (CI 1.58–2.39). Paquette et al, used a 192 SNP-based genetic risk score and reported that this risk score was better than prediction of CAD in familial hypercholesterolemia. Predictive accuracy of the genetic risk score was also reported by Mega et al. 5 Polygenic gene risk scores Subsequent to development of very large analytical capabilities and identification of larger number of SNPs involved in various processes of CAD more and more SNPs have been incorporated in the GRS. Genome wide association studies (GWAS) based identification of variants of risk accelerated this development. In one of the early studies using these capabilities, Abraham et al, developed a 49,000 SNP based genetic risk score that were evaluated using data from the FINRISK and Framingham Heart Study cohorts. The 49,000 SNP-based gene risk score was also evaluated in other prospective studies (all Caucasians). Significant associations were found in all these studies. In the case-control design the odds ratios of CAD varied 1.28 (CI 1.17–1.41) in Framingham Heart study to 1.74 (CI 1.63–1.86) in the Wellcome Trust Case-Control Consortium-CAD study ( ). These studies heralded the era of big data using extreme computer capabilities for calculation of genetic risk score and to predict its usefulness in prediction of CAD. Subsequent studies have become bigger and better. From the initial strategy of inclusion of variants that achieved genome-wide statistical significance in prior GWAS with 50–200 SNPs, the strategies moved on to linkage-equilibrium based thinning of variants from prior GWAS (40–50,000 SNPs), pruning based on statistical significance and linkage disequilibrium of variants from prior GWAS (100–200,000 SNP), to the currently available LDPred based computational algorithm that assign weights to all the available variants from prior GWAS via explicit modeling of linkage disequilibrium (millions of SNPs). In one of the early studies, Khera et al proposed that it may be important to identify polygenic predictors of conditions that also have significant monogenic variants. Five diseases were evaluated: coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes, inflammatory bowel disease and breast cancer. All these conditions have monogenic variants that increase the risk in addition to evidence of polygenic contributions. A genome-wide polygenic GRS, that incorporated more than 6 million SNPs, identified 8.0% population who were more than 3-fold greater risk of CAD. It was also observed that this GRS predicted CAD identical to rare monogenic mutations (e.g., familial hypercholesterolemia). In another large study using a meta-analytic approach, Inouye et al developed a metaGRS consisting of 1.7 million SNPs and applied the data in the prospective UK Biobank cohort. In this study of 22,242 CAD patients and 460,387 controls the GRS had hazard ratio of 1.71 (CI 1.68–1.73) per unit SD increase in metaGRS. Patients in top 20% of metaGRS had hazard ratio of 4.17 (3.97–4.38). Both the studies recommended inclusion of polygenic GRS-based risk prediction in clinical care. Similar studies have been reported from other regions of the world, predominantly among European and North American populations. , , , However, all these studies have focused on Caucasians and that is a major limitation regarding external validity of polygenic GRSs. It may not be very useful in other populations such as South Asians, East Asians, other Asians, Africans and native populations in the Americas and Europe. , , , Studies have reported that additional discriminant value gained from the polygenic risk score may not be superior to the information with use of traditional risk scores such as Framingham and SCORE (Europe). Mosley et al evaluated 2 US-based prospective cohorts (ARIC and MESA) for association of 6.6 million SNP-based GRS

, However, all these studies have focused on Caucasians and that is a major limitation regarding external validity of polygenic GRSs. It may not be very useful in other populations such as South Asians, East Asians, other Asians, Africans and native populations in the Americas and Europe. , , , Studies have reported that additional discriminant value gained from the polygenic risk score may not be superior to the information with use of traditional risk scores such as Framingham and SCORE (Europe). Mosley et al evaluated 2 US-based prospective cohorts (ARIC and MESA) for association of 6.6 million SNP-based GRS with incident CAD. There was a significant association of 10-year incident CAD in both ARIC (1.24, CI 1.15–1.34) and in MESA (1.38, CI 1.21–1.58) per unit SD increase in GRS, but there was no improvement in net reclassification index. The authors concluded that polygenic GRS did not significantly improve calibration in either cohort. Elliott et al also reported low predictive value of polygenic GRS as compared to clinical risk score in CAD. Editorialists and reviewers have criticized estimation of GRS as a more expensive method of estimating CAD risk. , , On the other hand, Wells et al used data from Framingham Offspring and CARDIA studies and evaluated usefulness of GRS in adults 18–35 years by comparing it with coronary artery calcium (as marker of atherosclerosis). It was concluded that PRS improved model discrimination for coronary atherosclerosis although the improvements were smaller than those associated with modifiable risk factors. In another study to identify importance of GRS in premature CAD, investigators used data from the UK Biobank. GRS was calculated using 1.14 million SNPs. For incident myocardial infarction the case-control comparison revealed hazard ratio per unit increase in SD of 1.52 (CI 1.50–1.54). The predictive value was the highest for men and women in age group 40–41 years (men 2.00, CI 1.86–2.16; women 1.57, CI 1.37–1.79). Both the studies, thus, showed usefulness of PRS in premature CAD. Studies among other ethnic groups are few and limited by small numbers. Case-control comparative studies in China and Japan have reported usefulness of GRS in CAD. , , A prospective study from China evaluated a 540 SNP-based GRS. In this study, Lu et al, developed a genome-wide association result with 540 SNP's in 2800 patient and 2055 control validation cohort in China. This was evaluated in 41,271 individuals prospectively followed for 13.0 years. It was calculated that individuals with the highest 20% of GRS had a 3-fold greater risk of CAD events (hazard ratio 2.91, CI 2.43–3.49). Moreover, addition of GRS to the clinical score yielded a significant improvement in net reclassification index. The GRS was most predictive of future cardiovascular events in the intermediate and high-risk groups ( ). It was concluded that the Chinese GRS could stratify individuals, especially the young at high risk, and could be applied for targeted interventions. 6 Indian data There are limited studies on utilization of GRS to predict CAD in India and South Asia and only in the recent years some studies have used South Asian cohorts. We performed a study to develop and validate a 6.6 million SNP-based GRS for Indian and South Asian CAD patients using GWAS's in Bangladesh, South Asians (UK Biobank), and India. For Bangladesh cohort, the reference population consisted of 491 South Asians in BRAVE consortium, in UK Biobank study there were 7244 South Asians, and in India 1800 CAD patients were studied. Using principal component analyses an ancestry adjusted GRS was developed. In the case-control validation of this GRS (comparison of top-percentile with middle quintile) it was determined that it was predictive of risk in BRAVE and UK Biobank cohorts. The odds ratio in top 2.5 percentile of GRS were 2.41 (CI 0.93–6.85) in BRAVE cohort and 5.56 (CI 3.40–8.98) in UK Biobank and for top 20.0 percentile GRS the odds ratio were 1.87 (CI 1.09–3.22) in BRAVE cohort and 2.16 (CI 1.56–3.03) in UK Biobank ( ). This GRS was evaluated in 1800 premature CAD Indian patients and 1163 age-matched controls, the odds ratio among top 2.5 percentile GRS was 3.30 (CI 2.11–5.33) and in the top 20 percentile was 1.79 (CI 1.42–2.28) ( ). This study demonstrated that the new GRS which was tested across three South Asian cohorts was useful in prediction of CAD risk. A few other studies are also available. In Pakistan, Shahid et al performed a case control study using a 21-SNP based GRS among 405 cases and 220 controls. The odds ratio of GRS in the highest quintile was 2.96 (CI 1.5–3.6). Another study reported that GRS developed using genetic analysis in Caucasians can be used for disease prediction in global populations. Although the studies highlighted above show that GRS can be successfully used for risk prediction in South Asian and Indian

that the new GRS which was tested across three South Asian cohorts was useful in prediction of CAD risk. A few other studies are also available. In Pakistan, Shahid et al performed a case control study using a 21-SNP based GRS among 405 cases and 220 controls. The odds ratio of GRS in the highest quintile was 2.96 (CI 1.5–3.6). Another study reported that GRS developed using genetic analysis in Caucasians can be used for disease prediction in global populations. Although the studies highlighted above show that GRS can be successfully used for risk prediction in South Asian and Indian populations almost similar to Caucasian and Chinese population, we need additional research to improve the transferability of GRS across various racial and ethnic groups and facilitate their integration into clinical practice. Larger prospective studies are required in our country to risk-stratify younger patients. This is all the more important as South Asian medical cohorts reveal high rates of homozygosity. In a study that evaluated whole genome sequencing (WGS) from 4806 individuals from healthcare delivery systems of Pakistan, India and Bangladesh and 927 South Asians from other cohorts, there were high rates of reproductive isolation, endogamy and consanguinity, especially marked in Pakistani and South Indian cohorts. A recent study utilized multi-ancestry GRS for CAD, based on ancestrally diverse GWAS and population specific optimization. It was observed that this multi-ancestry GRS (pruning and thresholding) demonstrated the strongest association with CAD in individuals of South Asian ancestry with OR per SD increase of 2.75 (CI 2.41–3.14) compared to European (OR 1.65, CI 1.59–1.72), East Asian, Hispanic/Latino and African cohorts. The GRS (continuous shrinkage priors) also demonstrated strongest association with CAD in South Asians (OR 2.67, CI 2.38–3.00) and Europeans (OR 1.65, CI 1.59–1.71) compared to other cohorts. It has also been reported that this multi-ancestry based GRS is better predictive of CAD in younger individuals. In view of these findings it is important to evaluate predictive importance of GRS in Indians with CAD and demonstrate its clinical usefulness in premature CAD. 7 Implications Genomic studies that have identified genetic risk factors and polygenes are important to guide risk stratification, especially to prevent premature CAD. This has demonstrated in the Harvard-based Partners Young-MI Registry more than 50% of patients with myocardial infarction ≤50 years were not identified using standard risk stratification tools. In this cohort more than 51% patients were not eligible for statin treatment if ACC/AHA 2013 guidelines were used and 71% would not qualify for statins using the 2016 USPTF guidelines. Similar data have been reported in the NORIN-STEMI study in Delhi. Many of these patients would have been eligible if genetic risk stratification tools had been available. Recent data across a number of different bio-banks have shown that addition of GRS to clinical risk tools improve net reclassification index in risk prediction by 5.9% (CI 4.7–7.0%), this increased to 15.4% (11.6–19.3%) in younger individuals. Early detection of genetic risk is not only important for risk stratification but also management, It has been reported that if these persons lead a healthy lifestyle they can reduce the risk substantially. , Moderate to high-intensity statins have been reported to be useful in reducing cardiovascular risks in very high genetic risk individuals. In conclusion, premature coronary artery disease is endemic in India. Standard risk factors identify less than 50% of patients with premature disease while imaging techniques miss even more of such patients. PURE-South Asia study has reported that traditional risk factors explain about 65% population attributable fraction of risk and about 35% risk is unexplained ( ). Genetic risk scores do not change from birth and it has been reported in prospective studies that those with high genetic risk have propensity for premature CAD. Promotion of aggressive lifestyle change in these individuals and prescription of statins in a selected few can significantly ameliorate cardiovascular risk. Individuals with strong family history of CAD (premature cardiac deaths, acute coronary syndromes, etc.) should be assessed for genetic risk early in life. Whether early intervention is helpful in prevention of CAD in high genetic risk individuals is a matter for future studies. One such study is going on in Finland. More studies are required in India and other developing countries to (a) assess the prognostic utility of clinical versus genetic risk scores, (b) use of machine learning tools to combine clinical and GWAS data for better risk prediction, and (c) to prospectively evaluate the influence of various lifestyle and pharmacological interventions in reducing this risk. chunks.content: Abbreviations BMI body‐mass‐index CI confidence interval COPD chronic obstructive pulmonary disease FORTA Fit fOR The Aged OR odds ratio PIM potentially inappropriate medication RCT randomized controlled trial Background Optimizing pharmacotherapy for older individuals is an ongoing challenge in our ageing society. In recent years, the focus has shifted away from merely reducing medication quantity to improving medication quality. This encompasses addressing three subdomains: overuse, underuse and drugs with an expected poor risk‐benefit ratio in older patients, so called potentially inappropriate medications (PIMs) [ , , ]. Accumulating evidence linking suboptimal medication quality to poor health outcomes, such as functional impairments, hospitalizations and premature death [ , , , ], indicates a necessity to improve overall medication quality in older adults. However, under‐ and overuse of medications have received little attention in prior research, and PIM use remains common, with a proportion ranging from 10.8% to 37.4% among older adults in the general German population [ , , , ]. Among a broad variety of medication assessment tools [ , , , , , , , , , , ], the Fit fOR The Aged (FORTA) list [ ] addresses all three subdomains of suboptimal medication quality and is tailored to the medication availability and prescribing patterns in Germany. It has been coherently evaluated by a large number of multidisciplinary experts and is regularly updated, reflecting its consolidated validity and recent advances in geriatric pharmacotherapy, and has been validated in a randomized clinical trial [ ]. The German National Cohort (NAKO) represents the largest German epidemiologic cohort study with recruitment in the whole country. The wide scope of available data, including self‐reported data, medical and functional assessments and blood‐based biomarkers [ ], enables the investigation of potential factors associated with PIM use, medication underuse or overuse more comprehensively than in any previous study [ , , , , , , ]. Therefore, we aimed to assess the frequency and factors associated with overuse, underuse and PIM use among older adults (60–74 years) who participated in the baseline assessment of the NAKO. Materials and methods Data source We conducted a cross‐sectional study based on data from the baseline assessment visit of the NAKO, a large national, multi‐centre, population‐based, prospective cohort study that recruited approximately 205,000 participants aged 19 to 74 years in 18 assessment centres between 2014 and 2019. Detailed methods have been published elsewhere [ ]. Study population Out of 204,666 participants with available baseline data, we included those aged 60–74 years, with available information on medication use, resulting in n = 54,296 participants eligible for our main analysis (Fig. ). Thereof, n = 5575 participants fully completed the NAKO vaccination data module. The upper age cut‐off was given by the inclusion criteria of the NAKO, and the lower age cut‐off was chosen in a trade‐off between sample size and fit of the population. Although the age cut‐off of 65 years is more commonly used, 60 years has also been used in prior research on medication quality among older adults [ , , ]. Data collection Sociodemographic information and lifestyle factors were collected through touchscreen questionnaires and interviews. Information about diseases was based on self‐reported data, where participants were asked if they had ever been diagnosed with a specific condition by a physician. The PHQ‐9 questionnaire was utilized to assess moderate to severe depressive symptoms (PHQ‐9 sum scores 15–19 and ≥20, respectively). Functional assessments (e.g., blood pressure measurement) were conducted during physical examinations. Medication use was assessed by computer‐assisted, face‐to‐face interviews. Participants were asked to bring packages of the medications they had used in the past 7 days, and if they forgot, they were called by phone after the study centre visit. In the interview, additional information was collected for each medication (such as prescription drugs and regular use or as needed). Vaccination information was extracted from participants’ vaccination booklets and additional questionnaires. Assessment of medication quality: overuse, underuse and potentially inappropriate medication (PIM) use We assessed medication quality considering the three subdomains, PIM use, underuse and overuse, as dichotomized exposures based on the 2024 version of the FORTA list, which classifies medications into four categories, encompassing A (indispensable), B (beneficial), C (questionable) and D (avoid) [ ]. The three subdomains were defined as follows: Overuse: any FORTA medication without an appropriate indication. Underuse: any untreated FORTA indication. To determine the need for medication, we also incorporated clinical biomarkers, for example, HbA 1c levels in participants with diabetes, as detailed in Table . PIM: any medication classified as FORTA C or D used in participants with the according indication. Out of 23 common geriatric indications listed in the FORTA list [ ], we included 17 indications predominantly based on self‐reported lifetime history of diagnoses and occasionally complemented by additional criteria such as diagnostic tools. The detailed definitions and assessments in the

were defined as follows: Overuse: any FORTA medication without an appropriate indication. Underuse: any untreated FORTA indication. To determine the need for medication, we also incorporated clinical biomarkers, for example, HbA 1c levels in participants with diabetes, as detailed in Table . PIM: any medication classified as FORTA C or D used in participants with the according indication. Out of 23 common geriatric indications listed in the FORTA list [ ], we included 17 indications predominantly based on self‐reported lifetime history of diagnoses and occasionally complemented by additional criteria such as diagnostic tools. The detailed definitions and assessments in the NAKO are listed in Table . Acute bacterial infections, nausea/vomiting and constipation were not included because these are not chronic diseases requiring long‐term medication. Anaemia, incontinence, bipolar disorder and behavioural/psychological symptoms of dementia were not included since relevant information about these diagnoses was not available. Insomnia requiring medical treatment could not be distinguished from other types of insomnia and was therefore also excluded from our underuse assessment. Possible alternative medications and indications not included in the FORTA list were also considered to mitigate the risk of misclassification of over‐ and underuse. The full list of potential medications to be used for these 17 indications and the assessed vaccinations is provided in Table . We only included pneumococcal and annual influenza vaccines in our vaccination assessment because herpes zoster, COVID‐19 and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccines were not part of the national recommendations for vaccination among older adults in the entire recruitment period (2014–2019). The recommendations for herpes zoster, COVID‐19 and RSV vaccinations were announced later in 12/2018, 12/2020 and 04/2025, respectively [ , , ]. Due to the small proportion of participants with complete available information on vaccinations (10.3%), we reported underuse of vaccines separately from underuse of other medications. We assessed the representativeness of this subpopulation with vaccination data by comparing the baseline characteristics of the included subsample with the baseline characteristics of those not included, and no major differences were observed (Table ). Statistical analyses We used multivariable logistic regression models to identify factors associated with PIM use, underuse, and overuse of medications as dependent variables. Results were presented as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals. Overall, 32 factors, including sociodemographic/‐economic factors, lifestyle factors, study centre and diseases, were selected based on subject matter knowledge. Multicollinearity and model stability were tested with the variation inflation index. After exclusion of self‐perceived general health status, no variable had a variance inflation factor ≥8. Therefore, the full model was adjusted for 31 independent variables, which are shown in Table . Additionally, models only adjusted for age, sex and study centre were computed. We utilized multiple imputations with the fully conditional specification method [ ] and created five imputed datasets to handle missing covariates. Indications for medication use were not imputed. Instead, we assumed the absence of the indication if this information was missing. No covariate had more than 30% of missing values. The proportions of missing values for imputed covariates (Table ) and medical indications (Table ) are listed in the appendix. Details about the imputation procedure are outlined in . We used SAS statistical software (version 9.4, SAS Institute, Inc.) for the statistical analyses. All statistical tests were two‐tailed, with a significance level set at α = 0.05 and p ‐values adjusted for multiple testing using the false discovery rate [ ] per model and outcome. Results Characteristics of the study population The baseline characteristics of the study population ( n = 54,296) are presented in Table . The median age was 65 years (interquartile range: 62–67), and half of the population was female (50.1%). The proportion of PIM users, individuals with underuse, and individuals with overuse in the total study population was 26.1%, 19.1% and 23.6%, respectively. Table also shows descriptively how these proportions vary according to baseline characteristics. Frequency of and factors associated with PIM use For the participants ( N = 14,182 (26.1%)) using at least one PIM, the ranking of the proportions according to indication is presented in Table . The largest proportions of individuals taking a PIM to treat the specific indication were observed among patients with Parkinson's disease (59.9%), epilepsy (39.9%), arterial hypertension (27.1%), atrial fibrillation (23.4%) and a history of depression (22.4%). The results of the age, sex and study centre–adjusted logistic regression model of potential factors associated with PIM use are provided in Table . Table lists the results of the full model. Among the sociodemographic/‐economic factors, we observed 12% lower odds for PIM use in males compared to females. In participants aged 65–69 and ≥70 years, 10% and 17% higher odds for PIM use were observed, respectively, compared to those aged 60–64 years. Furthermore, participants with middle and high income had 11% and 19% lower odds for using PIM relative

The results of the age, sex and study centre–adjusted logistic regression model of potential factors associated with PIM use are provided in Table . Table lists the results of the full model. Among the sociodemographic/‐economic factors, we observed 12% lower odds for PIM use in males compared to females. In participants aged 65–69 and ≥70 years, 10% and 17% higher odds for PIM use were observed, respectively, compared to those aged 60–64 years. Furthermore, participants with middle and high income had 11% and 19% lower odds for using PIM relative to participants with low income. We observed 14% lower odds for PIM use among participants with ≥13 years compared to <13 years of education. We also observed differences in the detected PIM rates in the 21 study centres. Compared to Augsburg, which was the largest study centre and recruited 10.2% of the study participants, 8 study centres had statistically significantly higher or lower odds for PIM use, with a range from 13% lower odds in Hamburg to 49% increased odds in Neubrandenburg. Obesity (defined as body‐mass‐index [BMI] ≥ 30; 38% increased odds compared to normal BMI) and alcohol abstinence (29% increased odds compared to low alcohol consumption) were the lifestyle risk factors with the strongest association with PIM use. We further identified overweight (BMI 25–29.9) and current smoking as additional associated factors, with 12% and 16% increased odds for PIM use. Conversely, participants with sufficient physical activity had 16% lower odds for PIM use compared to participants with insufficient physical activity. Overall, 18 out of 21 tested diseases were statistically significantly associated with PIM use. Parkinson's disease, arterial hypertension, epilepsy and depression were the most important factors associated with PIM use (OR ≥ 2), with 16.2‐, 4.5‐, 4.3‐ and 2.1‐fold increased odds, respectively. Acute coronary syndromes (39% lower odds) were the only morbidities that were inversely associated with PIM use. Frequency of and factors associated with medication underuse We identified 10,371 (19.1%) participants with underuse. The results from the age, sex and study centre–adjusted logistic regression model for the potential factors associated with underuse are presented in Table . In the full model (Table ), males had 8% higher odds for underuse compared to females. Compared to those aged 60–64 years, participants aged 65–69 and ≥70 years had 16% and 25% lower odds for medication underuse, respectively. Participants in 9 out of 21 study centres had statistically significantly lower odds for underuse compared to participants attending the study centre in Augsburg. The lowest odds for underuse were observed in Waren (Müritz) (49% lower odds). In contrast to other lifestyle factors, only obesity was statistically significantly associated with underuse, with 18% lower odds for underuse among obese participants compared to those with a normal BMI. We detected 12 out of the 21 tested diseases as being statistically significantly associated with underuse. Thereof, osteoporosis (9.5‐fold increased odds), atrial fibrillation (6.1‐fold increased odds), Parkinson's disease (2.6‐fold increased odds) and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) (2.0‐fold increased odds) were identified as particularly strongly associated with underuse (OR ≥ 2). The ranked proportions of participants with underuse per indication are presented in Table . We observed that more than half of the participants with osteoporosis (51.7%) and more than a third (38.7%) of the participants with atrial fibrillation had medication underuse for the specific indication. Parkinson's disease ranked fourth with 15.7% and COPD ranked sixth with 11.2% of patients with underuse. Conversely, a lifetime history of an acute coronary syndrome and renal impairment were inversely associated with underuse, with 33% and 25% lower odds. Frequency of and factors associated with medication overuse Medication overuse was detected in 12,787 (23.6%) participants. The most frequently overused drug classes are ranked in Table . No indication for low‐dose acetylsalicylic acid (ASA), hormone replacement therapy (HRT), proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) and antidepressants use could be found in 5.1%, 3.6%, 3.3% and 2.2% of the total study population, respectively. All other medication classes were identified as being overused in less than 2% of the total study population. For the factors associated with overuse, the results from the age, sex and study centre–adjusted logistic regression models are provided in Table . In the fully adjusted model (Table ), we observed 25% lower odds for overuse in males compared to females, and 21% and 46% increased odds in participants aged 65–69 and ≥70 years compared to those aged 60–64 years. Furthermore, six study centres were statistically significantly associated with overuse, ranging from statistically significantly 22% lower odds for overuse in Bremen to 21% increased odds in Regensburg compared to the study centre in Augsburg. No other socio‐economic/‐demographic factors were statistically significantly associated with overuse after adjustment for multiple testing. All assessed lifestyle factors were associated with overuse. Obesity and alcohol abstinence, as

In the fully adjusted model (Table ), we observed 25% lower odds for overuse in males compared to females, and 21% and 46% increased odds in participants aged 65–69 and ≥70 years compared to those aged 60–64 years. Furthermore, six study centres were statistically significantly associated with overuse, ranging from statistically significantly 22% lower odds for overuse in Bremen to 21% increased odds in Regensburg compared to the study centre in Augsburg. No other socio‐economic/‐demographic factors were statistically significantly associated with overuse after adjustment for multiple testing. All assessed lifestyle factors were associated with overuse. Obesity and alcohol abstinence, as well as current and ≤20 years since quitting smoking, were positively associated with overuse, whereas sufficient physical activity was inversely associated with it. After adjustment for multiple testing, 12 out of the 21 tested diseases were statistically significantly associated with overuse. Thereof, a lifetime history of depression (1.6‐fold increased odds) and epilepsy (1.5‐fold increased odds) were the factors exhibiting the strongest association (OR ≥ 1.5). Conversely, atrial fibrillation, acute coronary syndromes and pain were inversely associated with overuse, with 18%, 14% and 9% lower odds for overuse. Frequency of vaccination underuse In the subsample with complete available information on administered vaccinations, 90.6% and 62.7% of study participants did not have the recommended pneumococcal and annual influenza virus vaccinations, respectively. Discussion Summary of findings Our study summarized real‐world data of n = 54,296 participants aged 60–74 from the NAKO and showed that PIM use, underuse and overuse of medications according to the FORTA list [ ] were very common, with 26.1%, 19.1% and 23.6% exposed individuals. Furthermore, we observed 90.6% and 62.7% underuse with respect to the recommended pneumococcal and annual influenza virus vaccinations in participants with complete available vaccination information, respectively. In addition, we identified multiple factors associated with PIM use, overuse and underuse in the areas of sociodemographic/‐economic factors, lifestyle factors and comorbidities. Comparison of frequencies of FORTA‐based medication quality estimates with those from previous studies Multiple other, explicit medication assessment tools aim at improving optimization of pharmacotherapy for geriatric patients [ , ]. Given that they address different aspects of medication quality, we will not go into details about studies utilizing other lists. Despite the application of the FORTA list in previous studies [ , , , , , , , , , , ], our study is the first to assess the frequency of all three subdomains of suboptimal medication quality, including PIM use, underuse and overuse in the general older population. Proportions reported by previous studies [ , , , , , , , , , , , , , , ] ranged from 52.6% to 76.5% [ , , , ] for PIM use and from 48.7% [ ] to 62.8% [ ] for underuse. Only one study [ ] reported a prevalence for overuse, and two out of three participants (66.7%) were exposed. Although all these studies included participants with a mean age of 74 years or higher, our study population was relatively young (median age: 65 years). Furthermore, the morbidity was lower in the population‐based NAKO sample compared to the high‐risk populations included in the previous studies. Hence, it did not surprise that all previous studies reported higher proportions of exposed individuals [ , , , , , , , , , , , , , , ]. In addition, a healthy volunteer bias is apparent in the NAKO study population, which precludes the estimation of disease or medication use prevalences for the German population without using weights. We, therefore, only report frequencies rather than prevalences and recommend treating them with caution. However, although our observations likely underestimated the prevalences of PIM use, medication underuse and overuse in the ‘true’ older general German population, they are still quite high, calling for measures to reduce them. Factors associated with PIM use Since no previous study assessed factors associated with PIM use based on the FORTA list, we cautiously refer to studies that applied other tools [ , , , , ]. Previous research found inconsistent results on potential associations of PIM intake with sex and age [ , , , , ]. Our observation that older age and female sex were statistically significantly associated with PIM use is supported by three previous studies [ , , ]. The higher risk of PIM use among individuals with low income, with obesity, insufficient physical activity, alcohol abstainers and current smokers has not yet been shown by previous German studies [ , ], but they align with international research findings [ , , ], suggesting that individuals with lower socio‐economic status and less healthy lifestyles might be more likely to receive PIM. Abstinence from alcohol might be seen as an indicator for a healthy lifestyle. However, in population‐based studies, abstainers are usually less healthy than low alcohol

with PIM use is supported by three previous studies [ , , ]. The higher risk of PIM use among individuals with low income, with obesity, insufficient physical activity, alcohol abstainers and current smokers has not yet been shown by previous German studies [ , ], but they align with international research findings [ , , ], suggesting that individuals with lower socio‐economic status and less healthy lifestyles might be more likely to receive PIM. Abstinence from alcohol might be seen as an indicator for a healthy lifestyle. However, in population‐based studies, abstainers are usually less healthy than low alcohol consumers, as they also include previous alcoholics and individuals who quit drinking due to diseases or interactions with their medication [ , ]. It was not surprising that the vast majority of assessed diseases (18 out of 21) were statistically significantly associated with PIM use, as most of them are also FORTA indications. All cardiovascular diseases were among these factors, but arterial hypertension stood out with a particularly high 4.5‐fold increased odds for PIM use. However, all second‐ and third‐line antihypertensives are categorized as FORTA C or D [ ]. Hence, simply switching these medications to potentially more appropriate alternatives is not feasible in many cases and may partly explain the high PIM rate for this indication. We also identified three neurological diseases among the factors with the strongest associations with PIM use: Parkinson's disease, epilepsy and depression, with 16.2‐, 4.3‐ and 2.1‐fold increased odds for PIM use. The varying response rates and pharmacologic profiles of antiparkinson medications, antiepileptics and antidepressants are likely the challenging aspects for optimizing the indication‐specific therapy. For example, it would be essential to consider the differing pharmacological profiles of antidepressants, as all classes, except selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, are classified as PIMs according to the FORTA list [ ]. Factors associated with underuse Previous studies assessing factors associated with underuse have been based on guidelines for specific indications [ , , ] or the START criteria [ ]. Our finding that older age groups had higher odds of medication underuse resulted from the comprehensive adjustment for diseases. In the model adjusted for age, sex and study centre, only, no association between age and underuse was detected. This would be in line with a previous study from Germany, which found no association between age and underuse [ ]. The observed 8% higher odds for underuse among males compared to females might be explained by sex differences in symptom awareness, preventive health behaviours and the subsequent number of physician contacts [ ]. Obesity was the only lifestyle factor exhibiting an inverse association with underuse in the full model. This was also not observed in the age, sex and study centre–adjusted model and appeared after adjustment for the diseases. Maybe individuals with obesity as a comorbidity have more physician contacts and get more drugs prescribed. Regarding the diseases, osteoporosis, atrial fibrillation, Parkinson's disease and COPD appeared to be most relevant, as they were associated with more than 2.0‐fold increased odds for underuse. Over half (51.7%) of the participants with osteoporosis did not take the indicated medication, which aligns with previous studies [ , , ]. Given that osteoporosis‐related hip fractures are associated with higher mortality [ , ] and economic burden [ , ], undertreatment of osteoporosis has been recognized as an important national [ , , , ] and global [ , , , , , ] concern. As FORTA‐based prescribing has been proven to statistically significantly reduce underuse of osteoporosis medications in two randomized controlled trials [ , ], there is sufficient evidence to implement such interventions into standard care. The observed 6.1‐fold increased odds for underuse among participants with atrial fibrillation points to another area that requires clinical attention. Although we could not evaluate previous successful treatments through cardioversion or ablation, the 38.7% of medication underuse in patients with atrial fibrillation aligns with the 19% to over 50% underuse of anticoagulation among high‐risk patients identified by previous studies [ , , ]. However, given the increasing prevalence of atrial fibrillation with age, the complexity of bleeding risks, optimal stroke prevention and rhythm management in the oldest patient group [ , ], the observed high medication underuse rate should receive attention in clinical care. For some diseases with considerable indication‐specific underuse rates, for example, Parkinson's disease and COPD, lack of efficacy of the first‐line drugs or early‐stage diseases, for which the therapy had not yet been initiated, could be an explanation for underuse. Factors associated with overuse We only identified one previous study assessing factors associated with overuse, and this study only focused on antidepressants based on the START criteria [ ]. We found 25% lower odds for overuse among men compared to women. This sex difference was likely driven by HRT, ranking second among all

underuse rate should receive attention in clinical care. For some diseases with considerable indication‐specific underuse rates, for example, Parkinson's disease and COPD, lack of efficacy of the first‐line drugs or early‐stage diseases, for which the therapy had not yet been initiated, could be an explanation for underuse. Factors associated with overuse We only identified one previous study assessing factors associated with overuse, and this study only focused on antidepressants based on the START criteria [ ]. We found 25% lower odds for overuse among men compared to women. This sex difference was likely driven by HRT, ranking second among all overused medication classes. The FORTA list classifies HRT as overuse for subjects without osteoporosis if it is not used within 3 years of menopause [ , ], which typically occurs between the ages of 50 and 51 in Europe [ ]. HRT was subsequently classified as overuse in all study participants without osteoporosis, since our study population was 60 years and older. Periodically re‐evaluating the need for HRT and the individual risk profile is also recommended by the European clinical practice guideline [ ]. Regarding lifestyle factors, the clear pattern emerged that participants leading an unhealthy lifestyle appeared to be more likely to overuse medications. Maybe physicians tend to treat these patients with drugs rather than recommending lifestyle changes, which could be overuse if there is no clear indication. Furthermore, patients with an unhealthy lifestyle are often the most morbid and often receive polypharmacy. As the number of diseases increases, the medication gets more complex, and it is harder for the physicians to maintain an overview of all drugs (still) needed. Diseases were less prominent factors associated with overuse compared to PIM use and underuse, but history of depression and epilepsy (1.6‐ and 1.5‐fold increased odds) appeared to be most relevant. A large proportion of overuse among patients with depression can be explained by maintenance therapy or relapse prophylaxis [ , , , ] because 11.2% of participants with a lifetime history of depression used antidepressants but reported no moderate or severe symptoms, which we applied to define an indication for antidepressants. As previous research recommended maintenance therapy for at least 6 months after remission to effectively prevent relapse [ , ], the absence of at least moderate depressive symptoms could also reflect the effectiveness of an appropriate and indicated treatment. Distinguishing ‘true’ overuse from appropriate maintenance therapy requires evaluating each individual's treatment regularly in clinical practice. However, we had no information on whether these assessments took place. Antidepressants and antiepileptics used to treat pain could not have been a driver of overuse since pain was considered an alternative indication. When further exploring the underlying sources of overuse among patients with a history of depression or epilepsy, we found considerable overuse of low‐dose ASA and PPIs among participants with these indications. With respect to epilepsy, the high proportions of low‐dose ASA overuse might result from appropriate secondary stroke prevention, as stroke is the most common cause of epilepsy in older individuals [ ]. If the history of stroke remained unreported, this resulted in overuse. Additionally, PPI might have been initiated due to gastrointestinal symptoms linked to depression [ ] or caused by antiepileptic drugs [ ]. If these symptoms were not severe, the drugs to treat them appear to be an overuse. Regarding low‐dose ASA and depression, associations between cardiovascular symptoms and depression have also been established [ ]. However, if no cardiovascular disease has been diagnosed yet, the low‐dose ASA appears as overuse. Our finding that low‐dose ASA was the most frequently overused medication (in 5.1% of the study population) should also receive attention in clinical practice. This frequency was in agreement with an observational study from Spain, which found overuse of low‐dose ASA in 7% of the participants [ ]. Given the associated risks of bleeding, current guidelines have become very conservative regarding its use in primary prevention [ , ]. The US guidelines even recommend against initiating low‐dose ASA for primary prevention in adults over 60 years of age [ ]. In addition to the identified associated factors, an interesting finding was that 3.3% of the study population overused PPI. Concerns about their appropriate use have been progressively highlighted and addressed by specific deprescribing guidelines [ , ]. A previous drug utilization study of German claims data revealed a notable rise in PPI prescriptions between 2010 and 2016, and 52% of new PPI users had no documented on‐label indication [ ]. Underuse of vaccinations The low vaccination rates for pneumococcal (90.6% underuse) and annual influenza (62.7% underuse) vaccinations observed in our study align with recent data from the German vaccination monitoring: 88.2% and 68.6% of the citizens aged 60–64 and 65–69 years, respectively, had not received pneumococcal vaccinations. Furthermore, 61.8% of those aged 60 years and older

progressively highlighted and addressed by specific deprescribing guidelines [ , ]. A previous drug utilization study of German claims data revealed a notable rise in PPI prescriptions between 2010 and 2016, and 52% of new PPI users had no documented on‐label indication [ ]. Underuse of vaccinations The low vaccination rates for pneumococcal (90.6% underuse) and annual influenza (62.7% underuse) vaccinations observed in our study align with recent data from the German vaccination monitoring: 88.2% and 68.6% of the citizens aged 60–64 and 65–69 years, respectively, had not received pneumococcal vaccinations. Furthermore, 61.8% of those aged 60 years and older had no influenza vaccination [ ]. Implementing regular vaccination checks, ideally through easily accessible opportunities outside of standard physician visits, could help reduce the underutilization of vaccines. Regional differences Regional social inequalities between rural and urban German regions have been previously recognized, highlighting better accessibility to primary and specialist care in urban regions [ , , ]. Our findings might reflect these disparities by showing differences in odds for all three subdomains of medication quality by study centre. For instance, the odds for PIM use were considerably low in Hamburg, which is the second largest town in Germany and has a higher average socio‐economic status and a higher ratio of physicians per inhabitant compared to most other German rural regions. Consequently, participants from study centres in rural eastern German regions, that is, Neubrandenburg and Demmin, had the highest odds for PIM use. Interestingly, these rural regions also had the lowest odds for underuse. With respect to overuse, the pattern was less clear, as urban regions were among the study centres with the highest (Regensburg) and lowest (Bremen) odds for overuse. We consider these potential regional differences interesting signals warranting further investigation. Strengths and limitations To our knowledge, this is the first study investigating the frequency of and factors associated with all three dimensions of suboptimal prescribing in the general older population. The availability of a wealth of data enabled us to assess potential associations of a broad range of factors. Incorporating blood‐based biomarkers as well as diagnostic and physical assessments in our indication assessment is a unique strength that helped minimize potential misclassification for diagnoses. Moreover, the comprehensive brown‐bag review ensured a high level of reliability and completeness of the medication assessment. Finally, the high sample size ( n = 54,296) provided sufficient statistical power to address a large number of potentially associated factors ( n = 31) with correction for multiple testing. Although the identified associated factors provide a clinically relevant foundation for effectively identifying target populations for medication reviews, it should be noted that the cross‐sectional design mainly reflects correlations but does not imply causal inference. The main limitation of our study is the ‘healthy volunteer’ bias and a relatively young sample of older adults (60–74 years). Hence, our results cannot be extrapolated to older populations or all German adults aged 60 years and older. Another important limitation is the risk of information bias, including both over‐ and underreporting of indications (e.g., through recall bias or undiagnosed conditions) and (over‐the‐counter) medications. We addressed this by comprehensive statistical adjustment, completing indications with information from medications and biomarkers. We used the 2024 version of the FORTA list, whereas data collection was from 2014 to 2019. We think that the minimal changes during this time did not affect our results to a relevant extent. However, revisions and expansions of the FORTA list over time may influence prevalence estimates and complicate comparisons across studies using different versions. Our German study population and the use of the Germany‐specific FORTA list restrict the generalizability to other countries. However, a European version of the FORTA list is also available [ ] that largely aligns with the Germany‐specific version. A future study across European countries, preferably with available linkage to validated diagnoses (e.g., claims data), would be desirable. Clinical implications The results highlight critical areas, which clinical practice may need to address, such as untreated osteoporosis and low vaccination rates. In addition, the factors associated with the three subdomains of suboptimal medication can be used to assign resources for comprehensive medication reviews with the FORTA list to those patients with the highest odds for PIM use, underuse or overuse, which were patients with arterial hypertension, Parkinson's disease, epilepsy, depression, osteoporosis, COPD and atrial fibrillation. As arterial hypertension has a very high prevalence in older adults (49.7% in our sample), and all second‐ and third‐line antihypertensives are categorized as PIM, making changes in antihypertensive medication difficult, we recommend focusing on the other named, less common, six indications. As ‘only’ 0.4%, 0.7%, 15.7%, 7.3%, 7.5% and 15.2% of the older German NAKO study population were affected by Parkinson's disease, epilepsy, depression, osteoporosis, COPD and atrial fibrillation, respectively, and as they are also usually documented in electronic health records,

underuse or overuse, which were patients with arterial hypertension, Parkinson's disease, epilepsy, depression, osteoporosis, COPD and atrial fibrillation. As arterial hypertension has a very high prevalence in older adults (49.7% in our sample), and all second‐ and third‐line antihypertensives are categorized as PIM, making changes in antihypertensive medication difficult, we recommend focusing on the other named, less common, six indications. As ‘only’ 0.4%, 0.7%, 15.7%, 7.3%, 7.5% and 15.2% of the older German NAKO study population were affected by Parkinson's disease, epilepsy, depression, osteoporosis, COPD and atrial fibrillation, respectively, and as they are also usually documented in electronic health records, we suggest that they could be used to identify a high‐risk population for suboptimal medication quality quickly. If resources for comprehensive medication reviews with the FORTA list are limited, this disease‐defined high‐risk population could be prioritized. However, it should be noted that this recommendation is not based on evidence from RCTs showing a higher benefit from comprehensive medication reviews in these patient populations compared to others. Such RCTs are still needed. Moreover, further research could establish effective strategies that help clinicians address suboptimal medication quality in hard‐to‐reach groups, such as patients with lower socio‐economic status, leading unhealthy lifestyles or living in rural regions with barriers to healthcare access. Finally, the use of the FORTA list should only be regarded as a screening tool to detect suboptimal medication. It cannot replace clinical judgement, and the ultimate decisions regarding (de‐)prescribing should also be guided by individual patient goals and preferences. Conclusion PIM use, medication underuse and overuse were very common in this large, population‐based study of older adults from Germany. Arterial hypertension, Parkinson's disease, epilepsy, depression, osteoporosis, COPD and atrial fibrillation were identified as diseases with the highest odds of insufficient medication quality. If resources for medication reviews are limited, the latter six diseases could be prioritized because they have prevalences <16%. documents.title: USPSTF Screening for hypertension in adults

chunks.content: Hypertension is a leading modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular disease (CVD), and nearly 75% of United States (US) adults aged 60 years and older have hypertension with one-third of adults 60 years and older achieving the target BP goal . Control of blood pressure (BP) with antihypertensive therapy reduces risk of CVD , , and this CVD risk reduction benefit is present for both middle-aged and older adults . Concerns that intensive BP lowering may cause hypotension, either chronically or intermittently, and thus increase the risk for a fall, may be a barrier to achieving BP goals, particularly among older adults. Falls are a leading cause of injury-related hospitalization and death among older US adults, with more than one in three US adults ≥65 years of age experiencing a fall each year , . Although intensive BP lowering can increase risk of hypotension, the evidence that initiation or intensification of BP medication and intensive BP lowering targets lead to injurious falls is mixed , . Home blood pressure monitoring (HBPM) guided BP management can improve BP control and has the potential to reduce CVD risk while avoiding hypotension, falls, and serious injuries . BP has traditionally been measured in the clinic setting , and a major challenge that clinicians encounter in deciding to titrate antihypertensive medication is the inaccuracy and visit-to-visit variability of BP assessed in the clinic . The inaccuracy may be due to improper BP measurement and also the stress experienced by patients with being outside of their usual environment or because the clinic visit is only a single time and may miss variability within and across days . For example, 32% of adults 60 years and older have white coat hypertension, defined as high clinic BP (≥140/90 mmHg) but normal or controlled BP (<140/90 mmHg) when measured outside of the clinic . The United States Preventive Services Task Force and the 2017 and 2025 American College of Cardiology (ACC)/American Heart Association (AHA) BP guidelines recommend measurement of BP outside of the clinic setting to better assess BP and inform antihypertensive treatment , . HBPM is an inexpensive and highly feasible approach to measure out-of-office BP . It typically involves the measurement of BP two times in the morning and two times in the evening over a period of days to weeks while the person is seated and resting at home . However, it is unclear whether BP assessed by HBPM provides prognostic information on the risk for fall injuries among older adults. The goal of the current study was to determine whether mean BP on HBPM, differences between clinic and home BP (i.e. the white coat effect), and higher day-to-day BP variability are associated with an increased risk for falls among older adults with hypertension taking antihypertensive medication. 1 Methods 1.1 Study design and population This study included participants from the AMBulatoRy BlOod PreSsure In Older Adults (AMBROSIA) study, who completed HBPM through the AMBROSIA-HOME ancillary study. Details of the AMBROSIA and AMBROSIA-HOME studies have been previously published . Briefly, the AMBROSIA study was conducted at Kaiser Permanente Southern California (KPSC) which provides comprehensive services to over 4.9 million members through its integrated health care delivery system , . The KPSC electronic health records (EHR) were used to identify potential participants who were screened over the telephone prior to in-person study visits. Current KPSC members ≥65 years of age with hypertension defined as ≥2 outpatient ICD-10 diagnosis codes for hypertension in the prior 12 months and currently taking antihypertensive medication, were eligible for the study. Additionally, participants had to have outpatient systolic BP of 110–179 mmHg and diastolic BP of 50–109 mmHg recorded within the prior 12 weeks, no change in antihypertensive medication classes or doses between the participant's last clinic BP and the enrollment date, no serious fall injury since their last BP assessment, and enrollment in KPSC with a pharmacy benefit for at least 24 months. Participants meeting any of the following exclusion criteria were ineligible for the study: receiving skilled nursing, long-term, or hospice care in the year prior to enrollment; history of stroke in the prior 3 months; history of dementia; non-ambulatory; primary spoken and written language other than English; and systolic BP ≥180 mmHg or diastolic BP >110 mmHg or systolic BP <110 mmHg or diastolic BP <50 mmHg measured during the enrollment visit. For this analysis, we further limited the sample to those participants who completed at least 4 days out of 7 days of HBPM with 2 morning and 2 evening measurements. Days of HBPM could be non-consecutive. The study was approved by both the KPSC and University of Alabama at Birmingham institutional review boards. Each participant provided written informed consent. 1.2 Blood pressure measurement All clinic BP readings for the 12 weeks prior to study enrollment were extracted from

Each participant provided written informed consent. 1.2 Blood pressure measurement All clinic BP readings for the 12 weeks prior to study enrollment were extracted from the KPSC EHR. These measurements were conducted as part of routine clinical care during outpatient visits using an oscillometric device. All available measurements were averaged for systolic and diastolic BP, separately. During the first study visit, the ACC/AHA recommendations were followed to measure BP 10 using an Omron Model HEM-907XL (Omron Corporation, Japan) oscillometric device , . Specifically, participants were asked to sit comfortably with their legs uncrossed, feet flat on the floor and back supported. The BP cuff was placed on their upper non-dominant arm, when possible, with their arm supported. Fourteen participants used the dominant arm for BP. After 5 min of quiet rest, three BP readings were obtained at one-minute intervals and averaged. Orthostatic hypotension was defined as a decline of ≥20 mmHg in systolic BP or ≥ 10 mmHg in diastolic BP after either 1 or 3 min of standing , . Participants were given a Microlife WatchBP®home HBPM device with an appropriately sized cuff, which has been validated according to international BP measurement protocols . Following guideline-recommended approaches and prior validations studies , , , , the WatchBP®home device was set to automatically take 2 BP measurements 1 min apart. Participants were instructed to take 2 BP readings in the morning before breakfast and 2 readings in the evening, 2 h after dinner and before sleep, for 7 days. Study staff instructed participants to sit erect with their feet flat on the floor, arm supported on a table or pillow, with the BP cuff at heart level, and rest for 5 min prior to the first measurement being taken. To demonstrate their ability to measure BP with the HBPM, the research staff ensured that each participant was able to turn on the device and measure their BP twice using the appropriate body position and rest period. The systolic and diastolic BPs on HBPM were defined as the average of all available readings. White coat effect was defined as mean clinic BP minus mean BP from HBPM for systolic and diastolic BPs, separately. We calculated systolic and diastolic BP variability, separately, as the standard deviation independent of the mean (SDIM), a measure used in prior studies of HBPM BP variability and CVD outcomes , . To calculate the SDIM, we averaged the BP for all readings for each day and then calculated the day-to-day variability. The SDIM was calculated as SD/M a where SD is the standard deviation of BP, M is the mean BP, and a is derived by estimating the parameters of the equation ln(SD) = k + a · ln(M), where k is a constant . 1.3 Fall assessment Data on falls were collected following enrollment using monthly falls calendars, which have previously been validated and used as a reference standard for evaluating risk of falls , , . Participants were provided with prepaid postage envelopes, and instructions for completing and returning the falls calendars at the end of each month for 1 year after their initial study visit. Participants were asked to document “any fall where their body parts hit a surface, including falls that occur on stairs” by marking each day of the calendar, indicating if a fall had occurred or not. We chose a broad definition of falls to limit participants' variability in their interpretation of what constituted a fall , . In addition, participants were asked to provide information on the fall timing, location, and if they required medical care because of the fall. Participants who did not return a falls calendar within 2 weeks after the end of a month were followed up via a telephone, email, or text reminder. Serious fall injuries extracted from the EHR were a pre-specified secondary outcome. 1.4 Other data collection Data on participant age, sex, race and ethnicity, body mass index (BMI), presence of chronic conditions including diabetes mellitus, arthritis, and depression, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), and number of antihypertensive medication classes and other chronic medication prescribed were extracted from the EHR. The presence of diagnosis codes in the 2 years preceding the study visit were used to define chronic conditions. The presence of diagnosis codes in the 2 years preceding the study visit were used to define chronic conditions. Four participants, who used antihypertensive medications at the time of eligibility screening, did not have current prescriptions for an antihypertensive medication at the time of the study visit, but met the inclusion criteria and so were retained in the study. Data on self-reported history of falls, cigarette smoking (ever versus never), use of alcohol in the past year, and life-space mobility were collected during the study visit. Life-space mobility is a measure of community mobility and social participation based on self-reported movement from the room where one sleeps to areas outside of one's town over the last 4 weeks . The composite life-space mobility score takes into account how far people go, how often they go there, and how much assistance they need with higher scores indicating greater life-space. Cognition was assessed using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) . Frailty was defined as the presence of ≥3 of 5 characteristics assessed by the study staff during a study visit, based on the Fried frailty phenotype: (1) shrinking- unintentional weight loss ≥10 lbs. in the prior year, (2) weakness- grip strength in the lowest 20% according to age and BMI, (3) exhaustion- self-reported, (4) slow gait speed- being in the lowest 20% based on time to walk 15 ft according to sex- and height-specific norms, and (5) low physical activity- < 383 kcals/week for men and <270 kcals/week for women based on the Minnesota Leisure Time Activity questionnaire . Participants with no characteristics were considered robust while those with 1 or 2 of the characteristics were considered pre-frail. 1.5 Statistical analysis To evaluate the associations of systolic and diastolic BP from HBPM with falls, we examined the following pre-specified HBPM exposures: mean levels, BP white coat effect, and SDIM. We summarized participant characteristics using means with standard deviation or percentages for the full sample and by quartiles of mean systolic HBPM. For each HBPM exposure, we used Cox proportional hazards models to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) of time to first fall across quartiles. A priori, we chose the quartile that we hypothesized would have the lowest risk of falls as the reference category; quartile 4 for mean BP from HBPM and quartile 1 for white coat effect and SDIM. Model 1 was adjusted for demographic characteristics age, sex, and race/ethnicity. Model 2 included variables in Model 1 plus medical characteristics and health behaviors that might confound the associations of HBPM with falls: self-reported history of falls, any alcohol use in the past year, ever smoker, number of chronic medication classes, MoCA, depression, diabetes, arthritis, BMI, number of antihypertensive medication classes, and eGFR. Finally, Model 3 included variables in Model 2 plus geriatric assessments and BP characteristics: life-space mobility, frailty, orthostatic hypotension, and baseline clinic systolic BP. Next, we modeled the HBPM exposures using restricted cubic splines with 3 knots in the fully adjusted models and tested for deviations from linearity in the associations and overall statistical significance of the association. Due to the small number of serious fall injuries ( n = 8), we did not conduct analyses for this secondary outcome. The analyses followed a detailed, pre-specified statistical analysis plan. In addition, we conducted post hoc tests of whether associations between HBPM and falls varied by cognition, as people with cognitive impairment may be less accurate in reporting their falls, and by history of diabetes, because hypoglycemic episodes may lead to falls. Analyses were conducted in SAS version 9.4 (Cary, NC). P -values <0.05 were considered statistically significant. 2 Results A total of 499 of 541 participants (92.2%) had HBPM recordings with at least 4 days with 2 morning and 2 evening BP measurements (Supplemental Fig. 1). The mean ± standard deviation age of participants was 74.2 ± 6.1 years and 42.7% were men ( ). There were 45.5% Non-Hispanic White, 21.2% Non-Hispanic Black, 18.2% Hispanic, and 13.2% Asian or Pacific Islander participants, 38.5% had ever smoked, and 61.7% had consumed alcohol within the past year. In this sample, 29.7% had diabetes, 45.7% had arthritis, and 19.2% had depression. Mild cognitive impairment was present in 54.7% of participants. A total of 64.5% of participants were taking at least 2 antihypertensive medications and 63.7% were taking at least 2 chronic medication classes. The mean ± standard deviation eGFR was 72.6 ± 18.0 mL/min/1.73 m 2 and 50.7% of participants were prefrail
