A composite stigma severity rating will be assigned. Domain 4: Representation and Equity Where discernible, coders will note apparent race/ethnicity, gender, and age of individuals depicted. Structural barrier mentions (insurance, transportation, rural access, language barriers, racism, mistrust) will be coded. The focus population (general, specific communities) will be documented. A conservative “not discernible” classification will be applied when demographic attributes cannot be reliably identified. Domain 5: Tone and Emotional Framing Coders will assess dominant emotional valence (hopeful, fearful, neutral) and presence of alarmism or sensationalism. Domain 6: Engagement Metrics Platform-specific engagement data will be standardized to enable cross-platform comparison. Posts will be categorized into engagement tertiles (high, medium, low) within each platform to account for differences in engagement scale across platforms. Composite Rating Construction and Reporting Three composite ratings synthesize item-level assessments within their respective domains. The composite accuracy rating integrates item-level assessments across Domain 1 items (D1.1-D1.5). A post is rated “mostly accurate” when all verifiable claims align with USPSTF guidelines and no demonstrably false claims are present; “partially accurate” when the post contains a mix of accurate and inaccurate or incomplete claims; “mostly inaccurate” when the predominant claims are inconsistent with clinical evidence; and “cannot determine” when insufficient factual content is present for assessment. The composite stigma severity rating integrates Domain 3 items (D3.1-D3.5), ranging from “none” (no stigma indicators present) through “mild” (single implicit indicator), “moderate” (multiple indicators or one explicit indicator), to “severe” (explicit blame combined with nihilistic framing or shame imagery). The decision-support strength score (0‐2) is assigned based on the number and quality of decision-support features present across Domain 2 items: 0 indicates no decision-support features, 1 indicates minimal or implicit features, and 2 indicates explicit decision support. When item-level ratings within a composite do not converge clearly, coders will apply the decision rules detailed in [ ], which include worked examples of boundary cases. Unresolved borderline cases will be flagged for adjudication by the principal investigator (LC-B), with reasoning documented in the Coding Decision Log. Additionally, sensitivity analyses described in the Statistical Analysis section include reclassification of borderline composite ratings to assess whether findings are robust to these judgment calls. Item-level distributions will be reported for all accuracy, stigma, and decision-support items alongside composite scores, enabling readers to identify which specific components drive composite patterns. The complete codebook with operational definitions and decision rules is provided in [ ]. Coder Training and Reliability A minimum of 2 coders will independently code each post. Coders will be research assistants with prior content analysis experience selected based on demonstrated attention to detail and familiarity with social media platforms. Training will follow a structured 5-phase protocol: Orientation (2 h): Overview of LCS clinical guidelines (USPSTF 2021), eligibility criteria, and stigma/nihilism concepts using published literature [ ]. Codebook familiarization (2 h): Review of operational definitions with worked examples, boundary cases, and common pitfalls. Calibration coding (4 h): Group coding of 20 posts stratified by platform with real-time discussion and codebook refinement based on encountered ambiguities. Pilot reliability testing: Independent coding of 50 posts stratified by platform and content type. Gwet’s AC1 [ ] will be calculated for each domain; coders achieving AC1≥0.70 on all domains proceed; others receive targeted retraining on low-reliability domains. Drift monitoring: Every 100 coded posts, a random 10% subsample will be recoded by the alternate coder to detect coding drift. Drift exceeding 0.10 decline in AC1 from baseline will trigger a recalibration meeting with codebook clarification. Discrepancies will be flagged in real-time using a shared coding database. Coders will attempt resolution through discussion within 24 hours. Unresolved discrepancies will be escalated to the principal investigator (LC-B) for final determination; all adjudication decisions and reasoning will be documented in a Coding Decision Log to ensure transparency and support future replication. Interrater reliability will be calculated using Gwet’s AC1 [ ] coefficient, which is preferred over Cohen kappa for content analysis due to its stability in the presence of prevalence imbalances and high agreement [ ]. The threshold for acceptable reliability is AC1≥0.70 for accuracy and stigma domains. Percent agreement will be calculated for equity markers given the categorical and often conservative (“not discernible”) nature of these codes. Digital Opinion Leader Identification As an exploratory aim, we will identify DOLs who influence public discourse around lung cancer and LCS. DOL candidates will be identified during content analysis based on creator characteristics and engagement patterns. DOLs will be categorized by creator type for inclusion in engagement regression models, enabling direct comparison of content

to its stability in the presence of prevalence imbalances and high agreement [ ]. The threshold for acceptable reliability is AC1≥0.70 for accuracy and stigma domains. Percent agreement will be calculated for equity markers given the categorical and often conservative (“not discernible”) nature of these codes. Digital Opinion Leader Identification As an exploratory aim, we will identify DOLs who influence public discourse around lung cancer and LCS. DOL candidates will be identified during content analysis based on creator characteristics and engagement patterns. DOLs will be categorized by creator type for inclusion in engagement regression models, enabling direct comparison of content characteristics (accuracy, stigma) between DOLs and other creators. A structured scoring rubric (0‐9 points) will assess 5 criteria: (1) Credibility (0‐2 points): Verified status, professional credentials (clinician, researcher), or recognized organizational affiliation; (2) Reach (0‐2 points): Platform-specific follower/subscriber thresholds (eg, YouTube ≥5000; X/Twitter ≥10,000; TikTok ≥20,000); (3) Engagement rate (0‐2 points): Average engagement≥10%=2 points; 5%‐9%=1 point; (4) Relevance (0‐2 points): 5 or more lung cancer–focused posts in audit period=2 points; 2‐4 posts=1 point; and (5) Multiplatform presence (0‐1 point): Active on 2 or more platforms with relevant content. DOLs will be categorized into tiers: Tier 1 (7‐9 points)=high priority for partnership; Tier 2 (4‐6 points)=moderate priority; Tier 3 (<4 points)=monitor only. The DOL roster will be validated with community partners and patient advisory groups. The complete scoring rubric is provided in [ ]. We acknowledge that this scoring rubric is pragmatically derived for stakeholder mapping purposes and has not been psychometrically validated; the tiered roster represents a practical output for dissemination planning rather than a validated measurement instrument. Statistical Analysis Descriptive analyses will summarize distributions of accuracy, stigma/nihilism, decision-support strength, equity markers, and engagement by platform, content domain (screening vs general lung cancer), and creator type. Cross-platform comparisons will use chi-square or Fisher exact tests for categorical variables and Kruskal-Wallis tests for ordinal variables to identify significant differences in accuracy, stigma prevalence, and decision-support quality across platforms. Engagement modeling will use negative binomial regression (for count outcomes) or ordinal logistic regression (for engagement tertiles) to test the hypothesis that content characteristics predict engagement. Predictors will include accuracy rating, stigma severity, creator type (including DOL status), content type, platform, and equity markers. This analysis will test whether inaccurate or stigmatizing content is associated with disproportionate engagement, as specified in Primary Aim 3. We note that significant associations between content characteristics and engagement should be interpreted as evidence of differential visibility rather than causal evidence of algorithmic bias, as multiple mechanisms may contribute to observed engagement patterns. Subgroup analyses will compare screening-focused versus general lung cancer content; institutional versus individual creators; video versus static posts; and high- versus low-engagement content. Sensitivity analyses will assess the robustness of findings to reclassification of borderline accuracy ratings, exclusion of posts with missing engagement data, normalization of engagement by time since posting, and comparison of content characteristics between relevance-based and algorithmic samples to assess potential algorithmic bias direction. Qualitative synthesis will contextualize quantitative findings through thematic analysis of paraphrased content excerpts, identifying illustrative examples of key patterns. Ethical Considerations This study was reviewed by the Hackensack Meridian Health Institutional Review Board and determined not to constitute regulated research involving human participants under 45 CFR 46.102(e)(1) as it involves secondary analysis of publicly available data with no direct interaction with individuals and no collection of identifiable private information. While legally permissible, analysis of public health narratives raises ethical considerations beyond regulatory compliance. We adopt a minimization approach: (1) no direct quotations will appear in publications; content will be paraphrased and aggregated such that individual posters cannot be identified; (2) posts containing acute distress signals (eg, expressions of active suicidal ideation) will be excluded from analysis and not retained; and (3) the research team will not interact with or contact any content creators. These procedures exceed minimum regulatory requirements and align with emerging best practices for ethical social media research [ ]. All procedures comply with the platform Terms of Service. No informed consent is required as the study uses only publicly posted content with no direct contact with social media users. Data Management Data will be stored on institution-secured servers with role-based access restricted to approved research team members. The data management plan distinguishes three tiers: (1) raw data files containing post URLs and metadata will be retained for verification purposes but will not be shared publicly to comply with platform Terms of Service and protect user privacy; (2) analytic datasets will contain paraphrased content summaries, engagement metrics, and coded variables without direct identifiers linking to specific posts or users; and (3) aggregated summary datasets and the complete codebook will be prepared for public sharing. All data will be retained for 7 years following publication per institutional policy. Upon publication of results, the codebook, Coding Decision Log,

team members. The data management plan distinguishes three tiers: (1) raw data files containing post URLs and metadata will be retained for verification purposes but will not be shared publicly to comply with platform Terms of Service and protect user privacy; (2) analytic datasets will contain paraphrased content summaries, engagement metrics, and coded variables without direct identifiers linking to specific posts or users; and (3) aggregated summary datasets and the complete codebook will be prepared for public sharing. All data will be retained for 7 years following publication per institutional policy. Upon publication of results, the codebook, Coding Decision Log, aggregated summary statistics, and deidentified analytic datasets will be deposited in the Open Science Framework repository to support replication and secondary analysis. Results Data collection began in October 2025, following finalization of the sampling framework and completion of coder training and is projected to be completed by July 2026. As of March 2026, data have been collected from 181 posts across 7 platforms. During the initial phase, posts were systematically identified and captured across all 7 platforms using the predefined search strategy. Dual coding commenced with weekly calibration meetings to ensure consistency in codebook application and maintain interrater reliability standards. Preliminary quality checks indicate strong coder alignment, with reliability metrics meeting prespecified thresholds. Coding and adjudication will continue until the full dataset is complete. Formal quantitative analyses, including descriptive summaries, cross-platform comparisons, and regression modeling, will begin upon coding completion. The analytic phase is expected to conclude by mid-2026, with manuscript preparation and dissemination to follow. Discussion Principal Findings This study addresses a critical gap in lung cancer prevention and early detection research. While substantial investment has been directed toward LCS trials, implementation science, and health system interventions, the digital information environment that shapes public understanding, fear, stigma, and nihilism has been largely unexamined. This protocol describes the first systematic, multiplatform, theory-informed analysis of lung cancer and LCS content on social media. The study is expected to yield several novel contributions. First, by assessing accuracy across platforms and content types, findings will clarify the extent to which publicly visible LCS information aligns with guidelines, where inaccuracies cluster, and which creator types are most likely to disseminate misleading content. Second, the systematic application of a stigma and nihilism lens—operationalized through attribution theory—will provide the first empirical mapping of how blame, shame, and fatalism manifest and circulate in digital spaces. Third, the pairing of content characteristics with engagement metrics will illuminate whether stigmatizing or inaccurate content is associated with disproportionate engagement, which may reflect differential algorithmic visibility, user engagement preferences, or both, offering insights into the attention economy surrounding LCS. Fourth, documentation of representation patterns will quantify gaps in visibility for communities disproportionately affected by lung cancer but potentially underrepresented in online narratives. Importantly, interpretation of cross-platform differences will account for the inherent confounding between platform and content modality. Differences in stigma prevalence or accuracy between, for example, TikTok and Reddit may reflect the constraints and affordances of short-form video versus text-based discussion as much as community-level differences. The planned subgroup analysis comparing video versus static content will help disentangle modality effects from platform effects, though complete separation is not possible in an observational design. Comparison With Prior Work Existing research on lung cancer content in social media has been limited in scope. Alban et al [ ] analyzed YouTube videos related to lung cancer but did not assess stigma or decision-support features. Zhao et al [ ] examined LCS information on social media but focused on a single platform. Our multiplatform approach, theory-informed codebook, and integration of stigma assessment with engagement dynamics extend this work substantially. Translational Applications Findings will directly inform several ongoing initiatives. The characterization of dominant misconceptions, nihilistic narratives, and high-engagement misinformation will guide refinements to LungTalk, an evidence-based computer-tailored health communication and decision support tool for LCS. Real-world examples of stigmatizing content will be integrated into training modules for patient navigators and community health workers, enhancing their capacity to recognize and address digital influences on patient perceptions. The dual-coded, reliability-tested dataset will provide training examples that may inform future development of automated stigma detection tools. The labeled examples of explicit and implicit stigma in naturalistic social media contexts could serve as ground truth for supervised learning approaches. However, the feasibility of such applications depends on adequate representation of stigma-positive cases, class balance, and domain-specific model architecture considerations; this study is designed to characterize content patterns and is not intended to develop or validate automated detection systems. Finally, insights about platform-specific patterns will inform dissemination strategies for health systems and advocacy organizations seeking to reach eligible populations with accurate, stigma-informed messaging. Limitations Several anticipated limitations warrant acknowledgment. First, the study characterizes the publicly visible information environment—the content most likely encountered by individuals conducting typical health information searches—rather than

contexts could serve as ground truth for supervised learning approaches. However, the feasibility of such applications depends on adequate representation of stigma-positive cases, class balance, and domain-specific model architecture considerations; this study is designed to characterize content patterns and is not intended to develop or validate automated detection systems. Finally, insights about platform-specific patterns will inform dissemination strategies for health systems and advocacy organizations seeking to reach eligible populations with accurate, stigma-informed messaging. Limitations Several anticipated limitations warrant acknowledgment. First, the study characterizes the publicly visible information environment—the content most likely encountered by individuals conducting typical health information searches—rather than the totality of lung cancer discussions. This scope is intentional: publicly visible content shapes population-level exposure and is the appropriate target for public health communication interventions. Findings should not be generalized to private groups, direct messages, or content not surfaced by platform algorithms, which may differ substantially in tone and accuracy. Second, the cross-sectional design captures a specific temporal window in a rapidly evolving digital environment. We address this limitation through three strategies: (1) documenting search timestamps, platform versions, and procedural details to enable contextualization of findings within the specific data collection period; (2) focusing on structural patterns (eg, stigma prevalence differences across platforms, relationship between accuracy and engagement) that are likely to be more stable than specific content; and (3) providing methodological infrastructure (codebook, sampling framework, analytic code) that enables future replication to track temporal trends. We position this study as establishing a baseline against which future shifts can be measured rather than claiming to capture a permanent state. Third, representation coding is constrained by visual ambiguity; the conservative “not discernible” classification prevents inaccurate assumptions but may undercount certain demographic patterns. Fourth, the DOL scoring rubric is pragmatically derived for stakeholder mapping purposes and has not been psychometrically validated. Fifth, the inclusion of 7 platforms with substantially different content volumes may result in unequal sample sizes across platforms, particularly for Bluesky, which may yield fewer eligible posts. Should any platform produce fewer than the minimum posts needed for meaningful subgroup analysis, platform-specific findings will be interpreted descriptively rather than inferentially, and this will be noted transparently. Sixth, this study analyzes postlevel content and does not examine user comments or replies. Comment sections represent an important and often distinct dimension of public discourse, sentiment, and narrative framing—for example, stigmatizing or supportive responses to a patient’s personal narrative may substantially shape how that content is experienced by other viewers. Future research should examine comment-level content and sentiment to capture the full scope of public engagement with lung cancer and screening-related posts on social media. Despite these limitations, the systematic multiplatform design, dual-coding with reliability assessment, and theory-informed codebook collectively strengthen rigor. Conclusions This protocol establishes a rigorous, reproducible framework for characterizing the digital information environment surrounding lung cancer and LCS. By integrating clinical accuracy assessment, stigma and nihilism coding, decision-support evaluation, and engagement analysis within a theory-informed design, the study will generate foundational evidence to guide communication interventions, navigator training, and equitable dissemination strategies. The methodology provides a replicable framework for monitoring health information ecosystems and is adaptable to other cancer types, screening modalities, and emerging platforms. documents.title: USPSTF Tobacco smoking cessation in adults including pregnant persons

chunks.content: 1. Introduction Smoking continues to be the primary cause of preventable death and disease in the United States. It plays a significant role in the development of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, cardiovascular disease and at least 18 cancers[ ] [ , ]. Continued smoking after a cancer diagnosis is associated with increased cancer recurrence, increased mortality, increased adverse side effects from treatments, and a decrease in the effectiveness of first-line cancer treatments [ , ]. The growing awareness of the impact that quitting can have on a patient’s survival and long term quality of life has led to an initiative to include evidence-based tobacco treatment in cancer centers across the country [ – ] Best practice in tobacco treatment combines multiple intensive counseling (> 20 minutes) sessions with the provision and management of FDA-approved pharmacotherapy [ ]. Cancer patients face unique stressors and often require more intensive care than what is available through Quitlines [ , ] Traditionally, patients have been required to meet in person or over video with medical providers to receive prescription medication treatment for their smoking. The SARS-CoV-19 pandemic necessitated a shift away from this long-standing requirement, allowing these services to be offered by video or phone. [ ]. [ ] Tobacco treatment programs participating in the Cancer Center Cessation Initiative (C3I), supported by the U.S. National Cancer Institute Cancer Moonshot, reported increased utilization of services in response to the expansion of telehealth services [ , , , ]. Although most programs in the C3I experienced increased utilization, some patients continued to face barriers related to technology. For example, some programs who primarily offered group treatment still required patients to access services via a video platform. Disparities exist in both access to and comfort with video technologies among older adults, minority communities, rural communities, and individuals with public insurance [ , , ]. To our knowledge, there are only two studies that examined the effectiveness of tobacco treatment delivered by phone versus video with cancer patients. The first study used a pragmatic implementation design, giving cancer patients who smoke a choice between traditional Quitlines (N=39), in-person group treatment (N=14), or individual smartphone video telehealth (N=37) with remote CO testing [ ]. The median age was 58 and one-third were rural tobacco users. Importantly, the 1:1 telehealth patients rated the intervention most favorably, mainly due to the treatment’s convenience and high flexibility. Limitations include the fact that the study was not powered to detect differences in quit rates and there were low rates of follow-up, limiting conclusions around differential outcomes. The second study was a RCT conducted through ECOG-ACRIN comparing the effectiveness of sustained video telehealth counseling plus free nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) medication (Virtual Sustained Treatment) to referral to standard Quitline tobacco counseling (Enhanced Usual Care) in assisting recently diagnosed cancer patients to quit smoking [ ]. With a median age of 56 and a sample size of 306 patients, the telehealth group plus free NRT compared to enhanced usual care Quitline reported a significantly higher (P < .048) self-reported 7-day point prevalence abstinence at 3 months. Most studies to date that examined remote smoking cessation treatment did not involve patients with cancer. An RCT study comparing phone counseling, which was delivered to patients in their homes, versus video counseling, which was integrated into primary care clinics, where patients needed to travel to the clinic, found no significant difference in biochemically verified 7-day point prevalence at 12 months [ ]. While the counseling received was minimal, the primary significant finding was that more patients in the video arm had higher satisfaction and higher medication usage [ ]. Another study that delivered remote service to rural residents of Australia found no significant difference between phone counseling and real-time video counseling in achieving 7-day point prevalence abstinence at 4 months, although patients reported greater satisfaction with the video counseling [ ]. A pilot study of Korean-American women found that older women were less accepting of a video format compared to phone, but found no differences in 7-day point-prevalence at 3-months post-quit [ ]. Only one study, which involved women living with HIV, found that participants in the video arm were more likely to report long term abstinent at the 6-month follow-up than those in the phone arm [ ]. They also found that the video-call format was 30% less feasible than a phone call intervention for women in their 50’s and 60’s. Several limitations impacted the generalizability of these findings, including the small number of participants, the minimal amount of counseling delivered, and the high drop-out rate at the 6-month follow-up in the phone arm [ ]. A review of the literature asserted that no evidence of a difference for smoking cessation existed between phone and video counseling using the strictest definition of long-term follow-up defined as prolonged

the 6-month follow-up than those in the phone arm [ ]. They also found that the video-call format was 30% less feasible than a phone call intervention for women in their 50’s and 60’s. Several limitations impacted the generalizability of these findings, including the small number of participants, the minimal amount of counseling delivered, and the high drop-out rate at the 6-month follow-up in the phone arm [ ]. A review of the literature asserted that no evidence of a difference for smoking cessation existed between phone and video counseling using the strictest definition of long-term follow-up defined as prolonged abstinence at 3 months. [ ]. Given the likelihood that relaxing requirements for establishing patient care through tele-health has increased access to tobacco treatment and the lack of evidence supporting a significant difference in effectiveness between phone and video modalities, the aim of this analysis is to examine differences in abstinence between patients who established care via real-time video intake consultations versus real-time phone intake consultations during the SARS-COV-19 pandemic at MD Anderson’s TRTP. All initial intake visits were conducted based on patients’ preference for either telephone or video. The vast majority of follow-up contacts were conducted by phone. The data were gathered from 5/1/2020 through 4/30/2021. Before March 2020, most patients at MD Anderson established care in person. In 2019, we began testing a Zoom real-time video application (Zoom Video Communications, Inc., San Jose, CA, USA) for conducting the initial consultation to eliminate barriers for patients who found travel to our clinic difficult. In mid-March, all in-person services were discontinued. Texas issued a telemedicine emergency rule March 14, 2020, suspending occupation code 111.005 (a)-(b) and title 22, chapter 174–6 (a) (2)-(3) thereby allowing medical professionals to establish physician-patient relationships, diagnose, order tests, and prescribe via phone and video. This presented an opportunity for a real-world examination of which modalities patients preferred and the corresponding outcomes. 2. Methods MD Anderson Cancer Center’s Tobacco Research and Treatment Program (TRTP) was formed in 2006 with the primary mission to directly address the problem of continued tobacco use despite a diagnosis of cancer, and to expand the empirical basis for advancing the treatment of tobacco dependence among cancer patients and the general population. The TRTP operates as a center of clinical excellence and has continuously served patients, employees, and their family members since its inception, while also conducting extramurally funded clinical research with patients with cancer and community volunteers [ ]. 2.1 Patient recruitment A total of 4,689 potential patients were identified. Patients who were proactively identified in the electronic health record as currently using tobacco or having recently quit made up most of the referrals (3,931; 83%). The next largest source of referrals came from provider referrals within MD Anderson (758; 16%). Patients received a text message with brief program information and a more detailed message through their patient portal explaining the many benefits of quitting smoking for cancer patients. Tobacco treatment specialists trained in motivational interviewing made at least four initial calls to attempt to engage patients. Patients not reached were sent self-help materials, information on how to contact our program, and information related to the benefits of quitting. One final attempt to reach them by phone was made three months after the initial attempt. 2.2 Clinical Care and Follow-Up The program offers three levels of intervention. The most comprehensive program (Level 3, in which 995 unique patients participated) provides integrated counseling and medication management. An additional 153 patients received a motivational counseling call from an experienced clinician. A motivational interaction, self-help materials, and a follow-up call (level 2) were provided to 1,421 patients. Self-help materials and a follow-up call (Level-1) were provided to 1,458 patients. Comprehensive treatment (Level 3) involved consulting with both a counselor and medical provider to support the provision of fully integrated, evidence-based care [ ]. The initial consultation (typically 45 minutes to one hour) was followed by 6–8 follow-up (typically 30 minutes) counseling sessions and a medication check with their medical provider three weeks into treatment. The sessions were flexible in number and type to meet the needs of the patient. Since the program’s inception, most follow-up appointments (counseling follow-up, medication checks, and long-term follow-up with support staff) have been conducted by phone. A pilot project in 2019 utilizing Zoom for the initial consultation was initiated to extend care to patients in their homes. Although most patients were still seen in person, we wanted to extend the option of completing the initial consultation from home for patients who found travel difficult or simply preferred it. Support staff provided check-ins prior to the appointment to ensure patients could use the ZOOM platform. Our experience with the Zoom pilot and the telemedicine emergency rule allowed us to transition seamlessly to 100% remote service in the middle of March

Although most patients were still seen in person, we wanted to extend the option of completing the initial consultation from home for patients who found travel difficult or simply preferred it. Support staff provided check-ins prior to the appointment to ensure patients could use the ZOOM platform. Our experience with the Zoom pilot and the telemedicine emergency rule allowed us to transition seamlessly to 100% remote service in the middle of March 2020. For the entirety of the public health emergency patients have been given the option of establishing care via real-time video (Zoom) or by phone. The latitude to offer either phone or video provided information on preferences of several groups. For the initial consultation, patients self-selected their preferred method of establishing care. 2.3 Statistical Analysis In this study, we employed bivariate statistics and logistic regression models to analyze the data collected from the TRTP during the SARS-COV-19 pandemic. The primary comparisons were made between patients who established care via phone consultations and those who opted for video consultations. For group comparisons, we used chi-square tests to analyze categorical variables and independent t-tests for continuous outcomes. To analyze the outcomes related to abstinence from smoking at three different time points (3, 6, and 9 months), we used logistic regression with models adjusted for age, gender, ethnicity/race, and the number of sessions attended. The logistic regression was conducted using Stata version 18, and we used a two-sided p-value of 0.05 for statistical significance. 3. Results Patients smoked an average of 15 cigarettes per day for over 34 years. The most common cancer diagnoses were abdominal cancer, lung cancer, head and neck cancers, and breast cancer. Approximately 45% of our patients met criteria for one or more comorbid psychiatric diagnoses, with approximately 40% meeting criteria for more than one disorder. The descriptive statistics are summarized in . The gender distribution was similar between the phone (52.2% female) and video (55.2% female) consultation groups, with no statistically significant difference (p = 0.420). However, a significant difference was observed in race distribution between the two groups (p = 0.028). As shown in , participants in the phone group were more likely to be White (78.8%) compared to the video group (75.7%), while the video group had a higher percentage of patients categorized as other race (12.7%) compared to the phone group (7.1%). Additionally, there was a significant difference in age distribution between the groups (p = 0.001). Patients in the video group tended to be younger, with a higher percentage in the 18–34 (2.6%) and 35–49 (22.4%) age categories compared to the phone group. People who were 65 years and up were more likely to use the phone. The average number of sessions attended by patients in the phone group was significantly higher (mean = 7.7, SD = 4.1) than in the video group (mean = 6.8, SD = 3.7) (p = 0.005). The degree to which this difference is clinically meaningful since both groups received relatively high levels of tobacco treatment is unclear. and show the utilization rates and the number of sessions by consultation modality, with chi-square test results indicating significant differences. and illustrate the distribution of patients by age and gender across different consultation modalities, with significant differences identified through chi-square tests. presents the abstinence rates by group, outcome, and time-point for self-reported 7-day point prevalence abstinence at the 3-month (End of Treatment-EOT), 6-month, and 9-month follow-ups. In the respondent-only rates, at the 3-month (EOT) follow-up, 41.19% (201 out of 488) of the phone group reported abstinence compared to 44.20% (122 out of 276) of the video group. At the 6-month follow-up, 46.63% (180 out of 386) of the phone group reported abstinence compared to 43.72% (94 out of 215) of the video group. At the 9-month follow-up, 37.50% (144 out of 384) of the phone group reported abstinence compared to 37.85% (81 out of 214) of the video group. In the intention-to-treat analysis, at the 3-month (EOT) follow-up, 36.71% (187 out of 504) of the phone group reported abstinence compared to 41.55% (118 out of 284) of the video group. At the 6-month follow-up, 33.53% (169 out of 504) of the phone group reported abstinence compared to 32.39% (92 out of 284) of the video group. At the 9-month follow-up, 31.55% (159 out of 504) of the phone group reported abstinence compared to 33.45% (95 out of 284) of the video group. None of these bivariate comparisons were significant. At the 9-month follow-up, 31.55% (159 out of 504) of the phone group reported abstinence compared to 33.45% (95 out of 284) of the video group. None of these bivariate comparisons were significant. The logistic regression models ( ), adjusted for age, gender, ethnicity/race, and the number of sessions, showed no significant differences in abstinence outcomes at 3, 6, and 9 months between the phone and video consultation groups. As the 3 months odds ratio (OR) of abstinence between phone and video was 1.11 (95% CI: 0.80–1.54, p = 0.525). At 6 months, the OR was 0.88 (95% CI: 0.62–1.26, p = 0.482). At 9 months, the OR was 1.03 (95% CI: 0.73–1.45, p = 0.879). In the intention-to-treat analysis, the results were similar. At 3 months, the OR for abstinence was 1.14 (95% CI: 0.84–1.56, p = 0.394). At 6 months, the OR was 0.95 (95% CI: 0.69–1.30, p = 0.742). At 9 months, the OR was 1.03 (95% CI: 0.75–1.43, p = 0.841). This suggests that the modality of initial consultation (phone versus video) does not significantly impact abstinence outcomes, engagement, or patient demographics, except for some differences in age and race distributions. 4. Discussion The SARS-CoV-19 pandemic ushered in the relaxation of multiple requirements for the delivery of care across multiple disciplines. The most notable was the expansion of telehealth care delivered directly to patients in their homes. The most pressing concern was how much this change would affect the service’s quality and ultimately the outcomes for patients. Our analysis of data collected in a naturalistic design found no difference in abstinence for patients whose treatment was delivered completely over the phone vs. those who received their consultation via video and follow ups over the phone. There was also no meaningful clinical difference in the degree of engagement between groups as evidence but comparable number of sessions between the groups. Patients could select the initial consultation modality (phone or video). Almost all patients used the phone exclusively for follow ups, which was consistent with our practice prior to the pandemic. Older patients were more likely to request that all services be provided by phone, most likely due to ease of its use. This is consistent with studies of Medicare beneficiaries that found that older individuals had higher rates of audio only telehealth usage during the pandemic [ ]. Older patients interested in video may need support staff assistance and/or family member assistance to support the set up and use of this newer medium of communication. Our findings regarding the comparable efficacy of tobacco treatment delivered by phone exclusively vs video and phone are limited by the fact that this was not a randomly controlled trial. On the other hand, the naturalistic aspect of our data from a real-life setting offers a unique demonstration of what is possible to do, and the likely results. The complexity of factors affecting patients during the pandemic undoubtedly introduced additional variables that may have affected outcomes. Since our study ended in April of 2021, many patients have grown more comfortable with utilizing video formats. Our findings might not generalize to other geographical regions or to other less resourced cancer centers. Also, we only looked at telehealth for the initial consultation rather than the full course of treatment. Our follow-ups have always been conducted mostly by phone. Despite this, our findings are consistent with the congressionally mandated report of telehealth during the public health emergency that ended on May 11, 2023, which showed little change in quality, improved access, and slight increases of cost to the Medicare system [ ]. This conclusion was based on the review of services provided remotely across multiple disciplines and did not examine the difference between services delivered exclusively by phone vs video. Other reviews of telehealth found that in general telehealth exposure in primary care posed little risk to quality and may have improved care in the treatment of chronic disease management and preventative care such as tobacco counseling and medication intervention [ ]. These broader based reviews of the efficacy of telehealth during the pandemic further support reviews of tobacco treatment via phone which found no difference in the efficacy of phone-based vs video-based tobacco treatment [ ]. Perhaps the most important takeaway from the review of patient experiences during the pandemic is the fact that patients enjoyed expanded access to care without diminishing the quality of that care. This was true for our patients regardless of whether they established care via phone or via video. Establishment of care in our program included consultation with a physician or physician’s assistant and

[ ]. These broader based reviews of the efficacy of telehealth during the pandemic further support reviews of tobacco treatment via phone which found no difference in the efficacy of phone-based vs video-based tobacco treatment [ ]. Perhaps the most important takeaway from the review of patient experiences during the pandemic is the fact that patients enjoyed expanded access to care without diminishing the quality of that care. This was true for our patients regardless of whether they established care via phone or via video. Establishment of care in our program included consultation with a physician or physician’s assistant and the provision of tobacco treatment medications. While telehealth may not be preferable when a physical exam is required, our findings suggest phone and video telehealth are appropriate and effective for the treatment of tobacco use disorder. Our results do not diminish the preference many clinicians and patients may have for video visits over phone. When feasible, this modality more closely mirrors the in-person experience and has been shown to contribute to higher patients’ satisfaction [ ]. The concern relates to disparities which can result from limiting access to care through modalities that some groups find challenging or complex [ ]. Specifically, older adults, individuals with lower socioeconomic status and persons with severe mental health challenges may struggle to access needed care [ ]. The pandemic revealed the many benefits and potential difficulties inherent to the provision of remote care. Both clinicians and patients reported a desire for continued access after the public health emergency [ ]. The efficacy of tobacco treatment through telehealth is well established and the quality of both phone and video modalities for the provision of care has also been well established. Retaining clinicians’ ability to establish care for tobacco treatment whether by phone or video would ensure almost universal access to this essential medical service.

chunks.content: The integration of wearables in cardiac electrophysiology practice represents a unique scenario where technology adoption is outpacing clinical evidence, guidelines, and best practices. Consumers and patients are already widely using wearables capable of assessing cardiac rhythm, forcing clinicians to adapt in real time to this changing landscape. Today’s wearables vary widely in the signals and data they collect, ranging from those that use photoplethysmography (PPG) waveforms as surrogates for cardiac rhythm to single- and multilead electrocardiogram (ECG) recordings and multimodality data collection. Limited evidence from studies such as the Apple Heart Study, the Fitbit Heart Study, and the Huawei Heart Study, along with smaller studies in individual practices and health systems, has begun to shed light on the utility and limitations of these technologies, but many challenges and unknowns remain. Meanwhile, clinicians who have been early adopters of this technology have begun to recognize pitfalls in clinical utility. These include inconsistent and sometimes poor-quality tracings, an overwhelming influx of patient-generated data, a lack of unified data management systems, and an absence of well-established practice norms. These challenges highlight the need for robust data management systems and clear clinical practice guidance tailored to discrete clinical scenarios. Electrophysiology providers are especially well suited to take on this challenge, given their experience with medical-grade monitoring devices that have established algorithms for detection, verification, and response to arrhythmias. This white paper aimed to address these needs by compiling the insights and reflections of members of the Heart Rhythm Society Digital Health Committee who are navigating these complexities. Although we currently lack the data to formulate definitive recommendations, this document seeks to initiate a critical conversation within our field. By collectively examining these issues, we hope to take the necessary steps toward developing thoughtful, well-justified guidance for integrating wearables into our clinical practices. This effort is crucial as we strive to harness the potential of wearable technology to improve patient outcomes while managing its challenges in a clinically sound manner. In addition, there is a need for substantial guidance of patients in regard to the potential information a specific wearable and data transmission plans may offer in relation to individual clinical scenarios. Ideal data platform Although wearable devices have become increasingly popular among patients and consumers for health monitoring, their integration into clinical practice, particularly in cardiology, poses real challenges. Clinics often lack the infrastructure to efficiently process and integrate data from wearables into medical records. Despite these challenges, most health care providers who responded to a Heart Rhythm Society survey in 2020 had already recommended the use of a digital health device to facilitate management of atrial fibrillation (AF). This gap creates a disconnect between the potential of wearables for enhancing patient care and the current capabilities of health care systems to leverage these data effectively. The issues include difficulty in data ingestion, annotation, identification of relevant information, distinguishing important signals from irrelevant data, and generating concise reports for the medical record. Moreover, managing data from various sources is time consuming and not adequately supported by existing billing and reimbursement models, which sometimes makes the technology more burdensome than beneficial. From a patient perspective, the need to purchase and manage one’s own device has the potential to exacerbate existing health care disparities, particularly in patients with lower technological literacy. Addressing these challenges requires a well-engineered data platform encompassing several key features ( ). 1. Device-agnostic data ingestion engine: the system should be able to accept and process data from any wearable device, regardless of the manufacturer. 2. Automated system for identifying relevant signals: this includes machine learning algorithms capable of sifting through vast amounts of data to find clinically relevant information. The system needs to have good signal-to-noise optimization able to filter out irrelevant data while separating events detected by PPG, single-lead ECG, or relevant sensors owing to their different sensitivities and specificities. 3. Automated categorization of events by acuity: the system would need to prioritize data based on urgency so that clinicians can maximize efficiency of their work, addressing critical events or symptomatic events in a timely manner while allowing others to be addressed during routine care. Examples include AF alerts (need for anticoagulation, rapid ventricular rates) or heart failure events (increase in New York Heart Association III symptoms, need for diuretics). 4. Automated summary statistics and creation of standardized reports: summary reports will need to be generated and integrated into the electronic health record (EHR). Ideally, these reports would have a uniform structure to facilitate easy interpretation by a broad range of health care providers. 5. Intuitive dashboard for data display: an intuitive user interface should present data in an easily digestible format to reduce the cognitive load on clinicians. 6. Seamless EHR integration for various vendors: the system should incorporate features such as single sign-on; side-by-side data display; streamlined ordering and

New York Heart Association III symptoms, need for diuretics). 4. Automated summary statistics and creation of standardized reports: summary reports will need to be generated and integrated into the electronic health record (EHR). Ideally, these reports would have a uniform structure to facilitate easy interpretation by a broad range of health care providers. 5. Intuitive dashboard for data display: an intuitive user interface should present data in an easily digestible format to reduce the cognitive load on clinicians. 6. Seamless EHR integration for various vendors: the system should incorporate features such as single sign-on; side-by-side data display; streamlined ordering and billing processes; current medical problems, medications, and laboratories to facilitate clinical decision making; communication through patient portals; and an installation process that does not overburden information systems teams. 7. Overcoming health care disparities: the system should include open-source algorithms, a multilingual interface, and aids for individuals with visual and hearing impairment. 8. Addressing privacy concerns: incorporating data from consumer devices presents unique challenges compared with traditional health care-related data, including concerns over access to nonhealth mobile data. 9. Providing control to patients: patients should have the ability to link, unlink, and add additional devices as they change and upgrade. 10. Patient education and control: easily digestible information on patient-centric health metrics along with education tools. 11. Managing and resolving problems related to connectivity and data transfer: if problems with the platform or patient-specific data transfer occur, easy and fast problem solving is needed to not lose relevant information. Data integration with EHR and clinical workflow Once developed, the well-engineered platform requires integration into a workflow that facilitates patient care. Such a workflow would start with a decision between a provider and a patient to initiate monitoring with a wearable device. An order would be placed by the provider that signals to the ingestion engine that a patient may start transmitting data. The patient then agrees to send that data and links their device (or devices) to that ingestion engine. After the connection is made, tracings or other discrete data points flow to the ingestion and processing platform. The technology to make these connections exists, but specific applications to enable the ingestion of all types of wearable data require development. This initial ingestion likely involves preprocessing using machine learning models to reduce the rates of inconclusive tracings and improve diagnostic accuracy. Those preprocessed results would then pass into the second part of the platform to be displayed, cataloged, and prioritized for evaluation by clinical staff at the health care organization caring for the patient. Order generation is a key function in this processing portion of the platform. Creation of an order allows 2 key functions: (1) the result can be filed into the health care organizations’ medical record, allowing that result to be viewed across the organization, and (2) order placement facilitates billing. The clinical staff—likely nurses or certified technicians—review those preprocessed, prioritized tracings, creating a preliminary result. The preliminary results are finalized by attending physicians, billing is performed, the result is stored in EHR and the ingestion/processing platform, and the result is sent to the patient via the health care organization’s patient portal. This workflow overlaps in many ways with those already in place for ambulatory monitors—typically processed in ECG laboratories/heart stations—and remote monitoring for implanted devices. Therefore, the location of this clinical evaluation may vary between health care organizations. Current state Current commercial platforms are being developed to meet these requirements, but there is no dominant system that has been integrated at scale. Based on provider surveys, perceived barriers to adoption include limited awareness of billing codes available for interpretation of device-recorded ECGs, skepticism and uncertainty regarding the accuracy of the automated diagnoses from wearable devices, lack of understanding of the advanced data science techniques that lead to and improve those diagnoses, uncertainty regarding clinical utility, and data privacy concerns as we enter into a patient-centric rather than a provider-centric model for data. , Obtaining and installing third-party software to help manage patient-generated data come with an expense. Therefore, the onus is on vendors to demonstrate how the system can overcome existing barriers and lead to improved clinical outcomes. However, the current system that often relies on individual providers reviewing tracings sent through patient portals without preprocessing or mechanisms for formalizing interpretations and billing is not sustainable. Clinical scenarios for wearable monitor use in clinical practice Primary AF screening AF is an important and common cardiovascular disease, and oral anticoagulation (OAC) constitutes an effective, accepted treatment to prevent stroke in patients at high risk of thromboembolic events. The given incidence of new AF , , in the general population can vary owing to factors such as the monitoring modality, the population studied, the sensitivity of the monitoring method, and the duration of follow-up ( ). What is the monitoring going to achieve? Monitoring will detect subclinical or asymptomatic AF episodes, allowing for the initiation of guideline-directed anticoagulation and AF-directed therapies to prevent complications such as stroke, heart failure, and cognitive decline. Potential approach Screening modalities that accurately identify patients at high risk of developing AF are likely to be the most clinically relevant and cost-effective. Several risk scores for predicting incident AF have been reported, but most have not been replicated in large, diverse cohorts with various ethnicities. The CHARGE-AF risk score, which incorporates factors such as age, race, height, weight, blood pressure, smoking status, antihypertensive medication use, diabetes, and history of myocardial infarction and heart failure, has been tested on a large number of individuals across different ancestries, providing greater generalizability than other risk scores for AF prediction. These predictive models can be used to select high-risk individuals for trials of primary prevention of AF or intensive monitoring for AF detection and help select candidates for more aggressive risk factor modification. Promising screening techniques include machine learning based models to predict the development of AF based on sinus ECGs. Potential pitfalls Developments in wearable technologies allow for more extended intensive monitoring. These advancements frequently lead to the detection of more paroxysmal AF episodes with a shorter duration, potentially representing a lower AF burden and a more benign prognosis. The US Preventive Services Task Force and other professional societies believe that there is insufficient evidence to determine whether systematic ECG screening for AF will do more good than harm and recommend adequately powered randomized clinical trials to resolve this issue. Despite the potential benefits of screening for AF, appropriate care pathways for confirming the diagnosis and potential initiating guideline-directed treatment in individuals with positive findings have not been established. Wrist-based wearables use PPG sensors to measure pulse and process data frequently and passively during wear time. Although smartwatches continuously sample the PPG signal, most PPG-based algorithms only analyze periods when the user is not active. , Therefore, effective screening is reliant on opportunistic detection over long periods of wear time, including during sleep. When worn consistently, wearables have demonstrated the capacity to detect most clinically relevant episodes of AF (ie, AF episode duration >6 minutes). Although PPG-based approaches for AF detection are comparable with ECG-based approaches for AF diagnosis when there is adequate signal quality, further testing might be required to confirm AF. Secondary AF Beyond clinical AF, digital health holds promise in patients with secondary, or “triggered- induced” AF. These include patients who have new-onset AF in the context of postoperative cardiac surgery, acute pulmonary disease, acute coronary syndromes, or sepsis. However, some patients have abnormal substrate and are at risk of future AF episodes, and their long-term need for anticoagulation is unclear. Recent data show that continuous cardiac monitoring after cardiac surgery identifies previously unrecognized AF compared with usual care. Digital wearables might provide better insight to patients who would benefit from long-term anticoagulation and rhythm control and help avoid unnecessary bleeding risk for others. What is the monitoring going to achieve? Current multisociety guidelines provide limited guidance for management in this subset of patients, given that the net clinical benefit for anticoagulation after secondary AF has not been established. Wearable-based monitoring in this population can inform clinicians as to whether AF is truly provoked or whether it has unmasked substrate for AF that needs to be addressed, which may include anticoagulation or rhythm control. Potential approach A patient-tailored approach can optimize the positive and negative predictive value of wearable monitoring. For instance, in patients after cardiac surgery, PPG-based continuous rhythm monitoring may be ideal given the high likelihood of recurrent AF episodes. Meanwhile, in patients with sepsis and normal cardiac substrate, spot-check monitoring with ECG-based devices can serve as a high-specificity approach and reduce false positives. Those patients who are confirmed to have further AF episodes can then be evaluated for anticoagulation and rhythm control. Potential pitfalls Although wearable devices have been evaluated in prediagnostic AF screening capacities, their true performance in postoperative patients or patients with provoked AF is not known. Patients with recent cardiac surgery may be at higher risk of atrial ectopy, which may be falsely detected as AF. There is also limited

high likelihood of recurrent AF episodes. Meanwhile, in patients with sepsis and normal cardiac substrate, spot-check monitoring with ECG-based devices can serve as a high-specificity approach and reduce false positives. Those patients who are confirmed to have further AF episodes can then be evaluated for anticoagulation and rhythm control. Potential pitfalls Although wearable devices have been evaluated in prediagnostic AF screening capacities, their true performance in postoperative patients or patients with provoked AF is not known. Patients with recent cardiac surgery may be at higher risk of atrial ectopy, which may be falsely detected as AF. There is also limited knowledge on how long after an inciting event to still consider an AF episode trigger induced. Acknowledging these limitations is important for effective shared decision making when treating such patients. Patients at high risk of stroke or recurrent stroke The relationship between AF and ischemic stroke has long been established, with clinically detected AF increasing the risk of stroke more than 5-fold. In many patients, AF may be asymptomatic, with up to 20% of patients presenting with stroke as the first clinical manifestation of previously undiagnosed AF. As such, it has been proposed that rhythm monitoring may be a valuable tool for identifying AF in patients who would benefit from stroke prevention therapies, such as those at high objective risk of stroke or those who previously experienced an embolic stroke of unknown source. , , In these groups of patients at risk of adverse AF-associated outcomes, prolonged cardiac rhythm monitoring with wearable devices may improve the diagnostic yield by detecting actionable AF. What is the monitoring going to achieve? The goal of prolonged rhythm monitoring is the detection of actionable episodes of AF. In effect, the detection of occult AF would allow the consideration of stroke prevention therapies with the goal of reducing the incidence of AF-associated strokes, which are associated with greater long-term disability and a significantly higher mortality than non-AF-associated strokes. , , Potential approach AF detection is proportionate to the duration and intensity of arrhythmia monitoring, with intermittent rhythm monitors missing a substantial proportion of AF episodes. As a result, the ideal device for AF detection in high-risk individuals is a noninvasive device capable of real-time continuous rhythm monitoring over a prolonged duration of follow-up. Ideally, this should occur passively, meaning that the wearer is not required to perform an action to trigger the rhythm assessment (eg, rhythm strip activation). In this regard, an Internet-enabled smartwatch equipped with a PPG sensor and linked to real-time advanced rhythm analysis offers the best balance of convenience, continuous observation, and immediate notification. In individuals at high risk of AF, the detection of AF would be considered actionable and would suggest the need for OAC initiation for stroke prevention. In this circumstance, the relative balance of high pretest probability (eg, high risk of AF) would offset the relative inaccuracy of the PPG sensor, limiting the rate of false-positive detections necessitating ECG confirmation. Potential risks and pitfalls There are 2 concerns regarding the use of wearable cardiac monitors for AF detection and initiation of stroke prevention therapy. First, the current PPG-enabled devices are limited by a relatively low accuracy (∼95%), which is in part caused by a high proportion of uninterpretable recordings (eg, during exercise) and missed diagnosis owing to a lack of use (eg, patients not wearing the devices during sleep). Second, we do not yet know the threshold for clinically relevant AF episode duration or burden on wearable devices. Within the cardiac implantable device literature, there is debate regarding the biological relevance of shorter episodes of AF detected by continuous monitoring. Although these short AF episodes have been temporally linked to ischemic stroke events, the association is strongest for those episodes lasting longer than 24 hours. As such, it may be reasonable to consider an alternate approach of daily ECG rhythm strip assessment in lieu of continuous smartphone monitoring, at least until the accuracy of PPG monitoring improves. Research priorities and evidence gaps The major areas in need of research are (1) determination of the relationship between wearable device-detected AF and clinical outcomes (eg, stroke); (2) the relationship between AF episode duration (or AF burden over a certain period of time) and stroke risk, ideally with determination of a minimum duration of AF that increases the risk of stroke; (3) a randomized trial comparing OAC therapy for wearable detected AF; and (4) a pill-in-the-pocket OAC therapy for wearable detected AF (currently being tested in the REACT trial). Wearable monitors were initially validated to serve as prediagnostic tools for new AF via irregular pulse notifications from PPG. , However, these tools can play a potent role in prevalent AF management from identifying lifestyle factors and triggers to informing medical or

time) and stroke risk, ideally with determination of a minimum duration of AF that increases the risk of stroke; (3) a randomized trial comparing OAC therapy for wearable detected AF; and (4) a pill-in-the-pocket OAC therapy for wearable detected AF (currently being tested in the REACT trial). Monitoring of known AF What is the monitoring going to achieve? Wearable monitors were initially validated to serve as prediagnostic tools for new AF via irregular pulse notifications from PPG. , However, these tools can play a potent role in prevalent AF management from identifying lifestyle factors and triggers to informing medical or procedural intervention. They may also be valid tools for postintervention rhythm monitoring and have the potential for directing treatment options in this cohort during the early and late follow-up period. Multiple lifestyle factors have known associations with AF severity and symptomatology. For many patients, the convergence of wearable monitoring with other digital technologies may have an important role in reducing morbidity and mortality. Hypertension is one of the most frequently attributed risk factors for developing AF, and patients who self-monitor blood pressure to titrate antihypertensives were shown to achieve better blood pressure control than those assigned to usual care. Improved glycemic control may also help reduce the risk of AF recurrence ; this can be facilitated by application-based diabetes management. Large prospective studies have demonstrated that, in individuals with obesity, weight loss can significantly reduce AF burden and symptomatology. , Sleep disordered breathing and obstructive sleep apnea are associated with AF severity and AF-associated mortality, and continuous positive airway pressure therapy with improved sleep may ameliorate these risks. , In a randomized controlled trial with a series of n-of-1 participants, alcohol intake was associated with AF episodes and higher AF burden. Although wearable monitors have long recorded and summarized heart rate trends during wear periods, some devices now combine PPG-based AF detection to also provide estimates of daily AF burden. Monitoring these trends can provide real-time feedback to both patients and clinicians on lifestyle effects and inform appropriate interventions. Potential approach For clinicians seeking to use information from wearable monitors to guide patient management, wearable monitors can now demonstrate hour- and day-level heart rate trends, allow for point-of-care ECG measurements, and report trends in AF burden before and after clinical intervention. In patients with low-burden AF or chronic persistent/permanent AF on rate control alone, even simple wearable monitors can provide sufficient PPG-based heart rate trends to ensure that patients are achieving goal heart rate parameters. In patients with symptomatic AF, including those with previous catheter ablation or on antiarrhythmic therapy, symptom-triggered ECG recordings sent to a clinician can be useful in separating AF episodes from other arrhythmias or nonarrhythmic symptoms. For asymptomatic patients, maximizing wear time with the AF detection features enabled on wearable monitors can facilitate the detection of AF recurrence. Finally, more sophisticated consumer monitors can provide multilead ECGs, and these may be helpful in attempting to localize arrhythmias that are clearly not AF. Potential pitfalls When using wearable monitors for AF management, it is important to inform patients that AF detection is not enabled by default and must be turned on. As noted earlier, AF detection also relies on wear time, including during sleep, and irregular rhythms during activity periods may go undetected. For some wearables, ECGs must be obtained during a perceived episode and therefore may not be well suited for passive monitoring. Signal quality and interpretation algorithms also vary between devices, and there have not been head-to-head studies to compare their performance. Based on these issues, the decision on the specificities of data recorded by an individual wearable must be included in the device selection process. Research priorities and evidence gaps Prospective studies are needed to validate these and other potential features of wearable monitors in AF management, including titration of rate control, evaluation of AF episode duration and burden on rhythm control, and identification of potential adverse effects of medications. QT measurements from wearable monitors are not validated and should not be used as a proxy for true 12-lead ECG measurements. Symptom-rhythm correlation or undifferentiated arrhythmias believed to be low risk What is the monitoring going to achieve? Perhaps one of the most important use cases for wearables is in those patients who have intermittent palpitations but are either unwilling or unable (ie, owing to skin sensitivities) to use patch-based prescribed or implantable devices. In these patients, the use of direct-to-consumer wearables can provide a patient-centric approach to the acquisition of heart rate and ECG tracings that can guide diagnosis. A few subgroups of patients are ideally suited to this type of diagnostic approach: (1) patients with a high clinical index of suspicion for arrhythmia but infrequent symptoms and (2) patients with a low clinical index of suspicion for arrhythmia. In both patient groups,

use cases for wearables is in those patients who have intermittent palpitations but are either unwilling or unable (ie, owing to skin sensitivities) to use patch-based prescribed or implantable devices. In these patients, the use of direct-to-consumer wearables can provide a patient-centric approach to the acquisition of heart rate and ECG tracings that can guide diagnosis. A few subgroups of patients are ideally suited to this type of diagnostic approach: (1) patients with a high clinical index of suspicion for arrhythmia but infrequent symptoms and (2) patients with a low clinical index of suspicion for arrhythmia. In both patient groups, the ability to acquire heart rate and/or ECG tracings at the time of the event is important for having diagnostic certainty moving forward. In these cases, the diagnostic goal is to document symptom-rhythm correlation, which can then help guide therapy. These tracings can help support medical decision making and determine whether reassurance, medication, or referral for invasive diagnostics and treatment is most appropriate. Potential approach Shared decision making between the physician and patient when deciding on appropriate device selection is ideal. The role of the provider is to understand exactly what data are needed for diagnostic accuracy: does the device have to provide a heart rate or an ECG? Will a single lead suffice or are multiple leads indicated for diagnosis? What is the patient able to reasonably accomplish, both physically and financially? Addressing these questions forwardly, coupled with understanding the patient’s level of digital literacy before device acquisition, empowers the patient to purchase the most appropriate device to address the clinical question. Once data have been acquired, the next step is interpreting and sharing the data. Edge-based computing using proprietary algorithms can provide the patient with a relatively instantaneous interpretation of the data. Certain technologies have a subscription model that patients can opt in to that provides a physician overread for data. However, ensuring capture and presentation of the relevant data that are used in medical decision making remains an important hurdle that needs to be addressed. Although institutions may have local solutions to support this interoperability, this is not yet broadly available and will be an important step in implementing these technologies. Potential pitfalls Although the raw data gathered from these devices are often of high quality, the current algorithms have opportunities for improvement across a broader patient age range and more varied arrhythmia detections. In addition, appropriate signal quality is needed to make diagnostic decisions. Limitations of wearables Consumer-grade wearable devices are not currently recommended for the diagnosis of suspected arrhythmic syncope with high suspicion of either a tachy- or bradyarrhythmia. For high-risk syncope (eg, unheralded syncope, syncope during exercise, syncope in the setting of known infranodal conduction disease, or syncope during high-risk activities including driving and operating heavy machinery), those cases requiring symptom-rhythm correlation after appropriate clinical cardiovascular evaluation are best suited for continuous implantable or prescription-grade monitoring. Owing to the potential consequences of not capturing the heart rhythm associated with these high-risk events (including but not limited to recurrent syncope, injury, or death), wearables are not recommended at this time given the required element of patient willingness and compliance with wearing and reporting important findings documented by a consumer-grade device. Medical-grade continuous monitoring is better suited to these situations, including ECG patch monitors, mobile cardiac telemetry, or implantable loop recorders, depending on the frequency of symptoms and specific clinical scenario. Each of these prescription or implantable options allows for direct feedback to the prescribing provider, minimizing the risk of missing an important rhythm finding requiring further treatment including cardiac pacemaker or transvenous defibrillator implantation. One important consideration of wearable technology relates to the validity of the data that are returned, which includes an understanding that many of the clinical measures returned by wearables are the product of black-box computer algorithms applied to noisy raw data from sensors. For example, the PPG sensor measures patterns of light absorption across the skin, from which clinical metrics such as oxygen saturation, pulse rate and rhythm, or blood pressure are derived. The specific algorithms used in this process, whether well validated or not, are not directly available at the time of interpretation, nor are the raw data they process in deriving the clinical measure. The result is that many clinical measures reported by wearables carry a level of uncertainty that must be addressed if and when this information is reported back to the patient. A computer interpretation of an ECG tracing might falsely indicate AF owing to noise, but a clinician can directly inspect the raw tracing to confirm or refute the diagnosis. In contrast, a wearable PPG sensor can falsely indicate AF owing to motion artifact, but there is no mechanism for the clinician to review the raw data to make an equivalent assessment. In other words, the
