Figure shows the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 flowchart detailing the search and selection process. Characteristics of the included studies A total of 27 RCTs, involving 2314 participants (1192 in intervention groups and 1122 in control groups), were included in the meta-analysis. They were published between 2012 and 2025. Of the included studies, 11 trials enrolled patients with T2DM and comorbid MCI, while the remaining 16 trials involved diabetic patients without cognitive impairment. The design and detailed participant characteristics of the included studies are summarized in Table . Quality assessment The quality assessment results of the 27 included studies showed that 6 studies (22.2%) reported low risk, 15 studies (59.3%) reported some concerns, and 5 studies (18.5%) reported high risk. Twenty-two studies (81.5%) explicitly reported methods for random sequence generation. No deviations from intended interventions or bias due to missing outcome data were identified in any of the studies. Two studies (7.4%) clearly reported the bias in outcome assessment, and 17 studies (66.7%) reported some concerns, while the remaining 7 studies (25.9%) provided clear documentation. All studies demonstrated no selective reporting bias. Overall, the included studies were classified as a moderate risk of bias, with the evidence quality rated as moderate to high (Fig. ). Global cognitive function Combined effect sizes Twenty-one studies assessed changes in global cognitive function after interventions. To avoid double-counting participants from studies that used multiple tools, only one outcome per study was included in the primary meta-analysis. Where available, the MoCA score was preferentially selected due to its greater sensitivity compared to MMSE [ ]. For this outcome, a total of 1768 participants were included in the analysis, with 888 in the intervention group and 880 in the control group. As shown in Fig. , lifestyle interventions demonstrated a significant improvement in global cognitive function compared to usual care ( SMD = 1.66, 95% CI : 1.07 to 2.25, P < 0.001). Subgroup analysis This study further conducted exploratory subgroup analysis based on different measurement tools, countries, intervention types, intervention duration, and baseline MCI status. Since Renru Z (2022) was the only study that used 3MSE for outcome assessment and the only one conducted in Australia, it was excluded from the subgroup analysis by measurement tool and country. In addition, Asmaa E.S. (2024) was the only study conducted in Egypt, so it was excluded from the subgroup analysis by country. As shown in Table , statistically significant improvements in global cognitive function were observed in most subgroups of T2DM patients. Two exceptions were interventions conducted in Thailand (2 studies, SMD = 1.51, 95% CI : −2.80 to 5.82, P = 0.492) and those with a duration of ≥ 12 months (6 studies, SMD = 0.41, 95% CI : −0.51 to 1.32, P = 0.386), where the effects did not reach statistical significance. The forest plots of each subgroup analysis are shown in Figure S1. Sensitivity analysis and publication bias Sensitivity analysis demonstrated the stability of the pooled estimate for global cognitive function, as the overall conclusion remained unchanged and statistically significant. The result of the sensitivity analysis is shown in Figure S2. Visual inspection of the funnel plot did not reveal substantial asymmetry, suggesting a low likelihood of major publication bias. This was supported quantitatively by Egger’s regression test, which indicated no statistically significant evidence of publication bias ( P = 0.414). The funnel plot is shown in Figure S3. Executive function Combined effect sizes Eight studies assessed changes in executive function after interventions. For this outcome, a total of 827 participants were included in the analysis, with 417 in the intervention group and 410 in the control group. As shown in Figure S4, the meta-analysis did not demonstrate a statistically significant benefit of lifestyle interventions on executive function compared to usual care among T2DM patients ( SMD = −2.95, 95% CI : −8.79 to 2.89, P = 0.322). Subgroup analysis This study further conducted exploratory subgroup analysis based on different countries, intervention types, intervention duration, and baseline MCI status. Since Nicole J J (2022) was the only study on dietary intervention, it was excluded from the subgroup analysis based on intervention type. As shown in Table S3, three studies conducted in Asia ( SMD = −17.27, 95% CI : −30.13 to −4.41, P = 0.008) and three studies involving diabetic patients with combined MCI ( SMD = −17.27, 95% CI : −30.13 to −4.41, P = 0.008) had statistically significant improvements in executive function. The forest plots of each subgroup analysis are shown in Figure S5. The forest plots of each subgroup analysis are shown in Figure S5. Sensitivity analysis and Publication bias Sensitivity analysis demonstrated the stability of the pooled estimate for global cognitive function, as the overall conclusion remained unchanged and statistically significant. The result of the sensitivity analysis is shown in Figure S6. Visual inspection of the funnel plot did not reveal substantial asymmetry, suggesting a low likelihood of major publication bias. This was supported quantitatively by Egger’s regression test, which indicated no statistically significant evidence of publication bias ( P = 0.377). The funnel plot of publication bias is shown in Figure S7. Memory Combined effect sizes Six studies assessed changes in memory after interventions. For this outcome, a total of 464 participants were included in the analysis, with 238 in the intervention group and 226 in the control group. The pooled analysis found no statistically significant effect of lifestyle interventions on memory compared to usual care among T2DM patients ( SMD = −0.05, 95% CI : −0.42 to 0.33, P = 0.809). The forest plot is shown in Figure S8. Subgroup analysis Exploratory subgroup analyses were performed for memory outcomes based on different countries, intervention types, intervention duration, and baseline MCI status. Since Erin M. S (2018) was the only study conducted in America, and Nicole J.J. (2022) was the only study on dietary intervention, they were excluded from the subgroup analysis by country and intervention type. As detailed in Table S3, none of the subgroup analyses showed a statistically significant effect on memory of T2DM patients. The forest plots of each subgroup analysis are shown in Figure S9. Sensitivity analysis and Publication bias Sensitivity analysis indicated that t the overall finding for memory was robust, as the conclusion of no statistically significant benefit remained unchanged. The result of the sensitivity analysis is shown in Figure S10. Visual inspection of the funnel plot revealed no obvious asymmetry, indicating a low risk of publication bias. The quantitative evaluation through Egger’s regression test further confirmed that there was no significant publication bias ( P = 0.797). The funnel plot of publication bias is shown in Figure S11. Discussion The objective of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to summarize the available evidence on the effects of lifestyle interventions on cognitive function in patients with T2DM. A total of 27 studies met the inclusion criteria and were analyzed to assess the effects of lifestyle interventions on global cognitive function, executive function, and memory. Effects of lifestyle interventions on global cognitive function This meta-analysis found that lifestyle interventions were associated with a significant improvement in global cognitive function compared to usual care, with an effect size that was positive but should be interpreted cautiously. This finding is consistent with recent meta-analyses reporting cognitive benefits from exercise interventions in T2DM, including multi-component programs [ ] and interventions targeting elderly patients [ , ]. Our study adds to prior research by demonstrating that lifestyle interventions may improve global cognitive function in patients with T2DM, highlighting their value beyond glycemic control. The mechanisms underlying these effects remain incompletely understood, but evidence points to several primary neurobiological pathways. Exercise is a fundamental component of these interventions. It promotes neurogenesis and facilitates synaptic plasticity. These beneficial effects are potentially mediated through the upregulation of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and the amelioration of central insulin resistance, and the reduction of systemic inflammation [ , ]. Recent research also underscores the importance of the muscle-brain axis. In this pathway, myokines such as irisin and lactate act alongside neurotrophic factors to maintain neural homeostasis [ ]. However, the large effect size for global cognitive function needs careful consideration. While it suggests a potential benefit of lifestyle interventions, several methodological factors may explain such estimates. First, significant heterogeneity was present in these studies, indicating that the true effect likely varies across studies. Second, although MMSE and MoCA are validated tools for global cognition, differences in sensitivity and specific subdomains assessed may contribute to effect size variability. Third, the potential for small-study effects exists, where smaller studies with more positive results are more likely to be published. Finally, when control groups receive minimal contact or support, the contrast with structured lifestyle interventions may be amplified. Exploratory subgroup analyses suggested that the effect of lifestyle interventions on global cognitive function may vary by intervention duration. MoCA are validated tools for global cognition, differences in sensitivity and specific subdomains assessed may contribute to effect size variability. Third, the potential for small-study effects exists, where smaller studies with more positive results are more likely to be published. Finally, when control groups receive minimal contact or support, the contrast with structured lifestyle interventions may be amplified. Exploratory subgroup analyses suggested that the effect of lifestyle interventions on global cognitive function may vary by intervention duration. Interventions lasting less than 12 months were consistently associated with significant improvements, whereas programs lasting 12 months or longer did not show a statistically significant benefit. This may result from declining adherence over time, diminishing novelty effects, or the difficulty of sustaining behavioral support [ – ]. A 10-year follow-up of the Look AHEAD trial found that an intensive lifestyle intervention did not result in preserved cognitive function or slower rates of cognitive decline compared to diabetes support and education, suggesting that long-term sustainability of cognitive benefits remains challenging [ ]. Notably, the MCI subgroup showed a slightly larger effect size and lower heterogeneity compared to those without baseline impairment, suggesting that individuals with early cognitive decline may be more responsive to lifestyle interventions. Patients with comorbid MCI may benefit more from lifestyle interventions, highlighting a potential critical window for early intervention. During this window, residual neuroplasticity may be more optimally engaged [ – ]. What’s more, the positive effects across China, Japan, and Iran suggest that lifestyle interventions may be applicable in Asian populations. In contrast, the two studies conducted in Thailand did not show a statistically significant benefit. This finding should be interpreted with caution, given the small number of studies, the wide confidence interval, and the considerable heterogeneity observed. Future research with longer follow-up periods and more diverse geographic representation is needed to determine whether the cognitive benefits can be sustained over time and whether regional differences reflect true effect modification. Effects of lifestyle interventions on executive function The analysis of eight studies found no statistically significant effect of lifestyle interventions on executive function compared to usual care. This finding is consistent with a previous meta-analysis, which reported no significant effects of exercise interventions on executive function measured by the Stroop task or the TMT-B in patients with T2DM [ ]. Evidence showed that executive function mainly relies on prefrontal cortex networks and may require more targeted or intensive interventions to show measurable improvement [ ]. Therefore, the absence of a significant overall effect in this analysis does not rule out the possibility that specific subgroups or intervention types could yield benefits. Our exploratory subgroup analyses revealed that executive function improved in Asian populations and those with comorbid MCI. The finding in the Asian subgroup may reflect the cultural context of interventions. Mind-body practices like Tai Chi are common in many Asian studies. These activities combine physical movement with cognitive engagement and have been linked to improvements in executive function in older adults [ ]. This indicates that culturally adapted interventions may enhance engagement and effectiveness, although this hypothesis requires prospective testing. In addition, the benefits observed in patients with comorbid MCI support the existence of a potential critical window for early intervention. A recent meta-analysis found that exercise significantly improves executive function in patients with T2DM and cognitive impairment, suggesting that benefits may be more detectable in those with existing cognitive decline [ ]. These findings suggest that individuals with early cognitive decline may represent a priority population for targeted intervention. Given the exploratory nature of our subgroup analyses, future research should further confirm these findings through prospective studies. Effects of lifestyle interventions on memory Lifestyle interventions did not demonstrate a significant effect on memory in the overall pooled analysis. This finding is consistent with previous studies. Exercise-based interventions appear to benefit processing speed and executive function, with limited direct effects on hippocampal-dependent memory [ , ]. Improvements in memory may depend on factors such as intervention timing, intensity, and the specific memory processes being assessed [ ]. In contrast, short-term or low-intensity programs may not provide sufficient stimulus to produce measurable changes in memory performance, even when benefits in other cognitive domains are observed. What’s more, the lack of significant effects may also reflect measurement considerations. A review of cognitive assessments in diabetes research noted that memory is often assessed using limited tasks, and such measurement variability may contribute to inconsistent findings [ ]. Most included studies assessed memory using relatively brief instruments such as DST or RAVLT. While these tools are well-validated, they may not capture the full range of memory function or may be less sensitive to intervention-related changes compared to comprehensive neuropsychological batteries. of significant effects may also reflect measurement considerations. A review of cognitive assessments in diabetes research noted that memory is often assessed using limited tasks, and such measurement variability may contribute to inconsistent findings [ ]. Most included studies assessed memory using relatively brief instruments such as DST or RAVLT. While these tools are well-validated, they may not capture the full range of memory function or may be less sensitive to intervention-related changes compared to comprehensive neuropsychological batteries. Exploratory subgroup analyses did not reveal any significant effects on memory across the factors examined, including intervention type, duration, countries, or baseline cognitive status. The lack of effect across subgroups suggests that memory may be less responsive to lifestyle interventions than other cognitive domains within the intervention types or durations in this review. Whether longer interventions or more intensive cognitive engagement strategies can improve memory needs further investigation in the future. Implications for clinical practice and public health The findings of this review have potential relevance for clinical practice, particularly in older patients with T2DM. For this population, preserving cognitive function is closely tied to maintaining independence and quality of life [ , ]. In this context, lifestyle interventions may help slow cognitive decline and deserve consideration as part of diabetes care. From a public health perspective, lifestyle interventions represent some of the most accessible and cost-effective strategies for chronic disease management [ ]. A recent review highlighted the potential of multidimensional approaches that integrate metabolic management, nutritional optimization, physical exercise, and social engagement for preserving cognitive function in aging populations with T2DM [ ]. Integrating lifestyle interventions into diabetes self-management education programs may offer a feasible way to support cognitive health at the population level. Several suggestions may be relevant when considering lifestyle interventions for T2DM patients. First, those with comorbid MCI may derive greater benefit from lifestyle interventions, suggesting that routine cognitive screening could help identify individuals who might be prioritized. Second, regarding intervention content, combining aerobic and resistance training may be preferable, as both kinds of exercise intervention have shown to be associated with cognitive benefits in T2DM patients [ ]. Third, tailoring interventions to patients’ age and cultural background may enhance their effectiveness and should be considered when designing programs for specific populations. However, it is important to emphasize that these suggestions are preliminary. Given the heterogeneity of interventions and populations included in this review and the exploratory nature of subgroup findings, recommendations regarding intervention type, intensity, or duration require validation in further studies. Limitations This review has several potential limitations. First, the generalizability of our findings is limited by the characteristics of the included populations, which were primarily older adults with T2DM. Evidence on the cognitive effects of lifestyle interventions in younger adults with T2DM remains absent. Most included studies were conducted in Asia, particularly in China. This may limit the applicability of our findings to Western populations, where dietary patterns, physical activity norms, and health system infrastructures may differ substantially. Second, the primary outcome measures were exclusively behavioral neuropsychological tests. Although these instruments are well-validated and widely used, they provide only indirect measures of cognitive performance and are susceptible to practice effects. Third, substantial heterogeneity was observed across studies assessing global cognitive function, likely driven by several factors. The included lifestyle interventions varied in their components, intensity, frequency, duration, and delivery format. Participant characteristics, including baseline cognitive status, diabetes duration, and glycemic control, also differed substantially across studies. Variability in the sensitivity and scoring of cognitive assessment tools may have further contributed to measurement-related heterogeneity. Finally, the available evidence is limited by the short follow-up durations (most ≤ 12 months), restricting our understanding of the sustainability of cognitive improvements. Whether the observed benefits persist, diminish, or emerge only after longer intervention periods remains unknown. Conclusion This meta-analysis found that lifestyle intervention might be an effective intervention strategy for improving global cognitive function in patients with T2DM. Our findings may provide evidence for stratified risk assessment and personalized management strategies. However, with the limited inclusion and considerable heterogeneity of the studies included, the current evidence should be interpreted and applied with caution. Additional rigorous RCTs with larger samples are needed to confirm the efficacy and the mechanism of different kinds of lifestyle interventions in patients with T2DM in the future. chunks.content: Introduction Cancer presents a significant life-threatening challenge [ , ], with prolonged treatment periods imposing substantial disease burdens on patients and their families [ ], thereby constituting a major public health issue that demands increased attention [ ]. The disease burden is often described using metrics such as incidence rates, prevalence, DALYs (Disability-Adjusted Life Years) and QALYs (Quality-Adjusted Life Years). Cancer also brings economic burdens to patients and healthcare systems, highlighting the importance of understanding the characteristics and patterns of economic burden to inform policy making [ ]. China is experiencing a transition of cancer profiles [ ], shifting from the infection-related cancers that used to dominate in developing countries, towards the lifestyle-related cancers that are more prevalent in developed countries [ , ]. According to data from the China National Cancer Center, in 2015, 4.29 million new cases of cancer occurred in China [ ], the number of cancer-related deaths increased by 21.6% between 2005-2020 [ ]. The direct medical costs of hospitalized patients constitute an important component of economic burden, can provide an evidence-based decision-making foundation for policymakers to make well-targeted prevention and intervention strategies [ ]. Previous studies on the economic burden of cancer have predominantly focused on either single cancer types or aggregate regional estimates [ – ], while comprehensive analyses that examine the economic burden across all cancer patients within a specific region, particularly with a detailed breakdown by cancer types are lacking. A comprehensive study including economic burden analysis, incidence characteristics and medical quality (e.g., length of stay, surgery status) are of vital importance for policy making and controlling cancer-related medical expenditures. This study examines the trends in hospital visits and direct medical costs for inpatients with cancer, utilizing Electronic Health Records (EHRs) collected from all hospitals in Shenzhen, China, between 2016 and 2022. Aiming to provide robust data support, contribute to the evaluation of policy effectiveness and serving as a baseline reference for future cancer economic burden analysis in China. Materials and methods Data and study population The data for this study was collected from 167 hospitals in Shenzhen and collated by the Health Commission of Shenzhen Municipality. It contains Electronic Health Record (EHR) for inpatients, the database covers the period from January 1, 2016, to December 31, 2022, encompassing a total of 10,540,120 inpatient records (records related to each visit was processed independently). Records of cancer patients were extracted from the database using ICD-10 (International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision) codes (table of corresponding ICD-10 codes for cancers was presented in Appendix ), those records with incomplete information, furthermore, records with major diagnosis of pregnancy were excluded as it may lead to underestimation of cost analysis (Fig. ). Measurement Outcomes used in this study included demographic information, hospitalization information, and cost information. Demographic information included sex, age, region, insurance type, and marital status, records were classified into five age groups (0–5, 5–14, 15–45, 45–60, 60 and above), aligning with the pattern of increasing cancer incidence with age, patients aged 60 years and above were further stratified into 5-year age groups (60–64, 65–69, 70–74 …, ≥ 90). Hospitalization information included length of stay (LOS), number of hospitalized patients, and hospital visits. Number of hospitalized patients refers to a deduplicated count of unique patients, retaining only their first hospitalization record, while hospital visits refer to hospitalization records without linkage to specific patients. Cost information included total costs, out-of-pocket expenses, medicine fees, examination fees, and material fees. Total cost refers to the sum of all expenses incurred during a single hospitalization, including expenses such as medicine fees, examination fees, and material fees. Cost estimates represent total expenditures during hospitalization among cancer patients rather than cancer-specific treatment costs. Costs were adjusted to constant 2022 Chinese yuan using the national Consumer Price Index (CPI), which is commonly used for inflation adjustment in domestic time-series analyses. To further characterize the direct medical cost of cancer, we compared 25 sub-types of cancer by characteristics using the variables above. Statistical analysis We first conducted a descriptive statistical analysis of the patient demographic information (e.g., sex, age), hospitalization information (LOS, number of hospitalized patients, and hospital visits), and cost information (total costs, out-of-pocket expenses, medicine fees, examination fees, and material fees). Number of hospitalized patients, and hospital visits were calculated as mean admissions per year, LOS was reported as mean days per visit, and costs are reported as mean costs per visit. Continuous variables are described using mean values and standard deviation (SD), since cost data are typically skewed, median values were also used for the cost analysis to provide clarity and transparency. We further compared the rankings of the 25 sub-types of cancer by multidimensional characteristics. All analyses were conducted using R software (version 3.2.1, The R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). Statement of ethics This study was approved

Number of hospitalized patients, and hospital visits were calculated as mean admissions per year, LOS was reported as mean days per visit, and costs are reported as mean costs per visit. Continuous variables are described using mean values and standard deviation (SD), since cost data are typically skewed, median values were also used for the cost analysis to provide clarity and transparency. We further compared the rankings of the 25 sub-types of cancer by multidimensional characteristics. All analyses were conducted using R software (version 3.2.1, The R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). Statement of ethics This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Tsinghua University (NO. THU01-20240009). Informed consent was not required because anonymous and de-identified registry-based secondary data were used for our analysis. Results Characteristics of hospitalized cancer patients and all hospitalized patients Among all hospitalized patient visits, 4,619,291 (43.83%) were male, 7,279,218 (69.04%) were married. Those aged 30–34 years accounted for the highest proportion (12.8%), whereas those aged 90 years and above represented the lowest proportion (0.3%), shown in Appendix . Hospitalized cancer patient records were extracted from the database using ICD-10 codes for cancer, resulting in a total of 886,868 records, the distribution of demographic characteristics is shown in Table . 8,201,068 hospitalized patients had generated 10,540,120 inpatient records (average hospitalization rate was 1.29 admissions per person), while 318,506 cancer patients had generated 886,868 inpatient records (2.78 admissions per person). Total admission of cancer patients exhibited an upward trend during the study period, rising from 32,694 admissions in 2016 to 220,223 admissions in 2022 (Fig. A). Notably, there was a pronounced increase of growth in 2018, with a growth rate of 110.00%. In 2017, 2019, and 2021, growth rates exceeded 30% (Fig. B). The trend of changes in the number of inpatients is similar to that of visits (Appendix ). Expenditure status analysis Figure describes the medical expenditures of hospitalized patients during 2016 to 2022. The total costs and out-of-pocket expenses of hospitalized cancer patients increased from 2016 to 2021, and decreased from 2021 to 2022, respectively (The mean value, standard deviation, median value, and IQR are presented in Appendix & ). The total costs reached the highest point in 2016 ($4,151.8 per visit) and reached its lowest point in 2022 ($2,925.6 per visit); the out-of-pocket expenses reached its highest point in 2016 ($1,630.1 per visit) and reached its lowest point in 2018 ($970.5 per visit). Among all hospitalized patients, the total costs reached its highest point in 2021 ($2,007.2 per visit) and reached its lowest point in 2016 ($1,480.0 per visit); the out-of-pocket expenses reached its highest point in 2021 ($800.2 per visit) and reached its lowest point in 2016 ($604.2 per visit). Additionally, multiple comorbidities in cancer patients were observed, of which hypertension and diabetes stand out as the predominant comorbidities. During the study period, with the addition of hypertension, the mean total costs and mean out-of-pocket expenses per visit of inpatients with cancer were $3,136.0 and $1,121.9, respectively. And with the addition of diabetes, those expenses were $3,137.8 and $1,047.2, respectively. In the case of cancer patients concurrently affected by both comorbidities, those expenses were $3,459.7 and $1,190.4, respectively (Appendix ). Multidimensional characteristic analysis by cancer sub-types We summarized 25 types malignant tumors based on their anatomical locations and analyzed the total economic burden of all hospitalized patients for each cancer during the study period. Annual average total costs from 2016 to 2022 were presented in Fig. , while the detailed annual breakdown of these costs, is provided in Appendix . The top three cancer types with highest total costs were lung cancer, breast cancer, and liver cancer. Furthermore, we conducted a comprehensive statistical analysis encompassing cases (distinguished by sex and age groups), total costs, out-of-pocket expenses, examination fees, medicine fees and material fees (Fig. ). The results revealed the top three prevalent malignancies among hospitalized patients, with female breast cancer, lung cancer, and liver cancer leading the rankings. For male patients, lung cancer, liver cancer, and lymphoma were the most common. Among females, breast cancer, lung cancer, and thyroid cancer topped the list. The three cancers with the highest total hospitalization costs were colorectal cancer ($6,542.9), brain cancer ($5,372.6), and gallbladder cancer ($4,789.0). In terms of examination and testing fees, leukemia ($899.5), gallbladder cancer ($847.2), and colorectal cancer ($774.7) held the top positions. The three cancers with the highest occurrence of level-four surgeries, which refers to the most technically complex procedures according to standardized clinical classification system in China, were thyroid cancer, lung cancer, and colorectal cancer. The three cancers with the highest occurrence of level-four surgeries, which refers to the most technically complex procedures according to standardized clinical classification system in China, were thyroid cancer, lung cancer, and colorectal cancer. Discussion In this study, we analyzed multiple dimensions of hospitalized cancer patients, including direct medical costs, demographic and epidemiological characteristics, and cancer sub-type patterns. These data provide a descriptive picture of how cancer-related hospital care is organized and may support understanding inpatient demand and resource planning in cancer care. The overall hospitalized population in Shenzhen shows a unique age profile, which reflects the city’s distinctive demographic composition as a major destination for young migrant workers. This broader context informs our understanding of the demographic landscape within which cancer care is delivered in this study. The total number of hospitalization decreased in 2019 due to the COVID-19, but the number of hospitalizations of cancer patients kept rising during the study period, indicating that the timely medical treatment of cancer patients was guaranteed and the confidence of patients in local medical treatment was increased [ ]. Notably, in 2018, the growth rate of hospitalized cancer patient visits exceeded over 110%, and patients from outside Shenzhen demonstrated a rapid upswing, with a growth rate exceeding 140% (Appendix ). The substantial increase in inpatient admissions observed since 2018 may be partly associated with the implementation of the Early Screening and Treatment for Cancer program in Shenzhen [ ], researchers have suggested screening can reduce economic burden of cancer patients [ – ]. This program has expanded cancer screening coverage and facilitated the earlier detection of cases that were previously undiagnosed or detected at late stages. Subsequently, more patients, particularly those with treatable cancers detected at earlier stages, became eligible for inpatient interventions such as surgery or chemotherapy, thereby contributing to the observed rise in hospital admissions. The increase in the number of hospitalizations may reflect a substantial enhancement in Shenzhen’s capacity for receiving and treating cancer patients over the past few years, and instills confidence in local cancer treatment, thereby attracting patients from other regions to seek medical care in Shenzhen. Regarding types of payment, basic medical insurance accounts for over 80% of coverage, and the proportion of entirely self-funded patients is decreasing annually from 48.65% in 2016 to 20.62% in 2022. This reduction underscores the positive impact of improving medical insurance coverage on alleviating the economic burden on cancer patients [ , ]. In addition, Shenzhen, as a pioneering city in medical insurance reform [ ], incorporated cancer into critical illness insurance. Patients can seek secondary reimbursement for out-of-pocket expenses after basic medical insurance coverage, thereby further alleviating their financial burden. As expected, in comparison to the overall inpatient population, cancer patients consistently incur higher expenses in both total costs and out-of-pocket expenses. While these substantial absolute costs pose a significant risk of financial toxicity, our investigation notably revealed that the proportion of out-of-pocket expenses for inpatients with cancer remains consistently lower than the average for all hospitalized patients. This result can be attributed to the tiered reimbursement basic medical insurance scheme in China, which offers higher reimbursement rates for patients with greater healthcare expenses [ ]. Critical illnesses like cancer typically incur higher total hospitalization costs that surpass the annual deductible more easily, thereby qualifying for higher reimbursement rates. In contrast, hospitalizations for less severe conditions may incur lower total costs that frequently remain within the initial coverage tier with a lower reimbursement rate. This stepped mechanism creates a financial safety net for high-cost patients, potentially leading to a relatively lower out-of-pocket burden proportion for cancer patients. Consistent with previous studies, this tiered reimbursement strategy effectively mitigates financial toxicity [ , ]. Meanwhile, improved financial protection might effectively enhance the willingness of cancer patients to undergo comprehensive treatment [ – ]. Excluding tumors specific to female organs, females exhibit higher incidences than males only in breast cancer, thyroid cancer, and cutaneous melanoma. Male cases significantly surpass females in laryngeal cancer, liver cancer and esophageal cancer, while lymphoma, leukemia, colorectal cancer, lung cancer, renal cancer, gastric cancer and pancreatic cancer slightly exceed female occurrences. Excluding tumors specific to female organs, females exhibit higher incidences than males only in breast cancer, thyroid cancer, and cutaneous melanoma. Notably, breast cancer, ovarian cancer, uterine cancer, and cervical cancer in females collectively contribute to 221,648 hospitalizations, constituting a substantial 46.85% of the total. The disease burden of malignant tumors related to the female reproductive system is still at a high level, consistent with research on malignant tumors in Chinese women [ , ]. Future strategies on early screening projects should be informed by heterogeneity in cancer incidence and rigorous cost-effectiveness analyses. This could involve strengthening current screening frameworks (e.g., for cervical and breast cancer) and systematically assessing the feasibility of extending screening protocols to other cancers with a significant and growing cost burden [ , ]. Diverse age groups exhibit distinct predominant cancer types, with breast cancer, liver cancer, and lung cancer ranking as the top three cancers with the highest hospitalization frequencies in the overall malignant tumor population. The sub-type with the highest hospitalization frequencies vary among patients of different age groups (e.g., leukemia among 0–14 aged, breast cancer among 15–59 aged, lung cancer among ≥ 60), those results are consistent with multiple research findings [ – ]. Therefore, in subsequent research, more attention should be paid to the heterogeneity of cancer incidence based on different age groups. The results of the direct costs of different cancer sub-types are different from related studies in other regions [ , ]. For example, a study of Southwest China showed that the economic burden of lung cancer, liver cancer, and colorectal cancer are higher than those of other cancers [ ]. Another study in Beijing found that stomach cancer, colorectal cancer and gallbladder cancer are the top three types of cancer in terms of total costs per admission [ ]. Those differences are likely influenced by the varying levels of economic and medical development across regions. In terms of subdivision of expenditure, colorectal cancer and leukemia have shown quite a serious economic burden, consistent with multiple research findings [ – ]. The analysis of specific expenditures can provide assistance for implementing more targeted strategies to reduce the economic burden of cancer in the future [ , ]. There are some limitations to this study. First, this study is descriptive in nature and therefore does not establish associations or causal inferences. Second, this study is limited to analyzing direct medical costs during hospitalization and is unable to distinguish expenditure solely attributable to cancer treatment. Furthermore, as it only covers inpatient care, it does not include cancer-related costs in outpatient settings (e.g., chemotherapy, radiotherapy or day-case surgery), which are becoming an increasingly large part of cancer care in many countries. As a result, the estimates presented should be interpreted as reflecting the inpatient component of cancer-related healthcare expenditure. These limitations together constrain a comprehensive discussion on healthcare equity and the broader effectiveness of health policies [ ]. Future research should incorporate broader economic and societal costs associated with cancer to provide a more comprehensive assessment of its overall impact. Additionally, this study does not stratify patients by cancer stage, the inclusion of all cancer patients without stratification by disease severity or cancer stage limits the ability to assess how severity influences the economic burden and outcomes reported. Finally, it is imperative to note that Shenzhen, as a rapidly developing city in China with advanced healthcare standards, may not be entirely representative of other, particularly underdeveloped, regions in the country. Conclusion This study analyzed the direct cost of hospitalized cancer patients in Shenzhen from 2016 to 2022, including the levels of costs and their changing trends. Additionally, this study further examined the heterogeneity among patients based on sex, age, and sub-types of cancer. These descriptive findings enhanced our understanding of inpatient service demand, and informed hospital resource planning and insurance reimbursement design. Identifying cancer sub-types associated with higher inpatient expenditure may also help to prioritize future research into the economic burden of cancer, early diagnosis and prevention. Further integrating economic data with cancer epidemiology and screening evidence is essential to inform evidence-based cancer prevention and screening policies. chunks.content: Introduction Asthma is a common chronic respiratory disease characterized by multiple phenotypes, nonspecific symptoms, and a variable clinical course [ ].According to the 2021 Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study, the age-standardized prevalence of asthma worldwide in 2021 was approximately 3.34%, equating to about 26 million people living with asthma. By 2050, the age-standardized prevalence is projected to remain around 3.4%, with the increase in cases primarily driven by population growth [ ]. Furthermore, over 14% of children worldwide are affected by asthma, posing significant challenges to both individual health and public health systems [ ]. Childhood asthma often begins early in life and may persist into adulthood, exhibiting characteristics of long-term chronic inflammation [ – ]. It severely disrupts patients’ quality of life and is associated with socioeconomic burdens such as premature mortality, increased healthcare utilization and costs, and productivity losses due to absenteeism and school dropout [ – ]. Notably, childhood asthma is frequently accompanied by multiple pulmonary and extrapulmonary comorbidities, including allergic rhinitis, obesity, and gastroesophageal reflux disease. These comorbidities may influence the clinical severity of asthma, thereby increasing healthcare costs associated with its management [ – ]. Therefore, early identification and management of childhood asthma are crucial for preventing potential long-term complications. Understanding risk factors associated with childhood asthma is key to developing effective prevention and intervention strategies. Previous studies suggest that overweight and obesity influence asthma through multiple mechanisms, such as affecting lung mechanics and function at different stages of lung development. Additionally, the chronic low-grade inflammatory state induced by various pro-inflammatory cytokines secreted by adipose tissue, such as leptin, TNF-α, and IL-6, also plays a significant role [ ]. Conversely, asthma and its glucocorticoid treatment also promote the development of overweight and obesity. Over the past few decades, the global prevalence of overweight and obesity has surged at an alarming rate [ ]. In the United States, 19.7% of children and adolescents aged 2–19 years are obese [ – ]. Given the rapid rise in childhood obesity rates and its potential negative impacts on both childhood and future health, childhood obesity has become a major global public health concern [ – ]. Without specific interventions for these children, overweight and obesity often persist into adulthood, leading to an increased risk of developing noncommunicable diseases such as diabetes and cardiovascular disease at younger ages compared to their healthy-weight peers [ – ]. Currently, the dual epidemic of obesity and diabetes has become a major global crisis. Research indicates that the rising prevalence of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is closely linked to the surge in obesity, with approximately 90% of T2DM cases attributable to overweight [ ]. Furthermore, an observational study of children and adolescents revealed an upward trend in the overall prevalence of diabetes between 2001 and 2017 [ ]. The epidemiological association between asthma and diabetes has been frequently reported in previous studies. Among adults, asthma and diabetes often coexist in the same patient [ ]. However, the relationship between asthma and diabetes in children and adolescents requires further investigation. Concurrently, overweight and obesity appear to be associated factors linking asthma and diabetes; nevertheless, the interactions between these diseases, the underlying mechanisms, and the impact of obesity also warrant thorough exploration. It is noteworthy that existing evidence suggests a significant correlation between weight gain in adolescent girls and the risk of developing new asthma symptoms. This indicates that the relationship between overweight, diabetes, and asthma may be modified by factors such as age and gender [ ]. Therefore, this study aims to utilize relevant data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) from 1999 to 2023 to elucidate the association between overweight and diabetes and asthma in children and adolescents, and to explore the potential synergistic effects of these conditions. This research provides a reference for developing personalized, scientifically grounded asthma interventions and public health policies for children and adolescents in the future. Methods Study population and design The data for this study were derived from NHANES, a research program examining the health and nutritional status of U.S. adults and children [ ]. Through household interviews and examinations at mobile screening centers, it annually collects extensive information from a nationally representative sample of counties across the country. Cross-sectional sociodemographic records, dietary recalls, and biomedical measurements spanning 1999–2023 were extracted from NHANES cycles. Guardians and adolescents (≥ 16 y) provided written informed assent/consent prior to participation. Participants were removed if age at examination was < 2 or > 17 y, or if ascertainment of asthma, adiposity, or glucose homeostasis was incomplete. The remaining analytic sample comprised 14,281 youth; 2,326 (weighted prevalence 16.3%) met the case definition for active asthma, whereas 11,955 (83.7%) served as non-asthmatic comparators (Fig. ). sample of counties across the country. Cross-sectional sociodemographic records, dietary recalls, and biomedical measurements spanning 1999–2023 were extracted from NHANES cycles. Guardians and adolescents (≥ 16 y) provided written informed assent/consent prior to participation. Participants were removed if age at examination was < 2 or > 17 y, or if ascertainment of asthma, adiposity, or glucose homeostasis was incomplete. The remaining analytic sample comprised 14,281 youth; 2,326 (weighted prevalence 16.3%) met the case definition for active asthma, whereas 11,955 (83.7%) served as non-asthmatic comparators (Fig. ). Assessment of childhood asthma Physician-diagnosed, current asthma was operationalised through two affirmative items from the NHANES household questionnaire: (i) ever receiving a clinician diagnosis of asthma, and (ii) experiencing wheezing in the preceding 12 months. Responses for participants < 16 y were proxy-reported. Youth satisfying both criteria were classified as “active asthma” and constituted the case arm. Assessment of overweight/obesity status Stature and body mass were acquired by trained medical personnel following NHANES anthropometry protocols; BMI was computed as weight (kg)/height² (m²) and referenced to CDC 2000 growth charts. Youth with BMI ≥ 85th but < 95th percentile were labelled overweight, whereas those ≥ 95th percentile were categorised as obese [ ]. For the purposes of this study, the term “overweight” refers broadly to individuals with a BMI at or above the 85th percentile, thereby encompassing both the “overweight” (85th–<95th percentile) and “obese” (≥ 95th percentile) categories as defined by the CDC growth charts. Assessment of diabetes Diabetes was established when any American Diabetes Association (ADA) threshold was fulfilled: self-reported previous diagnosis, current glucose-lowering medication use, fasting blood glucose (FBG) ≥ 126 mg dL⁻¹, or glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) ≥ 6.5% [ ]. Covariates and data collection Potential confounders were captured from examination files, laboratory results, and structured interviews. Socio-demographics comprised age (continuous), gender, race/Hispanic origin, poverty–income ratio (PIR), and moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA). MVPA was dichotomised as “high” (≥ 60 min day⁻¹) or “low” (< 60 min day⁻¹) relative to the current physical activity guidelines [ ]. Household income was stratified at the poverty line (PIR = 1). Serum lipids, including total cholesterol, triglycerides (TAG), HDL-C, LDL-C, were assayed enzymatically; cut-offs for dyslipidaemia were TC ≥ 200 mg dL⁻¹, TAG ≥ 150 mg dL⁻¹, LDL-C ≥ 130 mg dL⁻¹, or HDL-C ≤ 35 mg dL⁻¹. For variables such as serum lipids and MVPA, records marked as “Don’t know” or missing in the NHANES database—typically resulting from missing laboratory specimens, assay failure, or unavailable interview responses—were categorized as “unknown” for subsequent analysis. Resting blood pressure (BP) was measured triplicate on the right arm after 5-min quiet sitting; the average of valid readings was converted to age-, gender-, and height-specific percentiles via American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) 2017 tables. Youth were considered hypertensive if mean systolic or diastolic BP exceeded the 95th percentile or if antihypertensive medication was currently used [ – ]. Statistical analysis All formal analyses in this study were conducted using survey-weighted logistic regression under a complex sampling design. Participants were cross-classified by asthma status (yes vs. no). Continuous variables were described as mean ± standard error (SE) after testing for normality via skewness/kurtosis, with intergroup comparisons performed using linear regression based on sampling weights. Categorical variables were expressed as frequency (%), with intergroup differences assessed using Rao-Scott corrected chi-square (χ²) tests. Regarding the handling of missing data for covariates, we did not employ multiple imputation. Instead, missing values were retained as a separate “unknown” category in the multivariable models. This approach was chosen to maximize the analytical sample size by retaining participants with valid primary exposure and outcome data despite missing covariates, while also allowing us to evaluate whether the missingness itself was associated with the risk of asthma. During the screening phase, asthma was the dependent variable. Univariate survey-weighted logistic regression was used to test covariates individually; those with P < 0.05 were included in subsequent models. For effect estimation, three sets of stepwise-adjusted multivariate survey-weighted logistic models were constructed: Model 1: Unadjusted; Model 2: Adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity; Model 3: Further adjusted for HDL-C, PIR, hypertension, and MVPA based on Model 2. To examine additive or multiplicative interactions between overweight and diabetes, exposure variables were grouped into four categories (none, overweight only, diabetes only, both present). All models incorporated NHANES 10-year stratification and cluster identification, with weights normalized according to the analytical sample size. To assess whether the combined effect of overweight and diabetes on asthma risk is modified, we conducted subgroup analyses. The analysis was stratified by prespecified factors such as age, gender, race, PIR and TC, and interaction tests were employed to examine the heterogeneity of these associations across different subgroups. Calculations were performed using R 4.3.3 + survey package. Statistical significance was defined as a two-sided p-value < 0.05. Results Demographic characteristics of the study cohort

Results Demographic characteristics of the study cohort This study ultimately included 14,281 participants, of whom 2,326 (16.3%) had asthma and 11,955 (83.7%) did not have asthma. Table details the demographic characteristics of participants. The mean age across all participants was 11.28 ± 0.08 years, with asthma patients averaging 12.08 ± 0.17 years and non-asthmatic participants averaging 11.12 ± 0.08 years. Gender distribution was comparable between groups. Among all children, 1,594 (10.38%) had a BMI ≥ the 85th percentile, and 48 (0.37%) had diabetes. Differences in the distribution of age, gender, race, BMI, HDL, overweight, PIR, hypertension, and physical activity level were statistically significant between the two groups (all p < 0.05). No significant differences were observed between groups for TC, TAG, LDL, or diabetes prevalence. Association between overweight/diabetes and asthma To separately assess the associations between overweight, diabetes, and asthma, this study constructed weighted multivariable logistic regression models. As shown in Table , compared with children without overweight, overweight children had a higher risk of asthma (unadjusted Model 1: crude OR 1.69, 95% CI 1.49–1.92; Model 2 [adjusted for race, age, and gender]: OR 1.65, 95% CI 1.45–1.87). After adjusting for gender, race, age, HDL, PIR, hypertension, and physical activity level in Model 3, overweight children were found to have a higher likelihood of developing asthma (OR 1.69, 95% CI 1.49–1.92). Table also revealed a significant association between diabetes and increased asthma risk (unadjusted Model 1: OR 2.34, 95% CI 1.27–4.32; Model 2 [adjusted for age, gender, and race]: OR 1.91, 95% CI 1.02–3.55). After adjusting for gender, race, age, HDL, PIR, hypertension, and physical activity levels in Model 3, children with diabetes were found to have a higher risk of asthma compared to those without diabetes (OR 2.34, 95% CI 1.27–4.32). Interaction between overweight and diabetes in children with asthma We also examined the interaction between overweight and diabetes in children with asthma. We categorized children with asthma into four distinct cohorts to examine asthma risk: individuals without overweight or diabetes, overweight individuals without diabetes, diabetic individuals without overweight, and individuals with both overweight and diabetes. Weighted multivariable logistic regression analysis revealed a significant synergistic effect of overweight and diabetes on asthma risk ( p < 0.001 in all models; see Table ). After adjusting for gender, race, age, HDL, PIR, hypertension, and physical activity levels in Model 3, children with both overweight and diabetes were found to have a significantly higher likelihood of developing asthma compared to children without asthma (OR 3.861, 95% CI 1.02–14.63). Additionally, we employed three models stratified by age, gender, and physical activity level to assess their impact on asthma, as shown in Table . Results indicate that among children aged 12–17 years, females, and those with low physical activity levels, overweight children without diabetes exhibited a significantly increased risk of asthma, while children who were both overweight and diabetic showed a further elevated risk ( p < 0.05). Conversely, among children aged 2–11 years, males, and those with high or unknown physical activity levels, only overweight status significantly influenced asthma risk; the presence of diabetes did not further increase this risk ( P > 0.05). Subgroup analysis We conducted subgroup analyses to explore differences in asthma risk between children without overweight or diabetes and other children (i.e., overweight children without diabetes, diabetic children without overweight, and children with both overweight and diabetes). Analysis using multivariable-adjusted models (Model 3), stratified by age, gender, race, TC, TAG, HDL, LDL, PIR, hypertension, and physical activity level, revealed a significant positive association between having overweight and/or diabetes and asthma incidence in most subgroups. However, no substantial association was found between having overweight and/or diabetes and asthma incidence in subgroups with TAG ≥ 150, HDL < 35, other Hispanic race, other racial backgrounds, and hypertension. Interaction analyses showed no statistically significant effects across all subgroups. Results are presented in Fig. . Sensitivity analysis using propensity score matching To address the high proportion of missing data in the original dataset, we conducted a sensitivity analysis using 1:4 propensity score matching (PSM). The baseline characteristics of the matched cohort are presented in Table . Following PSM, the association between overweight and asthma remained significant (Table ), whereas the association between diabetes and asthma was no longer observed.

Furthermore, Table demonstrates that both the “overweight without diabetes” and “overweight with diabetes” groups maintained significant associations with asthma risk. These findings collectively support the robustness of the relationship between adiposity and asthma, independent of diabetic status. Discusssion In this cross-sectional study, we utilized data from the 1999–2023 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) to examine the association between overweight and diabetes with asthma in children aged 2–17 years. Results indicated that after adjusting for confounding factors, children with both overweight and diabetes had a higher risk of asthma, and an interaction existed between the two conditions. Stratified analyses revealed that among children aged 12–17 years, females, and those with low physical activity levels, overweight children without diabetes had a significantly increased risk of asthma, while those with both conditions exhibited an even higher risk. Conversely, among children aged 2–11 years, males, and those with high or unknown physical activity levels, only overweight status significantly influenced asthma risk. Additionally, subgroup analyses revealed that children with at least one condition typically faced higher asthma risk compared to those without either overweight or diabetes. Our study identified significant differences between asthma patients and non-asthma patients in various factors, including age, gender, race, BMI, HDL, overweight status, PIR, hypertension, and physical activity levels. Asthma is one of the most common chronic respiratory diseases in children, with its prevalence varying due to differences in age, gender, race, and socioeconomic factors [ – ]. A survey of children in California found that boys and older children face a higher risk of developing asthma [ ]. Furthermore, extensive prior research indicates that boys typically exhibit higher asthma prevalence than girls during childhood-a pattern consistent with our study population characteristics-while women demonstrate higher asthma prevalence and severity than men in adulthood [ ]. Compared to girls, boys exhibit higher levels of allergic inflammation and serum IgE, smaller airway diameters relative to lung volume, and a more active lifestyle that increases exposure to allergens and irritants. These factors make boys more likely than girls to develop asthma symptoms [ ]. Following adolescence, gender hormones may serve as key mediators in the reversal of disease trends. Studies confirm that androgens such as testosterone or dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) can reduce asthma incidence and potentially alleviate symptoms, while estrogens may adversely affect lung function [ ]. In the United States, Black and Hispanic children experience higher asthma-related morbidity compared to White children. Racial health disparities may stem from socioeconomic factors, including higher poverty rates among racial and ethnic minorities, discrimination, and unequal access to healthcare [ ]. Furthermore, low socioeconomic status is also associated with higher childhood asthma prevalence and severity [ ]. Recent research indicates that children with asthma are more likely to develop hypertension than those without asthma. This may be related to asthma-induced systemic inflammation, which further contributes to vascular dysfunction and elevated blood pressure [ – ]. Regarding physical activity levels, a large European collaborative study indicated that children’s physical activity levels are unrelated to asthma [ ]. However, another study found that periods of higher physical activity in children were often associated with increased daytime and nighttime asthma symptoms, including bothersome asthma symptoms and asthma-related nighttime awakenings [ ]. However, this study did not observe significant differences in conventional lipid profiles or the prevalence of diabetes between asthmatic and non-asthmatic individuals, which contrasts with findings from most previous literature. Substantial evidence indicates an association between asthma and metabolic disturbances, such as elevated blood lipid levels and an increased risk of diabetes. For instance, prior research in adolescents has linked higher lipid levels to a greater prevalence of asthma [ ]. Other studies suggest that diabetes and insulin resistance are related to impaired lung function; peripheral insulin resistance and compensatory hyperinsulinemia may interfere with insulin’s anti-inflammatory effects and enhance bronchial reactivity, potentially contributing to the onset of asthma in children [ – ]. Our negative findings may suggest that, within the context of childhood and adolescent asthma, the mechanistic link between obesity and asthma is more complex and not solely linearly mediated through these common metabolic indicators. Some research points to a stronger association between obesity and non-atopic asthma (often related to non-eosinophilic inflammation and Th1 polarization)

Other studies suggest that diabetes and insulin resistance are related to impaired lung function; peripheral insulin resistance and compensatory hyperinsulinemia may interfere with insulin’s anti-inflammatory effects and enhance bronchial reactivity, potentially contributing to the onset of asthma in children [ – ]. Our negative findings may suggest that, within the context of childhood and adolescent asthma, the mechanistic link between obesity and asthma is more complex and not solely linearly mediated through these common metabolic indicators. Some research points to a stronger association between obesity and non-atopic asthma (often related to non-eosinophilic inflammation and Th1 polarization) compared to atopic asthma [ ]. This distinction might result in traditional metabolic abnormalities, such as dyslipidemia and diabetes, not always being the primary drivers in some adolescent asthma cases. Alternatively, their effects may not yet be fully apparent during the physiological developmental stage of childhood and adolescence, or they may be masked by other factors, including endocrine dysregulation, alterations in gut microbiota, or changes in lung mechanics [ – ]. Certainly, the discrepancies could also stem from this study’s design, population characteristics, or unmeasured confounding factors. Furthermore, given the cross-sectional design of this study, it may not capture metabolic changes that occur over time. These results underscore the need to consider more complex pathophysiological mechanisms when exploring the heterogeneity of asthma and its metabolic associations in younger populations. It is noteworthy that in this study, both overweight and diabetes were identified as risk factors for asthma in children and adolescents. Even after adjusting for confounding factors, the risk of asthma remained significantly elevated among overweight or diabetic individuals. The association between overweight and asthma has been extensively documented in epidemiological research, indicating not only a higher risk of developing asthma but also increased disease severity, poorer disease control, and reduced overall quality of life [ – ]. Additionally, overweight and obesity are associated with reduced responsiveness to inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) and potentially systemic corticosteroids, leading to diminished therapeutic efficacy [ ]. The underlying mechanisms linking obesity and asthma involve multiple levels. Obesity leads to alterations in lung physiology and mechanics, often manifesting as airway dysregulation (inconsistency between lung growth and airway caliber) in obese children. This airway dysregulation correlates with the high prevalence of asthma in obese children and reduced responsiveness to inhaled corticosteroids [ ]. Evidence indicates that obese individuals exhibit a generalized pro-inflammatory state characterized by elevated levels of multiple cytokines and chemokines, such as TNF-α, interleukin-6 (IL-6), and transforming growth factor-β1 (TGF-β1). Such inflammatory mediators may also diminish the anti-inflammatory effects of ICS [ , ]. Additionally, metabolic dysfunction, insulin resistance, and dyslipidemia are associated with obesity-mediated inflammation and may contribute to the development of asthma in obese children [ ]. Genetic studies indicate that obesity and asthma are highly heritable traits, with their parallel increase in prevalence suggesting potential shared genetic risk factors. Several genes associated with elevated BMI and asthma have been identified, including PRKCA, LEP, and ADRB3 [ – ]. Although diabetes affected only 0.37% of the study population, statistical models revealed a significant interaction between diabetes and asthma. This finding carries important clinical implications: even with a low absolute prevalence of diabetes among adolescents, its synergistic effects with respiratory diseases may profoundly impact individual health outcomes. However, due to the low prevalence of 0.37%, the study’s sample size was relatively limited for such comorbidity analyses, potentially restricting statistical power in this specific subgroup. Furthermore, the smaller sample size may increase the chance of random variation in results, necessitating further research for in-depth exploration. Meanwhile, growing evidence suggests that asthma may also contribute to the onset of obesity. Potential contributing factors include reduced physical activity, frequent use of systemic corticosteroids, and shared genetic predispositions between the two conditions [ ]. According to a US study, children with asthma have a 23% higher risk of obesity compared to those without asthma. Simultaneously, children with asthma who used asthma medications at higher rates had a 64% lower risk of obesity than those who used asthma medications at lower rates. This may be because standardized medication improves asthma management, helping to break the cycle where asthma increases obesity risk, obesity worsens asthma symptoms and related conditions, and ultimately leads to further weight gain [ ]. These studies underscore the complexity of the relationship between obesity and asthma. This study indicates that overweight and diabetes exhibit interactive characteristics. Compared to children without overweight or diabetes, those with both conditions are nearly four times more likely to develop asthma. Evidence suggests that overweight and obesity are associated with insulin resistance and the development of T2DM, while diabetes and insulin resistance are linked to impaired lung function [ – ]. Compared to children without overweight or diabetes, those with both conditions are nearly four times more likely to develop asthma. Evidence suggests that overweight and obesity are associated with insulin resistance and the development of T2DM, while diabetes and insulin resistance are linked to impaired lung function [ – ]. The increased incidence of childhood asthma may be directly attributable to peripheral tissue insulin resistance and compensatory hyperinsulinemia, which interfere with insulin’s anti-inflammatory effects while simultaneously increasing bronchial reactivity by inhibiting presynaptic M2 muscarinic receptors [ ]. These findings suggest that early combined screening and comprehensive management for overweight and diabetes may become an important public health intervention strategy to reduce the burden of asthma in children. The strength of this study lies in its ability to capture a wide range of demographic and health-related variables based on NHANES data, enabling a detailed analysis of the specific contributions of obesity and diabetes to childhood asthma risk. However, this study also has several limitations. First, our research is cross-sectional, so we cannot establish temporal associations or causality between exposures and outcomes; prospective studies may be needed in the future for further validation. Second, although our study adjusted for several potential confounders, residual confounding may still exist. Future research should account for other variables that could influence the relationship between these conditions. Additionally, while BMI is widely used as an indicator for assessing childhood obesity, it cannot precisely estimate body composition or distinguish between fat and muscle mass in children. Future studies may introduce other assessment tools suitable for childhood overweight and obesity to provide more detailed descriptions, ensuring accurate classification and more reliable results. Conclusion This study demonstrates that both overweight and diabetes are independent risk factors for childhood asthma. Further investigation indicates a synergistic interaction between overweight and diabetes on asthma risk in children, with the effect particularly pronounced in adolescents and those with low physical activity. These findings highlight specific high-risk subgroups and underscore the importance of integrated metabolic and respiratory health management in pediatric care.

chunks.content: Introduction Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) remain the number one threat to global health and the leading cause of mortality worldwide . In 2022, 19.8 million deaths were attributed to CVDs, accounting for 396 million years of life lost. This was despite significant investment and health policy aimed at addressing the increasing trend in CVDs through various strategies and measures . This is especially noteworthy given the preventable nature of modifiable CVD-related risk factors . The shift towards non-communicable diseases in Iran has received significant attention. Contributing factors include the aging population, the epidemiologic transition, and the consequent challenges in the health care system , . Atherosclerotic cardiovascular diseases (ASCVD) are at the forefront of this increase, with 40% of mortality attributed to CVD in Tehran in 2010 , . CVD has been the leading cause of mortality and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) in Iran . Iran is considered to have a high prevalence and incidence of ischemic heart diseases (IHDs) in the North Africa and Middle East (NAME) area . Although the DALYs and death rates trends of IHDs in Iran have had more favorable results compared to other countries, demonstrating effective secondary and tertiary prevention , , they were still considerably higher than the global estimates . These highlight the need for more comprehensive primary prevention measures and for addressing amenable risk factors. Besides, the current state of CVD and its future projections would play an essential role in helping health policymakers plan at a large scale and take measures to halt the rising disease burden. Several ASCVD risk estimators have been developed using clinical data from various populations to evaluate the future chance of developing atherosclerotic CVDs – . Among them, the 2013 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology (AHA/ACC) risk score has been validated in studies of the Iranian population , . However, it has not been used in any national-level study in Iran. While a previous report used data from 2016 studies to estimate future CVD status in Iran , no study has used the validated 2013 AHA/ACC risk score with the most up-to-date data from the country. Additionally, using the 2013 AHA/ACC risk score allows for a valuable opportunity to evaluate the population’s behavioral, metabolic, and environmental factors on a national scale. This assessment enables clinicians to identify areas for improvement . Herein, using data from the nationally representative Iran STEPS survey 2021 , we set out to evaluate the prevalence of ASCVD in Iran at the national and subnational levels. We also aim to examine various factors associated with ASCVD and to provide a clear picture of the future risk of ASCVD in the non-clinically-presented population over the next 10 years. Additionally, we assess the status of various cardiometabolic health factors across different populations. Methods STEPS survey overview This study was based on the data from the most recent nationally representative Iran STEPS Survey 2021, conducted according to the WHO STEPwise Approach to Non-Communicable Disease (NCD) Risk Factor Surveillance (STEPS) framework, whose protocol and details are provided elsewhere . In short, the STEPS 2021 cross-sectional study comprised three steps: questionnaires, physical measurements, and laboratory assessments for data collection. In the first step, the latest version of the WHO STEPS instrument, version 3.2, was used and further modified to meet survey requirements and reflect the population characteristics. To avoid issues linked to paper questionnaires, an electronic questionnaire was used by the trained staff via tablets. In the physical measurement, height, weight, waist and hip circumference, blood pressure, and pulse rate were measured according to the predefined criteria in the protocol. Finally, the laboratory measurement was done with an auto-analyzer (Roche-Hitachi Cobas C311, High–Technologies Corporation, Tokyo, Japan) at the survey headquarters. The study protocol adhered to the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the ethical committee of the National Institute for Health Research (ID: IR.TUMS.NIHR.REC.1398.006). All participants provided informed consent prior to participation in surveys. Inclusion criteria and study population Iranians aged ≥ 18 years residing in rural and urban areas of all 31 provinces of Iran were recruited using a clustered sampling method. For the first, second, and third steps of the survey, 27,874, 27,745, and 18,119 individuals participated. Analyses on ASCVD were performed on individuals without missing values regarding ASCVD questions in the first step. Analyses of 10-year ASCVD risk were conducted on the 40–75 age group with complete data based on the third step of the STEPS survey.
